text:
You don't exactly have to be Sherlock Holmes to notice the Republican Party is anti-EV. From murdering the gas tax to paying companies to end wind and solar efforts, it seems the oil and gas industry owns Trump and pretty much every other politician, for that matter. But while Republicans do their best to limit our choices here in the U.S., a new International Energy Agency report shows that globally, EVs are on track to account for nearly a third of new car sales in 2026.

According to the IEA's analysis, even with sales down in the U.S. and China, EVs will likely account for 29% of new car sales this year. Compared to 2025, that would be about a 10% increase in the share of new cars that are electric thanks to higher demand in Latin America, Europe, and Southeast Asia. In Australia, Brazil, India, Korea, and Vietnam, the IEA reports that March-through-June EV sales were essentially double what they were in 2025. And while China's seen a dip in new car sales like the U.S., it's still a huge market for EVs:

The pace of recovery of the Chinese car market remains the main constraint on global sales growth. Electric car sales in the country are expected to reach similar levels as in 2025, though the EV sales share is expected to grow to more than 60% in 2026.

Additionally, while China's new car sales dropped by about 20% in the first half of the year, its new car exports jumped by 65%. That boost in exports means the Chinese automotive industry only saw about a 6% drop in H1 2026. If you only look at EVs, exports jumped more than 120%, essentially erasing China's drop in domestic EV sales. That also means that while about 35% of the cars China exported in 2025 were EVs, through the first half of 2026, that figure has jumped to 45%.

The oil and gas industry has worked hard to limit EVs' appeal by spreading easily debunked myths about them. Heck, they even try to pretend we still haven't figured out how to recycle old EV batteries. In reality, people who buy EVs love owning them, and it's hard to beat old-fashioned word-of-mouth advertising. Still, the IEA report claims there's a much bigger factor behind EVs' growing popularity — Trump's no-end-in-sight war with Iran.

As the IEA noted, on-road vehicles account for about half of the world's annual oil consumption, and Trump's disastrous war with Iran created a global energy crisis that's driving increased interest in cars that aren't dependent on oil, or peace in the Middle East. If you're still paying less than $4 a gallon like we are in Georgia, calling what's happening right now an "energy crisis" may sound like hyperbole or communism, but that's what the IEA calls it. Look outside the U.S., and you can't miss it.

After years of failing to conquer Ukraine, Russia's experiencing a massive gas shortage. Australia is considering building a new oil refinery for the first time in decades. Egypt, Jordan, and Pakistan have been hit especially hard, as have Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, and rising fuel prices are already making daily life much more difficult in countries such as Chile, Nepal, Nigeria, and the Philippines. You can also expect the energy crisis in the Pacific to get worse now that Houthi forces have blockaded the Bab al-Mandab strait.

Before Trump attacked Iran, cargo ships could move freely through both the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Strait of Hormuz. Now, safe transit is no longer guaranteed. But hey, at least Trump and the Republicans who enable him have absolutely nothing to show for it, and there's no end to the war in sight.

No one can say exactly how the global transition to EVs will play out, but one thing that's clear is that legacy automakers don't dominate the same way they do with old-fashioned gas cars. The IEA found that legacy (they call them "incumbent") automakers still account for about 98% of internal combustion engine sales but only 55% of global EV sales. Those legacy automakers will likely remain dominant in the U.S. and, to a lesser extent, Europe for a while, but globally, you can expect Chinese EVs to continue to gobble up an even larger share of new car sales:

Chinese carmakers have expanded rapidly both at home and abroad, including in emerging markets, where they hold a particularly high share of EV sales. With China and other emerging economies set to represent 60% of global car demand over the next decade, success in these markets will increasingly determine future market leadership.

Legacy automakers have a huge advantage when it comes to developing engines, but as the IEA's report points out, "Value is shifting from traditional mechanical components towards batteries, electronics and software, with China occupying a leading position across much of the battery value chain." And in an industry where mastering logistics is so important, "Chinese manufacturers benefit from integrated supply chains, strong battery capabilities and production costs that are around 35% lower than in advanced economies."

That said, the IEA's report isn't all doom and gloom for automakers outside of China. We don't have to accept a total Chinese takeover of the new car industry, but it's going to require some changes in strategy. "Closing the competitiveness gap will require co-ordinated action by governments and industry, including stable demand signals, support for innovation, stronger battery ecosystems and improvements in manufacturing efficiency."

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

The U.S. EPA has announced $28 million in grant funding for tribes to build recycling and composting improvement projects across the country.

EPA selected 23 projects as part of the Solid Waste Infrastructure for Recycling Grants program. This year’s funding will go toward recycling infrastructure for a relocated tribe in Alaska, a new MRF project in Florida, and a composting program for a fishing community in Michigan. Grant funding will also support a curbside recycling data collection program in California, among other projects.

It’s the second round of SWIFR funding for tribes and intertribal consortia. In the first round, announced in 2023, EPA awarded 58 grants totalling about $83 million.

“These grants further energize our American economy by improving recycling, cutting disposal costs, reducing waste in landfills, and extending landfill life, and creating good paying local jobs,” Thomas Croci, acting assistant administrator for land and emergency management, said in a statement.

SWIFR was created by the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act a bipartisan bill passed in 2020 and funded by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act signed by President Joe Biden in 2021. The legislation originally allocated $55 million per year from fiscal years 2022 through 2026, and Congress has occasionally supplemented that total.

This latest round of SWIFR grants for tribes is the first to be disbursed under President Donald Trump’s administration. Federal grant applicants went through periods of uncertainty in the months after Trump took office in 2025. The administration paused or canceled numerous grant programs, particularly those funded by the Inflation Reduction Act, other climate-related laws, or programs connected to environmental justice efforts or diversity, equity and inclusion.

But the EPA said last year that it was still committed to disbursing SWIFR grants, including its tranche of funding specifically for tribes. EPA previously announced a separate round of $58 million in SWIFR funding for local governments in December.

Here’s a snapshot of a few of the 23 grant awardees and their upcoming projects. They were selected from a list of 151 applications.

Miccosukee Tribe in Florida plans major recycling upgrades

$1.5 million

Project highlights: The Miccosukee Tribe in the Miami region plans major upgrades at the Miccosukee Waste Facility, including building new recycling infrastructure on site.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Waste Dive free daily newsletter

The project calls for building a new, centrally located recycling pad and installing designated sorting stations. Part of that vision is providing 11 roll-away dumpster bays, which will give the facility more flexibility “to accommodate future materials management needs,” according to a fact sheet about the project. The updates will also help traffic flow and safety, it said.

The tribe previously received a $100,000 EPA Solid Waste Grant in 2022, which helped the community develop an integrated waste management plan, EPA said. That plan identified “large amounts” of recyclable materials that were going to landfills, in part because there was not enough recycling bin space and sorting areas were unclear, the fact sheet said.

Keweenaw Bay Indian Community to turn fish waste into compost in Michigan

$1.5 million

Project highlights: The group will repair and upgrade their recycling facility and establish a new composting program on the L’Anse Indian Reservation in Michigan. It will also provide curbside recycling services to about 850 households.

One part of the project will tackle upgrades such as paving the facility’s dirt floors and roads, repairing doors and lights and adding a fire suppression system. New heavy equipment and machinery is also on the list, according to the fact sheet. The Keweenaw Bay Indian Community is also creating a new composting program to divert fish waste to community gardens, and the grant funding will help purchase new composting equipment meant to divert about 49,000 pounds of fish waste annually.

Overall, the program is expected to divert another 4,000 tons of waste a year, according to the EPA. The community also plans to hire a full-time sustainability specialist and some additional part-time seasonal positions.

Read More in Recycling

Recycling infrastructure aims to help resettlement efforts in Mertarvik, Alaska

$939,629

Project highlights: Newtok Village will establish its first recycling infrastructure in the new town of Mertarvik. The community is in the process of relocating to Mertarvik because of ongoing coastal erosion and thawing permafrost, which is flooding Newtok Village.

The SWIFR funding will help the community establish a recycling and backhauling program and build a climate-controlled recycling center, according to a fact sheet. Funding will also help the community purchase equipment and materials such as balers, trucks and hazardous waste storage. In addition, funding will help hire five people and provide community job training.

The goal is to protect the region’s subsistence resources by diverting hazardous waste from the nearby landfill, which is unlined, according to the EPA. The project should divert 90% of household hazardous waste like batteries, lightbulbs, used oil and e-waste, it said.

Shinnecock Indian Nation plans curbside recycling on Long Island, New York

$765,299

Project highlights: The community aims to reduce recycling stream contamination and make collections more efficient by expanding on-site recycling and composting capacity for tribal households and offices. The group will also supply each home in the community with recycling bins, with plans to pick up recyclables on a weekly basis, EPA said in a news release. The goal is to establish new end markets for the materials it collects.

Funding will go toward the purchase of a collection truck, a pre-fab sorting and storage shed, and composting equipment. It will also fund safety and operations training for staff and hire three new employees.

Read More in Recycling

Pala Band of Mission Indians focus on data collection and education in San Diego County, California

$395,410

Project highlights: The Pala Band of Mission Indians aims to improve its curbside recycling programs through new data collection efforts and a long-term strategic plan. The community will conduct public outreach and education to encourage more recycling participation, and they will weigh and measure curbside recycling materials to track how effective the program is, according to the fact sheet.

The goal is to decrease landfill-bound waste by up to 20%, which the tribe says will help save money spent on tipping fees.

title: ERCOT: Texas' power grid meeting record demand now, but could falter when it doubles by 2032
authors: Paul Cobler | The Texas Tribune, www.keranews.org
description:
The demand on Texas’ energy grid by 2032 will be nearly double a record that was set last week, and state regulators say they will need more varied electrical generation to meet that demand.
The grid seamlessly met the demand because of solar and battery generation that has been added to the grid in recent years.
The PUC and ERCOT are also remaking their system for forecasting future energy demand on the grid as energy hungry data centers overwhelm their old system.
Texas’ deregulated energy market pays power generators only for actual power supplied to the grid based on pricing that goes up when demand is high.
Legislators on the committee said they were considering further legislative efforts to spur the development of natural gas power plants in Texas.
text:
The demand on Texas’ energy grid by 2032 will be nearly double a record that was set last week, and state regulators say they will need more varied electrical generation to meet that demand.

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) forecasts the statewide electric demand will reach roughly 175,000 megawatts — one megawatt can power 250 residential customers during peak hours — in six years, driven by a massive influx of data centers, along with Texas’ growing population and other industrial projects as the economy continues to boom, the council’s CEO Pablo Vegas told the state’s Senate Business and Commerce Committee on Wednesday.

Regulators said they are confident the grid will meet that demand thanks to an influx of solar power and battery storage, but also cautioned that the state needs more natural gas power generation to keep the lights on when the sun goes down and solar quits generating electricity.

“Texas is continuing to grow beyond data centers significantly,” said Thomas Gleeson, chair of the Public Utility Commission of Texas. “We’re doing great as a state and continuing to win on almost every front. There is still going to be a need to serve all the rest of the non-data center load, and that is going to require a balanced mix of resources to do that.”

The latest projection comes days after soaring temperatures statewide last week broke record demands on the ERCOT grid twice, the highest of which was 91,308 megawatts on July 22. That broke the record demand of 87,403 megawatts set the previous day, which broke the old high of 85,508 megawatts set in August 2023.

Those records, however, hardly registered in the consciousness of most Texans as ERCOT’s calls for energy conservation, a fairly regular occurrence during the hottest months of recent years, were not necessary on the two days of peak energy demand. The grid seamlessly met the demand because of solar and battery generation that has been added to the grid in recent years.

“We hit an all time peak, and we had no issue hitting that peak,” Gleeson said.

When the record was set around 5 p.m. July 22, the ERCOT grid had more than 20,000 megawatts of buffer between its demand and the capacity of electricity generation committed to the grid. This meant the grid had the capacity to serve an additional 5 million homes.

The grid’s ability to stand up during the hottest daytime hours was largely attributed to a massive growth of solar generation, which at times exceeded 45% of all electricity being generated. On July 21 and then again on Monday, the grid broke records for total electricity generated by solar, which now sits at 34,700 megawatts. And on July 22, the grid set a record of 11,980 megawatts of energy being discharged from batteries.

Since Winter Storm Uri in 2021 plunged most of the state into days of subfreezing temperatures that disrupted energy generation and forced ERCOT to implement rolling blackouts affecting millions of people, legislators and the public have widely scrutinized the power grid.

The Legislature has since passed laws requiring power generators to insulate themselves from the extreme weather that knocked them offline during Uri, as well as more recent laws that require data centers to disconnect from the grid during periods of strain.

The PUC and ERCOT are also remaking their system for forecasting future energy demand on the grid as energy hungry data centers overwhelm their old system. The forecast produced by ERCOT in April called for 367,790 megawatts of demand by 2032, a number regulators said was almost certainly flawed. ERCOT has since withheld official forecasts while its system for producing those numbers is reworked to better reflect the demands of large loads like data centers.

Solar and battery saving the day

Texas has become the nation’s leader in both solar energy and battery storage since 2021, providing new and significant sources of power to the grid.

Texas’ deregulated energy market pays power generators only for actual power supplied to the grid based on pricing that goes up when demand is high. Batteries typically charge during the day when electricity prices are at their cheapest and solar is providing large amounts of electricity to the grid. When the sun begins to set and the amount of power generated by solar dips, batteries release the power they have stored, keeping the grid stable and lowering energy prices. The nighttime hours are typically windier, allowing for wind farms to pick up some of the slack while natural gas power plants switch online and provide the majority of the state’s power needs.

Last year, ERCOT added 16,000 megawatts of new generation, most of which was solar and batteries, Vegas said.

The state’s solar capacity more than doubled between 2023 and 2025, and battery storage more than tripled, according to ERCOT.

”Texas has been fortunate to be able to develop in the last four or five years so much additional solar and battery storage which has helped make our grid more reliable, less costly and cleaner,” said Cyrus Reed, conservation director for the Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club. “Since 2021, even with record demands in the summer, we were able to meet those demands, and solar and battery storage was a big reason we were able to do that.”

While not all of it will come to fruition, there are 460,000 megawatts of interested generation in the ERCOT generation queue, Vegas said. About 70% of that potential load is made up of solar and batteries and about 78,000 megawatts are from natural gas power plants, Vegas added.

That amount of new solar and battery generation has pushed the period of highest concern for the grid back much later into the day than it was just five years ago, Vegas and Gleeson both said.

More gas needed at night

Rather than supply and demand being at their tightest point during the period of highest demand during the day, that now occurs late in the evening when solar is not generating electricity and batteries are running out of charged power to release back onto the grid. That is when natural gas power plants provide most of the state’s energy, and legislators and regulators said Wednesday they were concerned there may not be enough in the future.

“If that continues while load grows very rapidly, we’re going to get to a place where we have a lot more scarcity events,” Vegas said. “The ease at which we got through last week's peaks would not be the way I would characterize the future in two to three years. I think it will be much more difficult.”

In 2023, the Legislature created the Texas Energy Fund, a $10 billion program that provides low-interest loans to companies to develop new natural gas power plants in Texas.

That program saw a slow release of funds initially, approving only two new power plants in the first two years of its existence. However, it has since issued several more loans, now totaling 5,000 megawatts of new generation from eight separate projects, Gleeson said. A further 2,300 megawatts of generation from four projects are being reviewed by the PUC, Gleeson added.

Legislators on the committee said they were considering further legislative efforts to spur the development of natural gas power plants in Texas.

In Texas’ deregulated energy market, power plants only make money when their electricity is sold. If energy prices are low, potential power plant developers are less likely to invest in a new power plant, said Walt Baum, CEO of Powering Texans, a trade association that represents natural gas power generators.

Baum said ERCOT’s reworking of its load forecasting will be crucial to allow natural gas power generators to better understand the state’s future power needs, as well as potential reworking of ERCOT’s price structure for dispatchable power plants.

“That is going to help spur new development because we’re going to know these projects are real,” Baum said.

name: North Carolina Environment
title: NC leaders balk at chemical company's proposed deal over PFAS in river
description:
Reid Wilson filed comments Thursday opposing the proposed PFAS deal between the EPA and Chemours.
They outline several reasons why: North Carolina was excluded from negotiations, in violation of the EPA’s own guidelines.
However, the area around Chemours’ North Carolina facility was excluded for no reason.
The deal resolves 200 Clean Water Act violations at Fayetteville Works in exchange for no real benefit to North Carolina.
In 2019, NCDEQ reached a settlement with Chemours requiring the company to pay civil penalties, control PFAS air emissions, reduce PFAS contamination in the Cape Fear River and more.
text:
RALEIGH, N.C. (QUEEN CITY NEWS) – North Carolina leaders are calling foul on a proposed deal between the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and a chemical company that’s allegedly contaminated one of the state’s major rivers.

Gov. Josh Stein, Attorney General Jeff Jackson, and Department of Environmental Quality Sec. Reid Wilson filed comments Thursday opposing the proposed PFAS deal between the EPA and Chemours.

The comments urge the federal government to withdraw the proposed settlement, with the officials saying it would do “almost nothing” to address the alleged damage Chemours, a spinoff from DuPont, has done in eastern North Carolina.

Chemours would pay a civil penalty of $22.5 million for alleged violations and spend $90 million over 15 years to mitigate PFAS discharges in West Virginia, North Carolina and New Jersey.

“For decades, Chemours knowingly contaminated North Carolina’s air and water by discharging PFAS from its Fayetteville plant into the Cape Fear River,” said Stein. “Now, the EPA is cutting a deal with Chemours that does next to nothing for North Carolinians and allows polluters to choose what to clean up and where. I will continue to fight for North Carolinians’ clean air and clean water.”

For decades, state officials claim Chemours and DuPont, have been emitting GenX chemicals and other PFAS into the air and soil and discharging the chemicals into the Cape Fear River, which provides drinking water for 500,000 residents in eastern North Carolina.

PFAS contamination poses serious health risks. These forever chemicals don’t degrade. They accumulate in the body through water, soil, and air contamination. PFAS exposure has been linked to cancer, liver damage and birth defects.

“Chemours and the EPA negotiated this deal behind our backs,” said Attorney General Jeff Jackson. “It does nothing to fix the decades of damage Chemours has done to our state, and it’s offensive to the people who drink this water. That’s why I’m asking the federal government to throw it out. The people of eastern North Carolina deserve better.”

EPA says that its deal settles PFAS contamination claims from Chemours’ North Carolina, New Jersey, and West Virginia facilities – but it reportedly guarantees nothing for North Carolina and was reached without consulting the North Carolina Department of Justice or the Department of Environmental Quality (NCDEQ).

Stein, Jackson, and Wilson are urging the federal court to reject the proposed settlement and instead have EPA work with North Carolina to develop a settlement with real benefits for its residents. They outline several reasons why:

North Carolina was excluded from negotiations, in violation of the EPA’s own guidelines. The agreement includes sampling of water in New Jersey, Ohio and West Virginia around Chemours facilities. When that sampling finds PFAS contamination above a certain level, Chemours would be required to provide alternative drinking water. However, the area around Chemours’ North Carolina facility was excluded for no reason.

Chemours is not obligated to spend any of the $90 million in North Carolina. The agreement requires that Chemours spend up to $90 million over 15 years to fund PFAS pollution reduction and alternative drinking water projects, but it doesn’t require that any of that money actually be spent here.

The requirement to control GenX at the Fayetteville Works facility by 99.5% does not meaningfully reduce GenX pollution. GenX is toxic even at very low levels, and NCDEQ has already required Chemours to install technology to reduce certain GenX pollution at a 99.99% efficiency.

The deal resolves 200 Clean Water Act violations at Fayetteville Works in exchange for no real benefit to North Carolina. If the federal government actually wants to resolve these violations, it needs to do more for North Carolinians and provide concrete measures that will improve their lives.

In 2019, NCDEQ reached a settlement with Chemours requiring the company to pay civil penalties, control PFAS air emissions, reduce PFAS contamination in the Cape Fear River and more.

title: Mazda Plotting Electrified MX-5 Miata | The Truth About Cars
description:
Mazda’s top dog, Masahiro Moro, has reportedly stated the company is seriously considering offering an electrified version of the next MX-5 Miata.
Mazda could very easily change the fundamental characteristics of the MX-5 and where it resides on the market.
However, we’ve also seen fairly recent interviews where Mazda engineers stated that an all-electric MX-5 would be out of the question.
Going back to 2025, we have examples of Mazda leadership stressing how best to keep the next-gen Miata lightweight while also satisfying increasingly aggressive emission rules.
Power presumably wouldn’t be staggering but it would satisfy stringent European emission requirements while being more than sufficient on an extremely lightweight vehicle.
text:
Mazda’s top dog, Masahiro Moro, has reportedly stated the company is seriously considering offering an electrified version of the next MX-5 Miata.

Since the current generation of the MX-5 has been in production since 2015, it seems likely that Mazda would have already started development on such a vehicle. CEO Moro even told Auto Motor und Sport that the car needs to be ready for a possible future where it’s sold exclusively as an EV.

“The [MX-5] successor must also be ready for a scenario without an internal combustion engine. The challenge for us is to make the basic construction easier without using exotic materials such as [Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer],” he told the German outlet.

Considering that the whole point of the Miata was to exist as a lightweight and affordable roadster, the above is somewhat concerning. Pivoting to battery power is presumably going to add a lot of weight to the vehicle and we know that automakers have failed to sell EVs at competitive prices. Mazda could very easily change the fundamental characteristics of the MX-5 and where it resides on the market.

But Moro said that the company would be targeting a curb weight that’s not much different than today. "The target for the developers is between just under 1,000 and 1,200 kilograms. And I think we can do it," he explained.

While the Miata has gotten increasingly heavy since it launched in 1989, it always tends to be a featherweight relative to most other sports cars. Still, even a small battery pack can add several hundred pounds.

However, we’ve also seen fairly recent interviews where Mazda engineers stated that an all-electric MX-5 would be out of the question. Perhaps most recent was a chat between Christian Schultze, Director Research and Operations of Mazda Motor Europe, and Dutch outlet AutoRAI — which suggested that the car could instead become a hybrid to satisfy emissions.

Going back to 2025, we have examples of Mazda leadership stressing how best to keep the next-gen Miata lightweight while also satisfying increasingly aggressive emission rules. Chief Technical Officer Ryuichi Umeshita told Road & Track that the car absolutely had to be as lightweight as possible.

“I would say the most important thing is that it is lightweight," said Umeshita, "and that the second most important thing is that it is lightweight."

That sentiment was also echoed by Design Boss Masashi Nakayama.

“When I started designing this fourth generation, there was a request from the United States to make the car bigger, and to increase the power of the vehicle,” he explained via a translator. “I said, ‘Do you really want a Harley-Davidson?’”

“When we have to select an alternative out of two, there is a simple principle to make the selection,” Nakayama continued. “We tend to select the ones whose parts are less expensive, lighter and smaller. By doing so, we can prevent a car from being too big. When we consider the next-generation MX-5, we are considering making it less than one tonne in weight, and less than four meters in length.”

At the time, there was a lot of talk about using the latest version of the brand’s Skyactiv engines. While other brands were heavily focused on developing EVs, Mazda had continued trying to make internal combustion engines more efficient by running at higher compression ratios. The most advanced of these can run extremely lean and use extremely high pressures to help ignite the fuel similar to diesel engines.

The theory was that Mazda could simply install a smaller motor into the next MX-5 that leveraged the latest Skyactiv technology. Power presumably wouldn’t be staggering but it would satisfy stringent European emission requirements while being more than sufficient on an extremely lightweight vehicle. The formula would remain largely unchanged from previous generations.

Electrification, even if we’re discussing hybridization, risks undermining the core principles of the Miata. Balance could be retained thanks to EVs typically having a very low center of gravity and we know electric models can deliver blistering low-end acceleration. But there are other factors to consider.

For starters, the MX-5 has historically been one of the most-reliable sporting cars a person can buy. Pivoting to an entirely new powertrain (hybrid to pure EV) could result in some hiccups, especially since Mazda is kind of new to electrification. However, the assumption is that it’d be getting some help from Toyota — which has more experience with both.

While the MX-5 boasts a relatively small fuel tank and minimal storage, it’s also something a person could take on a long drive without many concerns. Fuel economy tends to be excellent and the cabin is comfortable enough to spend a lot of time in unless you’re exceptionally tall or particularly sensitive to road noise.

Hybridization wouldn’t impact much of the above. But full electrification certainly would, especially if Mazda strives to keep the vehicle as light as possible by making the battery pack small. Even though recharging has gotten significantly faster in recent years, pouring in a few gallons of gasoline is still the quickest and most convenient way to make a pitstop.

The more one looks into the situation, the more it seems like Mazda might need to tailor the car to appease various markets. Interviews taking place in the United States frequently have the automaker discussing how combustion engines are the best way to ensure the MX-5 will remain lightweight. These are often accompanied by claims that the car will receive a 2.5-liter Skyactiv-Z. European interviews are significantly more likely to discuss electrification and running with smaller displacement engines — the latter of which is something Mazda already does.

The current MX-5 is sold exclusively with a 2.0-liter motor in the United States, whereas Europe also receives the smaller 1.5-liter SkyActiv-G. There are also some minor differences in the hardware and software used on the 2.0-liter model, with the brunt having everything to do with satisfying emissions.

This is hardly unusual for global models, with the Miata historically following suit in order to cater to the rules of individual countries. Our guess is that the same will be true for any prospective electrification.

We doubt that an all-electric MX-5 would be a big hit in North America. But we may still see it as an option in the coming years. It just seems more plausible that an electrified Miata, which Moro seems to be confirming, would primarily exist to satisfy regional emissions. Europe would presumably continue seeing smaller engines and more electrification, while American customers should be able to nab something with more displacement.

The big concern is how taking a mixed approach will play out for the next-generation of the MX-5. Plenty of automakers are now manufacturing vehicles that can accommodate combustion engines and all-electric powertrains. But this has yielded mixed results, as developing a vehicle that can do both often means making sacrifices.

Automakers like the concept because it means they can more easily accommodate government emissions while limiting production costs. But drivers are occasionally saddled with vehicles that probably would have been a better EV or ICE model if the manufacturer had initially developed them as separate models.

We’ll see how the strategy plays out for Mazda in the coming years. Nobody expects to see the next-generation MX-5 until at least 2028, with some claims suggesting it might not arrive until 2030. While there’s a lot of lingering talk about how this will also be the final run of combustion models in Europe, which is plotting emissions restrictions that would practically ban combustion engines by 2035, the continent has repeatedly been forced to push back its previous targets. Meanwhile, the United States has aggressively walked back its own emissions targets to better suit consumer tastes.

text:
Daimler Trucks North America will end truck manufacturing operations in Portland by the end of the year, relocating production to facilities in North and South Carolina in a move that will affect approximately 375 employees.

The announcement comes just weeks after the company opened a new $40 million engineering hub in Portland.

In a message to employees, Daimler said the decision is part of a broader strategy to optimize its production network and better align resources with future business needs. The company added that it will work with affected employees to identify opportunities for other roles within the organization.

“Our commitment to Portland remains strong,” the company said. “Portland will continue to serve as DTNA’s North American headquarters and a key center for engineering, innovation, product development, testing, and validation.”

IAM Union (International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers) District W24 and Local 1005 released a statement following the announcement.

“Our employer’s decision to leave the Portland area does not remove the heart and soul that our members have put into their work at Daimler. And the IAM will support and fight for our members regardless of any decision their employer makes,” they wrote.

Although large-scale manufacturing will end, Daimler said it will continue building new trucks in Portland for testing and validation purposes, as reported by The Oregonian.

The decision highlights a setback for Portland’s manufacturing sector at a time when the city’s economy continues to recover slowly following the pandemic. Oregon lost approximately 4,600 manufacturing jobs last year, making Daimler’s planned production shift another significant change for the state’s industrial workforce.

Daimler Trucks North America has maintained its headquarters in Portland since the early 1980s, while truck manufacturing on Swan Island dates back to the 1940s. Today, the company employs more than 3,000 people throughout the Portland region.

Beyond its Oregon operations, Daimler operates five truck assembly plants in North and South Carolina, along with three manufacturing facilities in Mexico. Company officials recently said Daimler produces roughly 800 trucks per day across its North American manufacturing network.

RALEIGH, N.C. -- North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson is suing the chemical manufacturer Chemours in state court to recover damages for decades of PFAS contamination of the water supply. Attorneys General from across the country —and across the political spectrum —are backing the State’s efforts to hold Chemours (formerly DuPont) accountable for decades of water pollution and harm to public health.

A coalition of 10 Republican Attorneys General, including Texas AG Ken Paxton, filed an amicus brief today with the North Carolina Supreme Court supporting AG Jackson’s efforts to hold Chemours accountable. The brief notes that 30 Attorneys General have on-going litigation against PFAS polluters. The North Carolina lawsuit originated with Governor Josh Stein during his tenure as Attorney General.

Following is a statement by Corinne Bell, senior attorney for Environmental Health at NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council):

“Chemours has failed to fully address the on-going damage inflicted by decades of PFAS pollution. Despite past legal action, Chemours has not come close to cleaning up its mess and has fallen short of repairing the damages to communities and the state’s natural resources. This amicus brief is a reminder that protecting North Carolinians from toxic cancer-causing chemicals is not a partisan issue – it's a matter of public interest.”

See NRDC’s June press statement on US EPA's inadequate federal settlement with Chemours. NRDC and partners’ public comments opposing the settlement are available upon request.

text:
As long as they do not sell electricity or report as generating units to the U.S. Department of Energy, developers and operators of islanded power generators serving data centers are not subject to the acid rain program’s regulations, according to the guidance. If, however, a company develops a power generation facility that initially is off-grid but eventually becomes connected to the grid, the facility may be subject to the acid rain regulations under the guidance.

Regulations under the acid rain program, the nation’s first cap-and-trade program established under the amendments to the Clean Air Act signed into law in 1990, require major emission reductions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from the power sector. These emissions are the primary precursors of acid rain, according to EPA’s website. EPA said that its reading of the Clean Air Act and DOE definitions of “utilities” shows that ARP does not apply to off-grid power facilities.

“The guidance expands opportunities for companies to develop and operate islanded power generation facilities for data centers,” EPA said in a statement. The move will also give them greater flexibility in where to locate new facilities and speed up the process, the agency added.

The exemption helps to ensure that the U.S. will maintain its “AI dominance essential to national security and economic prosperity,” Aaron Szabo, EPA assistant administrator for Air and Radiation, said in a statement. It also safeguards communities from utility price hikes, he said.

The action has sparked criticism from such groups as the Sierra Club, which referred to it as the Trump administration’s selling out to data center owners at the expense of the health and wellbeing of Americans.

“Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides not only cause acid rain but also threaten the health of Americans when emitted into our air,” Sierra Club senior attorney Zachary Fabish, said. “Massive fossil power plants shouldn't get a free pass just because they are attached to data centers, and we will continue to push back against these reckless pollution passes being handed out to data centers and defend our public health and environment.”

EPA’s guidance aligns with President Donald Trump’s recently expanded Ratepayer Protection Pledge to support communities that "welcome” data centers. The pledge encourages companies to build, bring or buy all of the energy needed to power their facilities and pay all supporting costs, including infrastructure, a move that will cover 80% of all power delivered to U.S. homes and businesses, EPA said.

The pledge applies to all parties whose decisions determine the monthly rates consumers pay, EPA said. This includes electric utilities, developers and the states that regulate both. It also commits these parties to paying negotiated rates regardless of whether they use the electricity; invest in local hiring and workforce development; and coordinate with grid operators to strengthen grid resilience.

First announced last February in the president’s State of the Union address, the pledge’s signatories include Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI.

text:
A South Korean team has designed a Dual-Acting Hybrid Polymer (DHP) binder for thick-film lithium-ion battery electrodes.

Sungkyunkwan University and Seoul National University report that the novel binder enhances lithium-ion battery energy density and extends overall lifespan.

It solves a common issue where the binder drifts and ruins battery performance when making thicker, higher-capacity electrodes for EVs and smartphones.

In the testing, the binder demonstrated nearly double the adhesive strength compared to traditional PVDF binders.

Combining two materials

Range anxiety is real in electric vehicles. To push driving ranges past 400 miles, battery makers have been trying to make electrode layers much thicker. Thicker electrodes hold more power-dense materials like nickel.

There is just one problem. The process falls apart during drying. When battery manufacturers apply liquid mixtures to build thick electrodes, standard glue, known as a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) binder, floats to the top.

As the slurry dries, the binder unevenly distributes. And the electrode cracks, crumbles, and fails to conduct electricity properly. It is a chronic roadblock. Batteries built this way degrade rapidly after a handful of charge cycles.

“Previously, increasing electrode thickness and size was limited by binder and processing issues, which restricted overall battery performance. We overcame this hurdle by efficiently combining the advantages of spandex and poly(acrylic acid),” explained lead researcher Ki-Jae Kim, a professor at SKKU.

More from Innovation

See All

The solution came from combining two materials with opposite skill sets: spandex (SPDX) and polyacrylic acid (PAA). And it was dubbed the Dual-Acting Hybrid Polymer (DHP) binder. It works instantly.

Spandex brings flexibility. Its high elasticity gives the thick electrode the structural resilience it needs to resist snapping or fracturing under stress.

PAA brings chemical strength and forms tight molecular bonds with internal battery components.

During initial charge cycles, the hybrid binder does something even better: it spontaneously forms a special lithium-interface layer. This highway speeds up lithium-ion movement straight through the dense material.

Shows promise in testing

The numbers speak for themselves. The new hybrid glue delivers nearly twice the adhesive strength of PVDF. In tests using commercial-grade pouch cells, conventional thick batteries collapsed after roughly 95 cycles.

On the other hand, pouch cells using the spandex-infused binder maintained 86.8 percent of their original capacity past 200 cycles. Interestingly, this jump in cycle life enhances the battery’s operational lifespan.

The best news for the automotive industry is not just what the binder does. It is how it can be made.

Many next-generation battery developments require entirely new factories. It demands expensive dry-processing equipment or radical tooling overhauls. This binder does not.

It fits directly into existing wet manufacturing lines. Factory owners can swap the chemical glue without buying a single new machine or pausing assembly.

“This binder technology is highly adaptable for industry because it uses existing wet production lines without adopting dry-processing technologies, which have recently attracted attention as next-generation battery manufacturing methods. We expect it to play a pivotal role in extending the driving range of next-generation electric vehicles,” Kim concluded.

The study findings were published in the journal Nature Communications.

description:

Josh Stein, Attorney General Jeff Jackson, and Department of Environmental Quality Secretary Reid Wilson criticized the agency for excluding North Carolina from negotiations.

text:
North Carolina state leaders are asking a federal court to turn down what they call a “backroom deal” between the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and chemical manufacturer Chemours.

Chemours, formerly part of DuPont, has been manufacturing chemicals in its Fayetteville plant for decades. In 2017, scientists discovered that PFAS — sometimes known as “forever chemicals” due to their persistence in the environment — were being released from the plant into the Cape Fear river, as well as into other bodies of water from plants in West Virginia and New Jersey.

More than 2,600 plaintiffs sued Chemours for polluting their drinking water wells, air, soil, and groundwater. The pollution impacted about 500,000 North Carolinians and about 10,000 private drinking wells.

But plaintiffs won’t get their day in court if a proposed landmark $450 million settlement between the EPA and Chemours, announced last month, moves forward. It requires approval from a federal judge.

In their public comment on the settlement filed Wednesday, Gov. Josh Stein, Attorney General Jeff Jackson, and Department of Environmental Quality Secretary Reid Wilson criticized the agency for excluding North Carolina from negotiations.

“For decades, Chemours knowingly contaminated North Carolina’s air and water by discharging PFAS from its Fayetteville plant into the Cape Fear River,” Stein said in a statement Thursday. “Now, the EPA is cutting a deal with Chemours that does next to nothing for North Carolinians and allows polluters to choose what to clean up and where.”

Jackson previously encouraged North Carolinians to submit public comments to the federal government on how the agreement affects them. He shared the letter that he, Stein, and Wilson submitted on Wednesday.

NC AG Jackson calls on residents to weigh in on Chemours’ ‘backroom deal’ over PFAS

“Chemours and the EPA negotiated this deal behind our backs,” Jackson said in a statement. “It does nothing to fix the decades of damage Chemours has done to our state, and it’s offensive to the people who drink this water.”

The state leaders are asking the federal court to reject the proposal. Instead, they want the EPA to work with North Carolina to develop a settlement that benefits the state and its residents.

While the agreement requires Chemours to spend $90 million over 15 years to fund water cleanup and clean drinking water projects, none of that money is earmarked for the Tar Heel State.

“This proposed sweetheart deal that was brokered without even consulting North Carolina requires almost nothing more of Chemours than it’s already doing under the consent order it signed with DEQ,” Wilson said in a statement. “It’s offensive and unfair to the people of this state.”

A coalition of nine organizations represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center also filed public comments against the settlement. They say the deal absolves Chemours of responsibility for its actions.

Attorneys from SELC described the deal as a “remarkably poor bargain” for North Carolina, according to the letter.

“Rather than holding Chemours accountable, the deal appears designed to shield the company from meaningful consequences for the widespread harm its chemicals have caused,” said Kelly Moser, senior attorney and leader of the Water Program at SELC. “The message is hard to ignore: Chemours gets leniency while families get contamination.”

text:
North Carolina leaders are formally opposing a proposed federal settlement with Chemours over "forever chemical" pollution.

Critics argue the deal allows Chemours to avoid accountability for decades of knowingly discharging dangerous chemicals.

State officials contend the agreement's emission restrictions are redundant to requirements already enacted by North Carolina.

Following up on their initial criticism of a proposed settlement between the federal government and Chemours over "forever chemical" pollution, several of North Carolina's top leaders are putting their words into writing.

Gov. Josh Stein, N.C. Attorney General Jeff Jackson, and Reid Wilson, head of the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality, on Thursday, July 30, sent a letter attacking the proposed deal between the chemical maker and Washington.

In the letter, the officials say that Chemours for decades knowingly discharged dangerous manmade chemicals − formally known as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) − from its Fayetteville Works plant 75 miles upstream of Wilmington into North Carolina's air and water.

“Now, Chemours is cutting a settlement deal with the federal government that does next to nothing for North Carolinians and at the same time, is trying to evade the North Carolina Department of Justice’s lawsuit so it can avoid repaying the state for the damage it inflicted," Stein said in a news release. "Now is the time for the EPA and the state Supreme Court to do right by our people and our water and truly hold Chemours accountable."

Bad deal for North Carolina

In the deal announced in late June 2026, the federal government and Chemours agreed to better control emissions from plants in three states − North Carolina, West Virginia and New Jersey. It also involved commitments by the company to provide drinking water to communities around its plants, pay a civil penalty, and study new ways to further reduce PFAS emissions.

“This landmark settlement shows the administration’s commitment to protecting the public from harmful pollution,” said federal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam Gustafson in a news release. “Through this commitment, Chemours will better control PFAS at its plants, allowing the company to continue its manufacturing operations while protecting communities in North Carolina, West Virginia, and New Jersey from PFAS exposure.

"This agreement ensures that the company will manufacture these critical materials in a responsible manner.”

In a news release, Chemours said the agreement with the federal government continues the company's goal "to focus on responsibly resolving outstanding environmental and regulatory matters with terms that improve site operating certainty and include payment and remediation commitments that are structured over time."

"The settlement also recognizes the significant work already completed or underway across Chemours' sites to reduce emissions and strengthen processes," the company said.

But state officials, clean water advocates and environmentalists lambasted the agreement as not doing enough for North Carolina and largely allowing Chemours to get off with little more than a slap on the wrist.

"This deal is an insult to the people of Eastern North Carolina,” Jackson said in a release last month blasting the agreement. “Our state is ground zero for GenX contamination, but this deal does practically nothing to clean up our water. Chemours made this mess, and Chemours should clean it up. The EPA will be hearing from my office.”

'Neatly packaged illusion'

In their letter to the federal government, the state officials noted that the emission restrictions − listed in the agreement's Appendix B − practically add nothing to the requirements that North Carolina has already enacted against Chemours, including curtailing almost all PFAS emissions from Fayetteville Works.

"Appendix B may very well be just a neatly packaged illusion that amounts to little or no benefit for public health or the environment in North Carolina," the letter states. "As such, this provision is substantively inadequate, unfair and against the public interest."

The letter also states that the proposed settlement "provides no assurance of environmental benefits in North Carolina" and releases Chemours from facing charges on more than 200 violations of the federal Clean Water Act at Fayetteville Works.

Along with the letter to the federal government, Stein and the state environmental agency this week also filed a supporting document in Jackson's case against DuPont and Chemours that's currently in the N.C. Supreme Court. The case is looking at whether the state can hold Chemours and DuPont, which spun off Chemours and Fayetteville Works 11 years ago after operating the plant for decades, responsible for the damage the PFAS emissions have done to North Carolina's natural resources.

Reporter Gareth McGrath can be reached at GMcGrath@usatodayco.com or @GarethMcGrathSN on X/Twitter. This story was produced with financial support from Journalism Funding Partners. The USA TODAY Network maintains full editorial control of the work.

text:
An ambitious plan to build electric vehicles — and create thousands of jobs — in North Carolina has been dealt another major setback.

Chatham County commissioners on Monday voted to direct the county’s attorney to cancel an incentives agreement with a subsidiary of VinFast, — a deal that promised millions of dollars in tax breaks and other incentives for the Vietnamese automaker.

VinFast in 2022 pledged to invest more than $2 billion in a site in Moncure and create at least 7,500 jobs over a period of years. At the time, it expected to begin construction that year and begin production by the middle of 2024. In return, the county agreed to give the company about $400 million in incentives — if the company met investment and hiring targets and deadlines. None of the incentive money has been distributed to the company, county officials said.

A local economic development agreement signed by VinFast in 2022 allows the county to terminate its incentives agreement with VinFast if the company failed to develop enough of the project to increase its property tax value to at least $700 million and if VinFast hadn’t created at least 1,750 eligible jobs by Jan. 1, 2026. The company hadn’t made significant progress on construction and failed to meet the hiring goal by that date, state officials alleged in a recent lawsuit.

“VinFast has failed to meet the performance obligations and project deadlines outlined in the County’s economic development agreement,” Chatham County Manager Bryan Thompson said in a statement on Thursday. “As a result, the County determined that termination of the agreement is warranted.”

Spokespeople for VinFast and a lawyer representing the company didn’t immediately provide a comment on the termination of the Chatham County incentives.

The cancellation effort comes two months after the North Carolina Department of Justice sued the automaker on behalf of the state Department of Commerce — an effort to reclaim the land it sold to the company for its factory.

VinFast executives in 2022 agreed to a deal that would allow the state to buy back the property it originally sold to VinFast if the automaker failed to begin vertical construction by Jan. 1, 2024, or commence operations by July 1, 2026.

The state is now attempting to exercise that option, saying it wants to move on from the delayed project to free it up for future economic development opportunities. The state is also trying to claw back at least $80 million it has provided for site preparation related to the project.

Vinfast booked some of that money as a liability, “due to the uncertainty of certain events and conditions for recovery of funds as specified in the site development agreement” with the state, the automaker said in a regulatory filing last month. In a separate regulatory filing, the company said last month that it is evaluating the allegations in the state’s lawsuit and “intends to respond through the appropriate legal process.”

The company has until Sept. 2 to respond to the state’s lawsuit, according to court documents filed last week. The company and the state also requested this month that a judge seal an amended complaint to protect what VinFast describes as proprietary business information.

The state Department of Commerce also agreed to an incentives deal worth more than $300 million. A spokesperson for the department declined to comment Thursday, citing the pending litigation.

“Communities with development-ready mega-sites are rare,” Michael Smith, president of the Chatham Economic Development Corporation, said in an email to WRAL on Thursday. “If the site becomes available, Chatham County would have an opportunity to market it to a wide range of industries seeking large-scale locations. We are optimistic about its long-term potential for new jobs and investment in Moncure.”

Smith said VinFast’s planned investment in Chatham County has led to a surge of interest, which accelerated development in the area. He believes that positions the county well for any future projects.

text:
WISCONSIN – A new report from the Sierra Club, Thirsty Power: Coal and gas will leave us high and dry, analyzes Wisconsin’s current power generation, the water needed for that power, and the potential impacts on Wisconsin’s water as Big Tech tries to build more data centers across the state. These data centers require enormous amounts of power– and in some cases are prompting entirely new gas plants that will compound water and energy use at peak times.

The report found, among other things, that:

Wisconsin’s current dirty energy power fleet– including coal, gas, and nuclear plants– withdraws 1.34 trillion gallons of water annually. Meanwhile, solar and wind use so little water that the U.S. Energy Information Administration doesn’t even track their usage.

This is more than 7 times all of the municipalities in Wisconsin combined, and 18 times more than agricultural irrigation.

Five new gas plants, known or assumed to be proposed for data centers, would use 142 million gallons of water a year on average– the equivalent of the annual drinking water for 284 million people– and the majority of which would be needed during summer months when energy and water use has been strained by drought and heat.

The proposed Red Oak Ridge gas plant in Kenosha would consume an estimated maximum of 266,400 gallons of water per day– the equivalent of daily consumption of nearly 3,248 average Americans– and its owner, Invenergy, wants to use Lake Michigan water.

The proposed Foundry Ridge plant would use an estimated maximum of 55,152 gallons of groundwater from local wells per day.

The five new proposed gas plants confirmed or suspected of being proposed to solely power data centers in Wisconsin equate to 4 gigawatts of power– or enough electricity to power approx. 3 million average homes. There are only 2.84 million homes in Wisconsin.

Elizabeth Ward, Sierra Club Wisconsin Chapter Director, released the following statement:

“Water is our way of life in Wisconsin, but our dependency on fossil fuels for power generation drains our most precious resource. Across the state, Big Tech is looking to build out massive AI data centers and power plant builders are asking regulators to green-light expensive gas plants to power them. The potential cost to our environment, our water, and our wallets is enormous. Wisconsin isn’t Wisconsin without safe, clean water to drink, swim, and fish in. The fossil fuel and gas rush has to be stopped– we have to protect our most vital resources.”

text:
The startup Antora Energy just raised $550 million to build and deploy more of its heat-storing batteries for powering data centers and cleaning up factories.

On Thursday, San Jose, California–based Antora said it closed a Series C funding round co-led by climatetech investor G2 Venture Partners and the VC firm Eclipse, which backs manufacturing-focused startups. That brings Antora’s total corporate and project financing to around $1 billion, the company says, adding that the latest infusion will enable it to expand domestic production of its thermal batteries and accelerate the buildout of large-scale projects.

Eight-year-old Antora has likened its technology to an enormous toaster. Electricity runs through a large resistance heater to warm big blocks of solid carbon to extremely high temperatures for days on end. The blocks release controlled blasts of high-intensity light that can be used to either produce power on demand or generate steam for industrial processes.

Just two months ago, Antora began booting up its first commercial-size system: a 5-gigawatt-hour thermal battery at Poet’s biofuels plant near Big Stone City, South Dakota. The project will turn cheap wind energy into steam the plant needs to convert corn into ethanol, displacing some of the facility’s reliance on coal-fueled boilers.

Antora says this system will be one of the largest battery storage projects in the world when it’s fully operating later this year. Meanwhile, its San Jose manufacturing campus ranks among the country’s largest battery factories.

But the firm is hardly alone. Dozens of thermal energy startups in the U.S. and worldwide are developing systems with a variety of heat-trapping materials, including ceramic bricks, crushed rocks, and ​“stonelike” industrial waste.

The sector is expanding as countries are scrambling to meet power demand from data centers and industrial facilities — and struggling to limit the growing strain on grid infrastructure and household utility bills. In the U.S., high electricity costs have also hindered manufacturers from adopting cleaner, electrified heating technologies.

Energy storage systems in general can address those challenges by charging up when power is cheap and abundant, then dispatching that stored energy when it’s needed, such as by sending electricity to the grid during hours of peak demand. Thermal batteries can also deliver heat directly to factories to keep them from drawing lots of costly peak power.

“From factories to data centers, energy is the bottleneck to industrial growth,” Andrew Ponec, co-founder and CEO of Antora, said in a news release. ​“Antora has shown we can help break that bottleneck — delivering energy fast, at massive scale, with American innovation.”

The company launched its first pilot project in 2023: a 5-megawatt-hour system installed at a facility owned by the utility Wellhead Electric near Fresno, California. Months later, Antora raised $150 million from corporate and venture investors to scale up thermal-battery production at the San Jose factory, which it has expanded into a three-building manufacturing campus.

Antora built over 200 battery modules for the South Dakota storage system. But the project is notable for more than its technology. Antora is also pioneering an electricity tariff, designed with the local utility Otter Tail Power, that rewards Antora for charging up during periods of surplus local renewable energy production. The idea is to improve the bottom line for thermal energy systems while also ensuring they benefit everyone on the grid. Antora said it’s working with utilities across the country to develop similar rate structures for future projects.

With the $550 million fundraise, Antora said it plans to build a second U.S. manufacturing hub and to start fulfilling its ​“growing pipeline of signed agreements” with some of the nation’s biggest data center operators and industrial companies, including biofuels and chemical producers and food and beverage manufacturers. The company declined to share more specific details.

“We’re in the process of developing many more projects, very similar to the Big Stone project [with Poet], and those projects span a variety of sectors and are sort of a similar size,” Justin Briggs, Antora’s co-founder and chief operating officer, told Canary Media in a May interview.

“We’re also developing projects in the power sector that would provide the ability for data centers to come online much faster than they otherwise would,” he said, noting that those systems could be anywhere from five to 10 times the scale of its 5-GWh system at the South Dakota ethanol plant.

“Our energy system is at an inflection point, and very few companies can meet soaring power demand,” Jake Tauscher, partner at G2 Venture Partners, said in the news release. ​“Antora is meeting that demand today. They’re deploying at scale, on budget, and on the rapid timelines customers need.”
