text:
LANSING, Mich. (WLNS) — Michigan’s electric vehicle charging infrastructure is growing, expanding driver accessibility across the state, according to a new report released by the Anderson Economic Group.

There are three types of electric vehicle charging stations: Level 1, which can take two or more days to charge a battery-powered electric vehicle to 80% charge; Level 2, which takes between four and 10 hours to reach the same charge; and DC Fast, which takes between 20 minutes and one hour to reach that charge level. It should be noted that DC fast chargers do not work with plug-in hybrid vehicles.

Per the report, there are 569 public DC fast charging stations in Michigan as of July 7, 2026, a jump of 180 stations, or a 32% increase, from 2024. A total of 125 stations were added in 2025, and an additional 55 have been added so far this year.

Michigan’s implementation of DC fast chargers is matching the national growth rate of 31% in 2025. There are around 15,670 DC fast charging stations in the U.S. at the time of the report.

There are 1,721 Level 2 stations spread throughout the state. Statistics given on the number of Level 1 stations in Michigan were not shared in the report.

The report states that the majority of DC fast charging stations are located in the bottom half of Michigan’s Lower Peninsula, especially in urban areas such as Detroit, Ann Arbor, Lansing, Grand Rapids and Kalamazoo.

The distribution of DC fast charging stations in the Lower Peninsula’s upper region is sparse, with locations available in Traverse City and along a few highways.

There are 21 DC fast charging stations in the Upper Peninsula. They can be found in Marquette, Houghton, Hancock, Copper Harbor, Sault St. Marie, Brimley, Escanaba, Iron Mountain and Norway.

Michigan ranks sixth in the country for the most DC fast charging stations, behind California, Florida, Texas, New York, and Illinois. However, Michigan ranks 16th in the nation in DC fast chargers per capita.

July 29, 2026

SAN FRANCISCO, Calif. (July 29, 2026) – Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced $5,683,158 for Tribes within California through the Solid Waste Infrastructure for Recycling (SWIFR) program. EPA selected five projects to receive grants, with funding amounts ranging from $100,000 to $1.5 million.

“Solid waste infrastructure is especially important in tribal and rural communities across the Pacific Southwest” said EPA Pacific Southwest Regional Administrator Michael Martucci. “These funds enable Tribes to build long-term waste management capacity and increase recycling and composting in their communities, diverting waste from landfills.”

The goal of the SWIFR grants is to improve local waste management systems, meeting Congress’ goal to create a stronger, more resilient, and cost-effective U.S. municipal solid waste recycling system. The following Tribes in California will receive funding for projects including new and expanded recycling and composting facilities:

Kashia Band of Indians of the Stewarts Point Rancheria

Hoopa Valley Tribe

Torres Martinez Desert Cahuilla Indian

Coyote Valley Band of Pomo Indians

Pala Band of Luiseno Mission Indians

“These grants support the American economy by improving recycling, cutting disposal costs, extending landfill life, and creating local jobs,” said Acting EPA Assistant Administrator for Land and Emergency Management Thomas Croci. “By improving tribal recycling infrastructure EPA supports the recovery of domestic sources of raw materials, local economies and provides tangible health benefits to communities across Indian Country.”

By sponsoring a more efficient and robust solid waste management system in Tribal communities, these grants reduce the burden on landfill capacity, increase valuable materials for end-markets, establish collection services and composting programs, create new jobs, and improve quality of life.

text:
July 29, 2026

NEW YORK – Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced it has selected the Shinnecock Indian Nation to receive $750,000 through the Solid Waste Infrastructure for Recycling (SWIFR) to support the nation’s extensive recycling efforts. The Shinnecock Indian Nation is slated to receive funding for their project called "Shinnecock Enhancement of Recycling and Composting Initiative.”

“These grants further energize our American economy by improving recycling, cutting disposal costs, reducing waste in landfills and extending landfill life, and creating good paying local jobs,” said Acting Assistant Administrator for Land and Emergency Management Thomas Croci. “By improving tribal recycling infrastructure EPA supports the recovery of domestic sources of raw materials, local economies and provides tangible health benefits to communities across Indian Country.”

“The Shinnecock Indian Nation’s commitment to advancing recycling and composting demonstrates its commitment to improving the management of waste and improving the quality of life for all of its members,” said EPA Regional Administrator Michael Martucci. “This grant will create stronger local waste management systems, reduce landfill use, and support new economic opportunities while protecting the local environment for generations to come.”

The Shinnecock Indian Nation’s project will make recycling and composting programs on the Nation more efficient. Through this program, the Nation will supply every home with recycling bins and pick up recyclables weekly. The project will improve how recyclable materials, organics, and food waste are collected from tribal member homes and office buildings by offering direct pick-up services. The Nation will buy collection and storage bins and a truck to help with collection and transportation.

By sponsoring a more efficient and robust solid waste management system in Tribal communities, these grants reduce the burden on landfill capacity, increase valuable materials for end-markets, establish collection services and composting programs, create new jobs, and improve quality of life. The goal of the SWIFR grants is to improve local waste management systems, meeting Congress’ goal to create a stronger, more resilient, and cost-effective U.S. municipal solid waste recycling system.

title: OBBBA Abandons IRA's Technology-Neutral Clean Energy Credits | Legis1
description:
Why It Matters The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022 fundamentally rewrote how the federal government incentivizes clean energy.
A recent Congressional Service Report, published July 27, examines how the OBBBA departed from the technology-neutral framework that defined the IRA's approach to clean electricity tax credits.
The Big Picture The IRA created technology-neutral clean electricity tax credits that treated all energy sources equally if they met a single criterion: producing electricity with zero or negative lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions.
The Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit (CEITC) provided a 30 percent credit on capital investment costs for qualifying facilities placed in service in 2025 or later.
The IRA scheduled the two largest renewable energy tax credits (Production Tax Credit and Investment Tax Credit) to begin phasing out after 2024, thereafter replacing them with technology-neutral credits (CEITC and the Clean Electricity Production Tax Credit).
text:
Why It Matters

The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022 fundamentally rewrote how the federal government incentivizes clean energy. However, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), passed in 2025, moved away from the technology-neutral framework established by the IRA.

A recent Congressional Service Report, published July 27, examines how the OBBBA departed from the technology-neutral framework that defined the IRA's approach to clean electricity tax credits.

The Big Picture

The IRA created technology-neutral clean electricity tax credits that treated all energy sources equally if they met a single criterion: producing electricity with zero or negative lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions.

The Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit (CEITC) provided a 30 percent credit on capital investment costs for qualifying facilities placed in service in 2025 or later. The CEITC could be stacked with bonus credits of 10 percentage points for energy communities, 10 percentage points for domestic content, or 10 or 20 percentage points for low-income communities.

The IRA scheduled the two largest renewable energy tax credits (Production Tax Credit and Investment Tax Credit) to begin phasing out after 2024, thereafter replacing them with technology-neutral credits (CEITC and the Clean Electricity Production Tax Credit). Electricity facilities using solar, wind, nuclear, hydropower, geothermal, and marine and hydrokinetic technologies were automatically eligible, but the framework also extended potential eligibility to undiscovered zero-emissions sources, creating room for technologies not yet invented.

The Internal Revenue Service spent 2024 and 2025 clarifying how to measure whether technologies qualified. The agency established that greenhouse gas calculations would include all emissions from a facility's first decade of operation, excluding only backup generators, construction, and maintenance. It also created CO₂-equivalence scores for non-carbon greenhouse gases based on their global warming potential over 100 years.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act moved away from the technology-neutral framework in two significant ways. First, it allowed fuel cell property to qualify for the CEITC regardless of whether it produces positive greenhouse gas emissions. Second, the law also created a two-tiered timeline that disadvantages wind and solar. These technologies must have begun construction before July 5, 2026, or be placed in service before January 1, 2028, to qualify for either credit.

Wind and solar developers face deadlines that have already arrived or are rapidly approaching. Facilities that miss these windows lose eligibility entirely, while other technologies get nearly a decade more to reach construction milestones.

The Bottom Line

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act reveals that the technology-neutral approach established by the Inflation Reduction Act was not locked in place. Congress has already begun reverting to technology-specific incentives and timelines, creating urgency for some projects while extending deadlines for others.

The new additions come after Ceres joined other shareholder advocates in filing a regulatory petition to the Securities and Exchange Commission last week, urging the agency to “largely retain” the rule that governs the shareholder proposal process.

Ceres — which also runs networks for investors, companies and public policy — is adding the new board members to a group “with backgrounds in responsible investing, corporate sustainability, government and policy, environmental justice, and nonprofit advocacy.” The additions bring the total number of board members to 21, including Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford, New York State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli and Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs, according to Ceres’ website.

Ceres said its board members have an “active role” in setting the organization’s long-term strategy, while President’s Council members offer strategic oversight, specialized expertise, and public outreach to scale the organization’s impact.

Ceres CEO and President Mindy Lubber said in the release that the new members to the board and council will help Ceres as it looks to “grow [its] global networks, pursue new financial opportunities, and deepen [its] relationships and expertise.”

Levine was elected in 2025 to replace outgoing NYC Comptroller Brad Lander, now the Democratic nominee for New York’s 10th Congressional District. McCarthy, in addition to being a former EPA Administrator, was also the first White House national climate advisor and led the White House Office of Domestic Climate Policy that was created under President Joe Biden.

Rose McKinney James, a former commissioner for the Nevada Public Service commission, who is currently the managing principal for consulting firms Energy Works LLC and Mckinney-James & Associates

Aniket Shah, managing director and global head of the sustainability and transition team financial services company Jefferies Group

David Young, a former managing director at Boston Consulting Group — who still serves as a climate advisor to the firm — and executive managing director of a new venture called CascAldient.

text:
July 29, 2026 Whitehorse, Yukon Natural Resources Canada

The world is changing rapidly: global trade has been upended, and climate change is intensifying. In response, the Government of Canada is focused on what we can control: building an electricity grid that underpins energy security, affordability and competitiveness.

Building on the National Electricity Strategy, the Honourable Julie Dabrusin, Minister of Environment, Climate Change and Nature, and Brendan Hanley, Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern and Arctic Affairs, announced today nearly $7 million in funding for eight clean energy projects in Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut that will strengthen local electricity systems, reduce reliance on fossil fuels and support long-term economic growth for communities in the North. These investments will help ensure communities have reliable access to clean power that will support families, businesses, critical infrastructure and future economic development.

Generating reliable, affordable, low-emissions power is essential as electricity demand in Canada is expected to double by 2050. That is why on May 14, 2026, Canada announced a forthcoming National Electricity Strategy. This is our Team Canada plan to build a sustainable, affordable, prosperous and secure future, including in northern Canada, where access to electricity is more challenging, leading to northern and remote utility rates that are six- to ten-times higher than the national average. To that end, under the Strategy, the Government of Canada is working with territorial and Indigenous partners to support reliable, affordable electricity in the North that will secure our domestic economic and security interests and ensure an affordable future for Canadians.

Canada’s plan is clear: to build a stronger, more prosperous, secure and affordable Canada, including in the territories. Building new clean electricity capacity and optimizing energy efficiency in the North will reduce emissions, enhance energy security and create the conditions for new investment, good-paying jobs and more resilient northern communities.

text:
NORTHAMPTON, MA / ACCESS Newswire / July 29, 2026 / The aviary and pollinator habitat at MPLX's Martinsville tank farm.

Key Points

Marathon Petroleum has been recognized for its commitment to environmental stewardship through management of conservation habitats.

Six company habitat sites have re-qualified for WHC Certification®, powered by Tandem Global, an international, voluntary sustainability standard.

In all, the company has nine currently certified conservation sites that cover more than 750 acres.

Achieving WHC Certification®, powered by Tandem Global, involves far more than checking boxes on an application. It's a continual process. Documenting and maintaining ongoing benefits are required to meet the world's only voluntary sustainability standard for biodiversity enhancement and conservation education on corporate landholdings.

"Companies achieving WHC Certification are environmental leaders, voluntarily managing their lands to support sustainable ecosystems and the communities that surround them," said Margaret O'Gorman, Chief Executive Officer, Tandem Global.

At its 2026 annual conference, Tandem Global, formerly Wildlife Habitat Council and World Environment Center, recognized certification renewals for six conservation habitats owned and maintained by assets across Marathon Petroleum Corporation (MPC) and its midstream segment, MPLX:

Savage Branch Wildlife Reserve - Catlettsburg, Kentucky, refinery

Marathon Gardens - Detroit, Michigan, refinery

Pollinator garden - Garyville, Louisiana, refinery

Aviary and pollinator habitat - Martinsville, Illinois, tank farm

Washington Park - Robinson, Illinois, refinery

Prairie Park - St. Paul Park, Minnesota, refinery

WHC Certification has three tiers: Certified and Certified Silver that stay current for two years, and a three-year Certified Gold designation. The Catlettsburg and Detroit habitats earned Certified Silver status, and the other four sites received Certified honors.

Certified programs need to have at least one qualifying habitat, species or education project. Projects must exceed any relevant regulatory requirements, have a conservation or conservation education objective, and provide documented, measurable outcomes.

Managing the habitats across MPC and MPLX involves hundreds of employee volunteer hours. Tasks range from hosting school field trips to monitoring wildlife populations.

"Species observations include detailing the level of activity around nesting structures for birds," said Regina Cooper, a lead training specialist at MPC's Galveston Bay refinery in Texas City, Texas, and a volunteer at the refinery's conservation habitat. "Tandem Global wants to see continuous improvement from programs, requiring adequate monitoring to provide data that can be evaluated over time."

In all, MPC and MPLX have nine WHC-certified sites that cover more than 750 acres. Beyond the six highlighted this year, three locations gained certification renewals in prior years. The Galveston Bay refinery site has a Certified Gold designation that extends through 2027. Additionally, a second habitat at the Robinson refinery earned Certified Silver recognition and a site at the Canton, Ohio, refinery qualified for Certified status, both of which remain in effect through 2026.

title: Commission launches €1.5bn call for European battery manufacturing projects
description:
The European Commission has opened a €1.5bn funding competition designed to accelerate European battery manufacturing by supporting companies as they scale electric vehicle (EV) battery cell production.
The scheme, delivered through the Battery Booster Facility and financed by the Innovation Fund, will provide interest-free loans to eligible projects across the European Economic Area (EEA).
Focus on first commercial-scale EV battery plants The funding call is reserved for battery cell manufacturing projects serving the electric vehicle market and located within the EEA.
To be considered, applicants must be developing their first full-scale commercial EV battery cell production facility anywhere in the world.
Reviewers will consider whether projects are sufficiently mature to move into commercial production, whether financing plans are robust, and how each investment would strengthen the wider European battery ecosystem.
text:
The European Commission has opened a €1.5bn funding competition designed to accelerate European battery manufacturing by supporting companies as they scale electric vehicle (EV) battery cell production.

The scheme, delivered through the Battery Booster Facility and financed by the Innovation Fund, will provide interest-free loans to eligible projects across the European Economic Area (EEA).

Applications are now being accepted and will remain open until 30 September 2026. The funding is intended to help manufacturers overcome one of the biggest obstacles to commercial success: securing investment during the transition from demonstration-scale production to full industrial output.

The Commission expects the initiative to strengthen Europe’s battery industry by encouraging new production capacity, attracting private capital and improving the resilience of the region’s battery supply chain.

Closing a critical financing gap

While demand for EV batteries continues to rise, many manufacturers face significant financial pressure before production reaches commercial scale.

Large capital requirements, combined with limited revenue during the ramp-up period, can delay or even prevent projects from progressing.

The Battery Booster Facility, introduced earlier this year as part of the EU’s Battery Booster Strategy, has been established to address this challenge.

Rather than providing grants, the programme offers interest-free loans that allow companies to expand manufacturing while reducing the cost of financing.

Successful applicants can receive support covering up to 60% of eligible project costs, with individual loans of up to €500m.

Focus on first commercial-scale EV battery plants

The funding call is reserved for battery cell manufacturing projects serving the electric vehicle market and located within the EEA.

To be considered, applicants must be developing their first full-scale commercial EV battery cell production facility anywhere in the world.

Projects must already be progressing through the industrial ramp-up stage and be designed to achieve an annual production capacity of at least 10GWh.

By concentrating support on first-of-a-kind commercial facilities, the Commission hopes to accelerate the emergence of new large-scale manufacturers within Europe.

Projects will compete on quality and industrial impact

Applications will not be awarded solely on the basis of size. Instead, the Commission will assess each proposal against a range of technical, financial and strategic criteria.

Reviewers will consider whether projects are sufficiently mature to move into commercial production, whether financing plans are robust, and how each investment would strengthen the wider European battery ecosystem.

The latest funding call reflects the EU’s broader industrial strategy to expand European battery manufacturing, reduce dependence on overseas suppliers and build a competitive domestic industry capable of supporting Europe’s transition to electric mobility and clean energy technologies.

The home of BMW’s X models is getting ready to begin building high-voltage batteries for the new iX5 premium SUV.

BMW’s new Plant Woodruff is located 15 miles from its existing Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina, responsible for manufacturing the X3, X5, X6, X7 and XM luxury SUV models.

Due to open fully in December 2026, Plant Woodruff will see 300 employees working alongside some 250 robots, making use of artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality technology to assemble EV batteries.

With constant monitoring of the manufacturing processes by in-house AI agents and assistants, BMW promises that Plant Woodruff will deliver ‘zero-defect battery production’.

Seeking perfect EV batteries

Before beginning work on the production line, all new employees will undergo training within a virtual reality simulation.

This creates a digital replica of Plant Woodruff, allowing production employees to perform actual manufacturing operations in realistic conditions.

Multiple safety and quality checks are performed throughout the real manufacturing process, before the completed batteries are transported to Plant Spartanburg.

The new sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries will be used to power the recently announced BMW iX5 electric SUV.

With an output of 144 kWh for US-spec models, and 141 kWh in the EU, the BMW iX5 60 xDrive boasts the largest high-voltage battery of any electric BMW to date.

Boosting electromobility in the USA

text:
With gas prices remaining high due to the war in Iran, California officials are hoping a new rebate program for electric cars can make the math work for buyers at a time when federal incentives have gone away under the Trump administration.

California has long been the leader in electric-vehicle adoption, which has continued this year despite the elimination of federal tax credits. The state is now poised to assist drivers with the purchase of their first new or used electric vehicle, starting next month.

Experts say the program is meant to provide a shot in the arm for EV sales in the state but might not move the needle much at a time when the supply of electric vehicles is low nationwide. EV prices remain higher in general than gas-powered cars, and that price has been a barrier to new adoption to those with low or moderate incomes.

This month, the California Energy Commission announced that during the second quarter of the fiscal year, April through June, Californians purchased 86,857 new zero-emission vehicles — 75,597 bought EVs, 81 purchased hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles, and 11,179 people bought plug-in hybrids.

This represents 19.1% of new-car sales in the state and a 3.3 point jump over the first quarter, the strongest EV share ever recorded without a federal tax credit, said Gil Tal, director of the Electric Vehicle Research Center with UC Davis.

“At $5.77 a gallon, the operating-cost math swings decisively to the EV, about $125 a month for a typical driver, and buyers acted on that price signal within weeks,” he said.

When the Trump administration ended the $7,500 federal tax incentive for new electric vehicles in September, Tal said, the percentage of new electric vehicles sold or registered in the state fell to 15.8% in the first three months of the year, its lowest since 2021.

The reported rebound comes at a time when gas prices are soaring well above the national average in California a result of the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran.

The commission and Gov. Gavin Newsom point to gas price volatility as one reason why so many Californians decided to turn in their gasoline-powered vehicles for electric ones.

“While Donald Trump makes Americans pay the bill for his Iran war at the pump, California is giving families the freedom to choose a cheaper way forward by going electric,” Newsom said in a statement.

But, Tal noted, the whole automotive market tends to trend upward every spring, so the sale of EV units rose with it.

Regardless, California’s latest push toward getting more EVs on the road is the MyFirstEV instant rebate program, which will knock $3,500 off the purchase price of a new EV and $1,750 off a used model.

It’s an important incentive to get people into their first electric vehicle, and it continues to support the state’s transition to zero-emission vehicles, said Jeremy Michalek, director of the Vehicle Electrification Group, a research group at Carnegie Mellon University.

But one roadblock consumers may face is a lack of EVs in the dealership lot.

“We have no supply because we have no regulation that forces supply,” Tal said. “The federal government dismantled everything that was creating the supply, and the car companies started to announce backpedaling, undoing things, and we lost a lot of the supply.”

Last year, the U.S. Senate revoked California’s clean-car mandate waivers — including a rule that would have effectively banned the sale of new gas-powered cars by 2035.

The state is currently fighting the action, which removed the pressure on automakers to sell EVs within the state.

Another wrinkle is how likely consumers are to purchase an EV.

Even though consumer spending on the vehicles has ramped up, Michalek said, “it’s not that people started liking electric vehicles more. ... It’s because electric vehicles kept getting better and cheaper.”

Ultimately the program will have a couple of effects on the EV landscape in California, Michalek said. By incentivizing the purchase of a new electric vehicle, that will encourage new production, which means more EVs on the road.

Secondly, the used-EV incentive will allow some consumers to go electric who couldn’t afford to do so before.

However, incentivizing buying used EVs doesn’t result in new production, he noted: “That’s just a change of hands.” But by supporting both new and used EVs, it lessens equity concerns — that only people with higher incomes are able to take advantage of the program, Michalek said.

How the MyFirstEV program works

Newsom signed Senate Bill 168 into law this month allocating $135 million for the MyFirstEV program; the funding will be matched by 13 major automakers combined.

Through this program, eligible buyers will get an instant discount when purchasing a new or used electric vehicle — a major difference from the federal incentive that required that buyers apply for the credit after the purchase.

Eligibility is open to all Californians buying or leasing their first EV — this is confirmed through a buyer’s attestation.

Not all electric vehicles qualify for the rebate. It only pertains to new EVs with a manufacturer’s suggested retail price of $50,000 or less and used EVs sold through a manufacturer’s pre-owned vehicle program at $25,000 or less.

There is one exception to the vehicle eligibility rule: EVs sold from a company with headquarters in California can claim the discount regardless of the vehicle price. Companies include Newark-based Lucid and Irvine-based Rivian.

Solar energy is likely to provide more electricity to Texans this year than coal, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

text:
Even as the relentless sun parches plants and turns sidewalks into griddles, solar power has been helping Texans stay cool this summer.

Data from ERCOT, the independent agency that manages the electrical grid for most of Texas, show just how critical solar and wind have become for coping with high demand. On Sunday and Monday around noon, for example, more than half of the electricity flowing across the grid came from solar and wind. Natural gas supplied less than one-third. Solar energy is likely to provide more electricity to Texans this year than coal, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Political leaders in Austin should celebrate this accomplishment. That diversity of energy sources improves overall grid resilience and reliability and allows power production to keep pace with population and industrial growth. Republican lawmakers ought to embrace and encourage renewables as part of the state’s overall energy success story.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

They didn’t do that in last year’s regular legislative session. One state senator introduced a bill that would have added layers of permits and environmental regulations to the siting of solar and wind farms. The proposed regulations were more burdensome than those the state applies to oil and gas production.

Another bill would have required half of all new electricity flowing through the grid to come from “dispatchable” sources, such as coal or natural gas plants or batteries, which can be turned on or off as demand requires. Neither bill became law.

It’s easy to understand why many of the state’s most prominent GOP politicians dislike renewable energy. Some work in the oil and gas industry. Some of their biggest donors own oil and gas production or related service companies. The state makes a lot of money, directly and indirectly, from fossil fuels.

And it’s true: Wind and solar are not “dispatchable” energy. You can’t force the sun to shine at night or the wind to blow on a calm day, but you can predict those natural phenomena and adjust to their fluctuations. Battery arrays help, too.

And yes, as the renewable energy industry matures, its leaders must reckon with its waste products: scrapped solar panels and decommissioned turbine blades. That problem seems less worrisome than the rising costs of plugging and remediating Texas’ abundance of orphan oil and gas wells.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The growth of wind and solar power is part of the reason Texans haven’t had to worry about the possibility of rolling blackouts during our streaks of 100-degree days. According to a Reuters news story, ERCOT predicted only a 0.3% chance of rolling blackouts in August 2025, down from 12% in 2024. That fact alone should make Texans grateful. No air conditioning in August isn’t just uncomfortable, it’s dangerous.

Federal energy policy may no longer encourage renewable energy production, but it’s in Texans’ best interest to allow the industry to flourish here.

text:
Gap Inc. hit its sustainable cotton sourcing goal and exceeded its recycled polyester target in fiscal 2025, while renewable power use and some greenhouse gas emissions slipped, according to an annual report.

The apparel brand sourced 100% of its cotton from sustainable sources in the fiscal year ending Jan. 31, surpassing the 98% reported last year, according to the 2025 Impact Report published in June. While continuing its eco-friendly sourcing this year, the company aims to double its use of traceable U.S.-grown cotton, tracked through the TextileGenesis platform, which follows materials from fiber to retail.

Meanwhile, the company obtained 65% of its polyester from recycled sources in 2025, beating its goal of at least 45%. The company also signed a letter of intent to use Syre’s polyester, made from recycled textiles rather than new oil-based materials.

Gap also cut scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 70% from a 2017 baseline, less than the 74% reported in 2024. The company’s goal is to reach a 90% reduction by 2030.

Scope 3 emissions from purchased goods and services fell 20% from 2017, higher than the 13% reduction reported in 2024. Gap aims to cut these emissions 32.5% by 2030 by working with suppliers on energy efficiency and renewable power.

Gap is also working toward its goal of having net-zero emissions across its value chain by 2050 and has reduced overall emissions 20% toward that target since 2017, an improvement over 2024’s 17% drop, the company reported.

The apparel brand slipped in terms of sustainable power use, as it obtained 46% of the electricity for company-operated facilities from renewable sources in 2025, compared with 52% in 2024. The company’s goal is to reach 100% renewable electricity by 2030.

In 2025, 420 of the company’s Tier 1 and Tier 2 facilities invested in renewable energy, including two in Vietnam that completed rooftop solar panel installations covering about a third of their electricity needs, the report says. Comparative numbers were not given in 2024.

Roughly 40 of Gap’s Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers enrolled in or completed Cascale’s Manufacturer Climate Action Program. The company did not provide a number for 2024. Cascale is a global nonprofit alliance of brands, manufacturers, retailers, suppliers and other stakeholders working to improve sustainability in the consumer goods industry.

Also in 2025, Gap transitioned diesel-powered shunt trunks, used to move containers, to electric models at four distribution centers, saving more than 31,000 gallons of diesel, according to the report. The company plans to extend the conversion to its remaining campuses in 2026.

Gap also replenished 39% of its total freshwater withdrawals across its supply chain in 2025, up from 14% in 2024. The company says that progress keeps it on track to replenish 100% of the freshwater used in apparel manufacturing and in company-operated facilities by 2030.

text:
Since the start of the year, four high-speed charging stations have opened in Bentonville, Ark., even though the state has been a laggard in transitioning to electric vehicles.

Bentonville, however, is Walmart Inc. country and these are Walmart chargers — three at stores near the company’s headquarters and one at the airport.

In a matter of months, Walmart has become a major player in the burgeoning business of quickly fueling electric vehicles, speeding past Costco as well as more established charging companies with its in-house network of electron pumps. Walmart has hosted chargers from brands like Electrify America since 2018. But now the company is building its own network — and quickly. As of March of last year, every EV station at a Walmart is under the company brand.

While the blitz of infrastructure will fuel in-store sales, it will also redraw the American charging map, making public electrons cheaper and easier to find.

“They’re steamrolling,” said Bill Ferro, cofounder of Paren, a charging consultancy. “It’s the right time to do this and they’ve got the right locations.”

Through June this year, Walmart opened about 46 high-speed public charging stations with 380 cords, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. All told, there are now EV chargers at about 326 of Walmart’s 4,600 or so U.S. stores, and Paren estimates another 300 or so stations are under construction.

(Walmart Inc.)

Walmart declined to answer questions or provide any detail on how much more charging it will build, but acknowledged in a statement that it has one of the critical ingredients in an electric pump empire: scads of valuable and widespread real estate.

“Our broad footprint positions us to make EV charging more accessible for communities while expanding the way we serve customers,” a Walmart spokesperson wrote via e-mail.

Charging an electric vehicle typically takes a little bit longer than fueling a gas car. That bit of technological lag has been a bug to EV sales, but to retailers like Walmart, it’s a feature — a perfect window of idle time for someone to pick up a few odds and ends.

“The fact that Walmart knows the indirect value of having charging at their facility is all the evidence you need to know that there is a real viable business there,” said Nick Nigro, cofounder of Atlas Public Policy, a Washington, D.C.-based climate consultancy.

Walmart’s charging plans are spooling up even as EV sales falter in the U.S. Demand for electric cars and trucks slumped after federal incentives expired in September, though they have started to recover since the Iran war spiked gas prices.

Analysts are split on where the EV market goes from here, but the installed base is sizable. There are now 7.6 million plug-in vehicles on U.S. roads, according to S&P Global, and an estimated 90% of Americans live less than 10 miles from a Walmart.

As battery-powered machines gain traction among mainstream buyers and proliferate on the second hand market, they’ve spread from the American coasts into rural areas in the Midwest and Deep South. They’ve also gathered momentum among apartment dwellers who don’t have access to charging at home. Florida, Illinois and Texas are adding EV charging infrastructure faster than nearly anywhere else.

Target has 150 high-speed charging stations in the U.S. (Target)

Walmart, meanwhile, isn’t alone in its play for EV pilots. If anything, it’s a little late to the game. Target Corp. has 150 high-speed charging stations spread around its U.S. stores, according to Paren, while Costco Wholesale Corp. is selling electrons in 42 of its lots. Home Depot Inc. and Lowe’s Companies Inc. have 101 stations between them.

Shiri Levi-Laor, CEO of Driivz Inc., a consultancy, says adjacent charging generally increases a store’s sales by 5%. By 2030, she estimates one in five fast-charging stations in the U.S. will be in the parking lot of a big-box retailer.

“It’s a double-dip of revenue,” Levi-Laor said. “Retailers are not investing in charging to sell electricity; that’s not their intention. They are investing because it strengthens their core business.”

While Walmart’s chargers will no doubt juice its in-store sales, selling electrons has been good business of late. Despite a rash of new charging stations, America’s EV plugs have stayed busy, used about 16% of the time in recent months, according to Paren. In June, U.S. drivers plugged into public fast-chargers 16 million times.

To be sure, Walmart is still a blip on the U.S. charging map, though maybe not for long. Among charging networks expanding in the second quarter, Walmart was second only to Tesla.

Meanwhile, Walmart’s charging rates are cheaper than the national average, and cheaper still for loyalty members. Ferro, at Paren, expects the ubiquity of the new stations and the low prices will spur EV adoption in places where gas has been resilient, like Arkansas.

“Honestly,” he explained, “I wouldn’t be surprised if you start to see people trying to do a Walmart road trip.”

text:
Ken Salazar has a climate and energy message for Democrats gearing up to fight President Donald Trump’s machine in 2028: Unite the countries of North America — and particularly work with Mexico — to counteract the Trump administration’s retreat on global climate action.

The lawyer, who led the Interior Department during the Obama administration and served as U.S. ambassador to Mexico under former President Joe Biden, makes the case for a new era of collaboration in a memoir that explores his Colorado roots and role as one of that state’s pioneering Hispanic politicians.

“What I’m calling for is this new American alliance,” Salazar said in a wide-ranging interview about his new book, “Borderlands: My Fight for an Inclusive America.”

Advertisement

The interview, like the memoir, ranged from his views on the current era of anti-immigration policies in Washington, how his upbringing on a ranch in Colorado shaped his political trajectory and the role Mexico’s current leader — President Claudia Sheinbaum — could play in creating a different politics around climate action.

“We are a North American continent that has so much potential to bring our peoples together,” Salazar said. “Right now, we have a present administration that has turned its back on that very positive agenda.”

Salazar was raised in the San Luis Valley — his family’s roots in that valley in Colorado and New Mexico span back to at least the 1600s — in a single-story adobe house with limited electricity and running water. He went on to become a lawyer working on water issues and eventually won election to become Colorado’s first Hispanic attorney general on the cusp of the state’s transition from mostly politically red to mostly blue. After winning that seat in 1999, Salazar recalls embarking on a road trip through the state blasting folk songs, Mexican norteño music and Bruce Springsteen’s version of “This Land is Your Land.”

The memoir explores Salazar’s relationship to the Western landscape, recounting how his family’s stewardship contrasted sharply with the “exploitation” he witnessed from nearby absentee cattle ranchers. Salazar said in his book that he came to believe that “when land is treated sustainably, it can be both healthy and productive. There is no need to sacrifice one for the other.”

That ethos of both using and conserving the environment could be seen when Salazar later became the director of Colorado’s Department of Natural Resources under former Gov. Roy Romer (D), and when he became the U.S. senator for Colorado from 2005 to 2009. But some environmentalists criticized his openness to mineral development on public lands when former President Barack Obama tapped Salazar to be his first Interior secretary.

“Ken Salazar is very closely tied to ranching and mining and very traditional, old-time Western extraction industries,” the Center for Biological Diversity’s Kieran Suckling told NPR in 2008. “We were promised that an Obama presidency would bring change.”

Salazar’s period as secretary from 2009 to 2013 boosted natural gas development on federal lands, even as the administration also hammered out some of the nation’s first climate regulations to deal a blow to coal dependency. At the time, coal was responsible for about half of the country’s electricity supply, and Salazar argued that natural gas was a bridge fuel away from the more carbon-heavy power source.

Salazar told POLITICO public lands still have room for natural gas development but that the U.S. also needs “to recognize that fossil fuels have had a tremendous effect on our planet.”

“We need to address those realities,” he said.

During Salazar’s tenure, Interior developed the nation’s first federal offshore wind program and held the first national wind lease sale in 2013, just a few months after he left the post. Offshore wind would make little progress until the Biden administration supercharged the program as part of its all-of-government approach to climate change. The nascent industry, however, has faced tremendous setbacks under the Trump administration, and companies have been pressured by the White House to relinquish their offshore wind leases and invest instead in fossil energy.

Salazar, 71, politely declared Trump’s attacks on renewables as “the wrong way to go.”

Asked if his book launch precedes a return to politics, Salazar said his immediate passion is convincing Democrats of the “Borderlands agenda,” both in the upcoming midterms and in the presidential race of 2028.

Pressed on whether he will run for office, the former secretary quoted his granddaughter saying, “Papa, one thing at a time.”

This interview was edited for clarity and length.

You speak at length of the need for a new deal between the U.S. and Mexico, where you served as the U.S. ambassador under Biden. What would that relationship look like?

If we had a new energy and climate pact for North America, we could frankly set an example for the entire world of what we can do with renewable energies — also with traditional energies that we need, because you’re not going to transition from one day to the next.

You think about Arizona, which is one of the best places for solar energy in the world, and you take the state to the south, [Mexico’s] Sonora, they have huge, huge solar energy resources. The interconnectivity of the power grid becomes important.

You think about minerals like lithium — the state of Sonora has some of the largest lithium deposits in the world — and how we use lithium for batteries for the future. That’s all part of integrated supply chains.

Why do you think that kind of collaboration hasn’t emerged already?

Because of historic inattention.

We need to create a stronger Western Hemisphere, and different presidents have given it attention. President Bush did a lot, in some areas. I think President Obama did an outstanding job.

I helped lead some of this, at Big Bend National Park and the [Mexican] state of Coahuila, all the things we’re doing with our national parks to try to create this bi-national conservation area [and] our agreements on the Colorado River Minute 319 [a pact between the U.S. and Mexico on managing Colorado River water].

Unfortunately, 2016 comes around, and this president, who’s never been to Mexico as president, is continuing this agenda of inattention. It’s a wrong-headed approach, and I hope it gets turned around.

Your Hispanic heritage appears to have had a profound impact on your life and career — your family’s footprint in the West dates to when the land belonged to Mexico, as you talk about in your book. How has that relationship to the land shaped you?

I’m proud to be Mexican American, proud to be a U.S. citizen. My family has been in what is now the southwestern part of the United States since the 1600s. They settled the upper reaches of the Rio Grande in New Mexico under places like Santa Fe and north into Española. After the Mexican-American War, they moved to the ranch in the San Luis Valley, and we’ve been there 170-plus years. We’re not going anywhere.

When you look at where we are today, there are some 50 million Mexican Americans in the United States, 70 million Latinos and 130 million Mexicans. It’s important to recognize history to understand where we are now, and to plan for a future where we have respect for the sovereignties and histories of both countries. You also understand the importance of them working together.

There’s been a ton of ink spilled about the Trump administration’s border wall, most recently because of plans to put border infrastructure in Big Bend National Park. What are your thoughts about the border wall and its presence on public lands?

The creation of a physical wall is not the solution here. The solution has to go beyond the border itself, it has to look at the realities of flows of illicit products, including drugs from the Americas to Mexico.

We need to have a secure border and a modern border, and that’s where I think the United States, both Democrats and Republicans, have gotten it wrong. We need to have a secure border, we need a modern border, we need to have technology that fixes the border. But it needs to be done by both the United States and Mexico. You can’t secure the border only on one side.

Do you view climate as a potential political unifier in your vision of “North American energy independence”?

It is a positive, powerful, unifying challenge and opportunity that we have.

There’s a reality in Mexico that you have the first president who really understands climate better than almost anybody, because she’s a scientist, Claudia Sheinbaum. She was part of the [U.N.’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change] report. She, through many conversations I’ve had with her, recognizes the imperative of dealing with the realities of climate change. The table is set, except that we don’t have the right leadership with us.

The Trump administration has doubled down on fossil fuels on public lands, arguing that we face an energy emergency due to rising energy demand. What are your thoughts on that?

They just took our country back to a place where it was in probably the 1950s, maybe 1960s. Since then, we’ve been making progress to diversify our energy resources, to become energy independent.

When I got to the Senate, I remember sitting down with former Sen. Tim Wirth — a progressive Democrat — and a conservative —Republican C. Boyden Gray — who’d been a White House counsel. And our agenda on the table was called Set America Free.

That means set America free from the dependence on oil from Iran and Iraq and the Middle East and Venezuela. But it also made sense for us to embrace this broad portfolio of energy through technology, and we have been doing that. The unfortunate reality is that since Donald Trump came into office, all that has been given a 180-degree about face.

When politicians talk about ending fossil fuel dependency, they very often don’t have a concrete route to get there. Do you have a road map for that?

It’s a tough nut to crack, because it can’t happen instantaneously, but it’s happening. If you think about electric vehicles and fuel efficiency, we’re a lot better today than we were 10 years ago and 20 years ago. When you think about the power of wind and solar energy — the top states for wind are Texas and Iowa. So it can be done, but it doesn’t happen in a year or five years. It takes a long-term commitment, and that’s the greatest danger of this time, this president. His people have basically done away with, or are trying to do away with, all the progress that’s been made.

title: Chatham County landowners are uniting against a proposed natural gas pipeline
description:
The company planned to survey their 22-acre property for a proposed natural gas pipeline.
Soon after, the Guniperos joined hundreds of Chatham County residents opposing the project.
But very few of us use natural gas,” Chatham resident Jenna Dunning told The N&O.

text:
Eileen and James Gunipero opened a letter on April 16 from Enbridge Gas North Carolina. The company planned to survey their 22-acre property for a proposed natural gas pipeline.

Soon after, the Guniperos joined hundreds of Chatham County residents opposing the project. With different maps being circulated in the community, residents still don’t know, months later, whether the pipeline would cross their property, or whether wetlands, culturally significant land or farms they’ve spent decades caring for would be disturbed.

“We’re almost always kept in the dark, and it causes anxiety,” Eileen Gunipero told The News & Observer.

On July 17, about 40 people gathered at the Chatham Community Library in Pittsboro, where the Haw River Assembly environmental group hosted a meeting on the pipeline’s permitting process and strategies to oppose the project. Attendees discussed eminent domain laws and the proposed data center that many believe is driving demand for the pipeline.

“We’re going to be working together to stop this pipeline,” Emily Sutton, executive director of the Haw River Assembly, told the crowd as she outlined next steps.

Persida Montanez, spokesperson with Enbridge, told The N&O that the company needs the 28-mile pipeline to meet growing residential and business demand in Chatham and Lee counties. The company has surveyed about 200 landowners and says each has been assigned an agent to discuss routing and property concerns.

Montanez said the number of customers it serves in Chatham County increased 2.7% over the past year, one of the fastest-growing counties in its service territory.

During the community meeting, Sutton told attendees that Enbridge cannot apply for environmental permits until a route is finalized. She said the Army Corps of Engineers relies heavily on company-funded archaeological surveys and suggested residents consider hiring their own experts to document culturally significant sites before the route is complete and permits are issued.

She also urged residents to ask the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality to require individual permits for each stream and wetland crossing instead of issuing one general permit. Once Enbridge does apply for permits, DEQ has 15 days to review an application followed by another 15 days to consider public comments.

‘Our property is being usurped’

The Guniperos moved from New York to Chatham County with their Icelandic horses in 2007. The property was intended to be a long-term retirement property and family farm compound after James, 72, retired as a podiatric surgeon and Eileen, 71, from administrative work and running an Icelandic horse tack store.

The proposed pipeline, 12 inches in diameter, would stretch from Siler City to Moncure. The Guniperos said Enbridge has downplayed the long-term restrictions that easements could place on their land. For instance, the pipeline would prohibit families from farming or building on their land, and Enbridge would own the right to expand the pipeline at any time without resident input.

The typical permanent easement is expected to be 50 feet wide, according to Montanez. Additionally, an easement would allow Enbridge to operate and maintain the pipeline, but would not transfer ownership of the property, she noted.

“It just feels like our property is being usurped,” Eileen Gunipero said. “The area of the farm that is most threatened by the pipeline still has the survey flags evident from recent work to subdivide approximately two acres that were intended for a young couple we consider family.”

“It was envisioned that we would have several members of the family living here as we age,” she explained. “The newly surveyed section would not be used should the pipeline come through.”

Eminent domain

Governments can use eminent domain to acquire private property for projects that are deemed to benefit the public. They must pay the landowners for their property. Private utility companies can also use eminent domain for purposes such as pipelines.

Montanez said Enbridge is “committed to doing all we can to work with property owners to reach a positive outcome.”

James Gunipero said he understands the purpose of eminent domain, “but to me it seems that corporations are twisting it and using it more as legalized thievery.”

Many residents have also questioned whether the project primarily serves future industrial development rather than existing residents.

“We all use propane or solar or a mixture of both. But very few of us use natural gas,” Chatham resident Jenna Dunning told The N&O. “It’s not a public need.”

Among other concerns, the Guniperos are worried about leaks and pollution during the process of installing the pipeline.

“We don’t know what can be left over. [Enbridge doesn’t] exactly have the best track record for any of this, and I’m not convinced they would do anything in our favor. Once they leave that pipeline in, we’re living on a landmine, essentially,” James said.

Enbridge, a Canadian energy infrastructure company, owns gas and energy divisions across North America, including Enbridge Gas North Carolina. The company has a controversial history in Wisconsin. The Bad River Band of Lake Superior Chippewa sued the company over its 41-mile oil pipeline after it crossed into tribal land. A federal judge ruled in 2023 the company has trespassed on the reservation since 2013 and ordered it to reroute.

Separately, in 2024, Enbridge detected a crude oil spill of 70,000 gallons in a small town in Wisconsin, prompting cleanup efforts that cost $1.1 million. And in 2019, Wisconsin regulators accused the company of violating state law by waiting more than 15 months to report a pipeline leak near Fort Atkinson that released 1,200 gallons of petroleum into groundwater.

In Chatham County, Enbridge has operated safely since 1955, according to Montanez.

‘Over my dead body’

For 85-year-old Dorasue Christian, the pipeline threatens more than just her property.

Christian, a widow, lives on 22.5 acres with her 66-year-old son, who has a disability. The property, which her family has owned for generations, is filled with chickens, birds, a pond and wildlife that she says provide the quiet environment her son depends on.

She also worries construction could cross beneath her pond and permanently alter the land.

“I’ve never been arrested in my life. … I’ve never even had a parking ticket,” she told The N&O. “If Enbridge takes this land, they’re going to have to come over my dead body.”

Christian, who retired as a dental hygienist in 2001, has said she is running out of savings and had planned to sell parcels of her land to support her son, but she said if Enbridge constructs a pipeline through it, buyers will not want to purchase it, due to the liability.

At the community meeting, residents repeatedly discussed the prospect that the pipeline would cross creeks, rivers and tributaries.

Retired biologist John Alderman, who is currently being sued by Enbridge, has been vocal in saying the pipeline would threaten the Rocky River-Deep River system, which is a habitat for the federally endangered Cape Fear Shiner fish. In a letter to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, he urged them to prepare an environmental impact statement, warning that the pipeline would increase sedimentation and erosion, require blasting, contribute to unwarranted deforestation and affect water runoff, among other issues.

Crystal Cavalier-Keck of 7 Directions of Service, an Indigenous-led environmental justice organization, told The N&O the proposed route also crosses documented Tuscarora village sites. She said many Tuscarora live in New York and have lost a bond to North Carolina. She believes the pipeline could cut any connections Tuscarora have left to their land.

“It’s just really all about trying to connect back to our ancestors and our way of being as Indigenous people, because that really reminds us of the sacred responsibilities given to us from the Creator, and so when people start to lose that connection they really start to lose respect for everything — the environment, the animals, the other people,” she said.

Montanez said any concerns with cultural sites and farms will be addressed before the final route is selected.

“We take cultural and archaeological resources really seriously,” she said. “The route has not been finalized, and the intent is to avoid environmental and cultural resources to the greatest extent possible.”

Enbridge held an open house July 28 that gave residents an opportunity to provide feedback on the route to land agents.

In a public packet provided to The N&O, Enbridge wrote that residents may receive additional survey notifications, requests for property access and potential easement discussions as the next steps. For larger rivers and sensitive areas, the company wrote it would consider horizontal directional drilling, a trenchless construction method that bores beneath the water to reduce surface disturbance.

Enbridge denies data center claims

Near the end of the July 17 meeting residents said the pipeline may have ties to a proposed 740-megawatt EcoTip data center planned for Chatham County.

The data center would include cryptocurrency mining and is managed by Kirk Bradley, owner and CEO of real estate firm Lee Moore Capitol Co.

Montanez disputed this claim, and told The N&O the pipeline will not support a data center, and could not do so because the gas that would flow through its 12-inch diameter pipe would not support the level of energy a data center demands.

Still, residents feel Enbridge hasn’t been transparent.

Dunning said the study corridor map stops directly at the EcoTip site where the proposed data center may go.

“That’s not a public need, that’s an industrial need, but if that is the case, then eminent domain is not justified,” she said.

Dunning also pointed to Enbridge’s 2025 annual report, which says the company’s long-term strategy is to expand natural gas infrastructure and mentions data centers as a driver of future pipeline development.

“We continue to work with customers on opportunities to supply gas for new power generation that supports data centers and overall demand growth, and capitalize on strong gas fundamentals to deliver safe, reliable, and lower-carbon energy to North Americans while simultaneously growing (liquified natural gas) exports,” the document said.

Still, in a frequently asked questions section on the company’s website, it denies that the proposed pipeline could support a data center and says “no such request has been made to date.”

Chatham County Manager Bryan Thompson told The N&O the county will evaluate the pipeline project to determine its role under applicable law and potential impacts.

“The County has received many comments from residents expressing concerns about the proposed Enbridge pipeline project,” he said in an email.

In response, the Chatham County Board of Commissioners has scheduled a meeting on Aug. 5 to receive further public comment on the pipeline.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Five states have agreed to accept nuclear waste from around the country in exchange for federal help developing nuclear energy to create thousands of jobs.

The states — Tennessee, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Utah and Idaho — all have Republican governors who say they welcome the chance to help America reclaim its leadership in civilian nuclear energy.

If built, the storage sites would represent significant progress in a multi-decade effort to store more than 95,000 metric tons of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste. Plans for a permanent underground storage facility at Nevada's Yucca Mountain have long been stalled because of staunch opposition from most residents and officials.

Spent fuel is currently stored at nuclear plants and former nuclear sites nationwide and is piling up. New storage sites would move the radioactive material away from population centers, fault lines and flood plains. Experts say the plan also should help officials gain consent from communities that will host the repositories.

Under the non-binding agreements, the states could host Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses that would include waste sites as well as uranium enrichment, spent-fuel reprocessing and fuel fabrication. The campuses may also host advanced reactor deployment, power generation and data centers, the Energy Department said.

Nuclear campuses could boost state economies

The campuses have the potential to attract up to $50 billion in private investment and generate as much as $10 billion in state and local tax revenues, the Energy Department said in a statement. Eligible projects could access federal loans worth billions of dollars, the department said.

“These campuses will be massive generators of economic growth ... and be crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance,'' Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a statement. He called the proposed campuses an “innovative concept” that will "get America’s nuclear industry growing again.''

Tennessee is home to the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which enriched uranium during World War II as part of the Manhattan Project, while Idaho hosts the Idaho National Laboratory, a key research site for nuclear energy and national security. Utah was a source of raw uranium for the Manhattan Project and a training site for crews that dropped atomic bombs on Japan in 1945.

“As the global epicenter of nuclear energy, Tennessee is honored to be selected as a potential host for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus,” said Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee. "As our state answered the call during the Manhattan Project and helped shape the course of history, Tennessee stands ready once again to advance the safe, reliable energy solutions our nation depends on.”

Solution for storing waste needed to expand nuclear power

The announcement comes as President Donald Trump attempts to quadruple domestic nuclear energy production because of surging electricity demand due to a data center and artificial intelligence boom. Trump also has moved to reshape the independent Nuclear Regulatory Commission to speed up nuclear reactor development. Under Trump’s direction, the commission has proposed eliminating a foundational safety principle that for 50 years minimized the radiation people in the United States are exposed to.

The NRC proposal would abandon a philosophy to keep radiation exposure “as low as reasonably achievable,” instead setting a separate standard on maximum radiation exposure that includes several actions facilities must take depending on the potential dose of radiation to workers.

California Rep. Mike Levin said the nuclear fuel announcement was a long time coming and required bipartisan collaboration to fix difficult nuclear waste challenges. Levin, a Democrat, has pushed to allocate funding to safely remove and dispose of spent nuclear fuel from decommissioned nuclear plants, including the closed San Onofre nuclear power plant in Southern California.

“Today’s selection of states is a monumental step in the right direction,” Levin said in a statement. “For the first time in decades, states are raising their hands” to accept nuclear waste.

Scott Roecker, a former official at the National Nuclear Security Administration who now advises the Nuclear Scaling Initiative, a pro-nuclear group, said the campuses are a good idea, though he cautions that spent nuclear fuel should not be reprocessed there to be recycled for new fuel because of the cost and security issues.

“Getting a community to accept a long-term repository for nuclear waste has been a big challenge in the United States politically. It’s been a hard pill to swallow for certain communities,” he said in a recent interview. “The fact that they’re talking about sort of the whole fuel cycle at these centers is a positive thing. Basically, you’re getting the consent of that community for that long-term repository.”

Congress now must work to authorize the campuses and establish clear oversight, Levin said.

text:
On July 27, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s final rule, Phasedown of Hydrofluorocarbons: Reconsideration of Certain Regulatory Requirements Promulgated Under the Technology Transitions Provisions of the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020, took effect. The rule removes the federal installation deadline for qualifying nonvariable refrigerant flow residential and light-commercial air conditioning and heat pump systems that use R-410A or another refrigerant with a global warming potential, or GWP, of 700 or greater.

The now-eliminated deadline stemmed from the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020, which Congress enacted as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021. The law directed the EPA to phase down the production and consumption of hydrofluorocarbons and authorized the agency to restrict their use in designated sectors and subsectors. Acting under that authority, the Biden EPA’s implementing rule generally prohibited the installation of new residential and light-commercial air conditioning and heat pump systems using refrigerants with a GWP of 700 or greater beginning Jan. 1, 2025

The EPA later issued a December 2023 interim final rule that allowed contractors to install qualifying equipment through Dec. 31, 2025, if manufacturers produced all specified components in the United States or importers brought them into the country before Jan. 1, 2025. As that deadline approached, the Trump administration announced in December 2025 that the deadline would remain in force but that the EPA generally would not prioritize enforcement while it completed the rulemaking.

The Trump administration’s 2026 final rule formally removes the installation deadline. Distributors may continue selling qualifying legacy inventory and contractors may install systems made entirely from eligible components without a federal expiration date. The EPA also preserved contractors’ ability to service existing R-410A systems with replacement components labeled “for servicing existing equipment only.”

The rule does not allow businesses to use R-410A components manufactured in the United States or imported on or after Jan. 1, 2025, to assemble a new system. However, manufacturers and importers may continue supplying properly labeled R-410A components, with limitations, to repair existing systems. New non-ariable refrigerant flow systems that do not qualify for the legacy-inventory provision must use refrigerants with a GWP below 700.

text:
Editor’s note: Dr.Richard Feldman is an Indianapolis family physician and the former state health commissioner.

Columns such as this, published on a printed page or website section labeled Opinion, are solely the opinion of the author. Send comments on this column to dr-editorial@greenfieldreporter.com.

I was impressed by a recent perspective published in the New England Journal of Medicine, entitled “The Dismantling of Environmental Protections – A Grave Threat to America’s Health,” which serves as a major source for this column.

In 1970, President Richard Nixon lamented that Americans were being “suffocated by smog” and “poisoned by water.” He declared that clean air and water should be “the birthright of every American.” With the president’s encouragement, Congress established the Environmental Protection Agency and enacted the Clean Air Act, both with bipartisan support. The authors maintain that the resulting environmental improvements “are among the most effective health interventions of the past half-century, having reduced U.S. air pollution by 75% and saving 200,000 lives per year.” Progress of that magnitude may now be in the rearview mirror.

During President Trump’s first term, about 100 environmental and occupational protections, including air-quality mandates, were rescinded. Although President Biden reversed some of those actions, the authors believe they caused significant adverse health consequences. The second Trump administration’s actions “have been even more aggressive, portending greater harm.”

In March 2025, the EPA announced 31 new regulatory reversals that would accelerate climate change, increase air and water pollution, make workplaces more dangerous, and ultimately cause disease and premature death. These outcomes are determined by established science, not opinion. Some examples include:

-Lowering the fine airborne particulate matter standard, which would increase childhood asthma, heart attacks, strokes, chronic respiratory conditions and deaths.

-Undermining regulations governing air pollution from oil and gas extraction.

-Increasing allowable releases of airborne neurotoxins and carcinogens, including arsenic and benzene.

-Terminating the “Good Neighbor Plan,” which protects downwind states from nitrogen oxide emissions that promote ozone formation, thereby exacerbating respiratory disease and increasing mortality.

-Adopting policy changes that favor fossil fuel combustion (primarily coal) while discouraging clean-energy sources, harming long-term planetary health and increasing cardiopulmonary disease in the short term.

-Increasing allowable greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, accelerating climate change and increasing particulate matter and ozone formation, leading to greater cardiopulmonary morbidity and mortality, premature deliveries, and stillbirths.

-Lowering limits on mercury emissions from coal-fired power plants. Mercury enters the food chain as methylmercury (different from the mercury in vaccines). Pregnant women who ingest methylmercury risk causing brain damage and diminished cognitive function in their infants.

-Enactment of the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which ended federal subsidies for solar- and wind-powered energy production, further increasing fossil fuel utilization.

-U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement, resulting in adverse global consequences.

-The proposal to end the greenhouse gases “Endangerment Finding,” which determined that greenhouse gases are pollutants. This will terminate the EPA’s authority to regulate “climate-forcing pollution.” These climate-change-denying actions will result in further increases in heat waves, wildfires, floods, and other natural disasters.

-Relaxing automotive emission standards.

-Weakening drinking water quality standards by allowing greater levels of PFAS (“forever chemicals”), lead, mercury and arsenic; thus, increasing the incidence of cancer, cardiovascular disease, pediatric cognitive dysfunction, and other conditions.

Pollution is largely an invisible health threat and is therefore easily dismissed or overlooked by everyday Americans. Undermining science, eliminating agency research capabilities, and reducing staffing at the EPA and other agencies compromise essential evidence-based policy development.

The authors conclude that “…this administration’s actions will undo the work of generations. Its policies will result in dirtier skies, befouled waters, rising temperatures, more dangerous workplaces, and diminished quality of life….”

The price will be paid in the currency of disease and death.

Dr.Richard Feldman is an Indianapolis family physician and the former state health commissioner. Send comments to dr-editorial@greenfieldreporter.com.

text:
Download PDF

The National Association of Clean Water Agencies (“NACWA”) submitted June 29th comments on the United States Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) Interim Guidance on the Destruction and Disposal of PFAS and Materials Containing PFAS – 2026 Version (“Interim Guidance”). See EPA-HQ-OLEM-2020-0527.

EPA states that the Interim Guidance’s 2026 update provides the currently available information on the destruction and disposal of Perfluoroalkyl and Polyfluoroalkyl (“PFAS”) substances and materials containing PFAS.

The Interim Guidance focuses on updates to the current state of science and what it describes as associated uncertainties for three large-scale capacity technologies that can destroy PFAS or control PFAS release into the environment, which include:

Thermal treatment

Landfills

Underground injection

The Interim Guidance also discusses:

Emerging technologies

Framework for evaluating these technologies for PFAS destruction or disposal

NACWA states that it represents the interests of more than 360 publicly owned clean water utilities of all sizes across the United States. Further, their services are noted to include treating billions of gallons of our nation’s wastewater and stormwater and managing the millions of tons of biosolids generated as a byproduct of the wastewater treatment process in a manner that ensures continued protection of human health and the environment.

NACWA states by way of introduction that the organization:

Appreciates the inclusion of several new studies and data while also urging additional context regarding the findings

Appreciates what it states are important insights into how PFAS impact clean water agencies and each of the biosolids management approaches while:

Underscoring the complicated landscape PFAS creates

Lack of a clear solution for the clean water community

Overall need for greater source control alongside advanced destruction technologies

Clean water utilities are passive PFAS receivers, and the organization is working to understand and mitigate PFAS entering and leaving clean water collection systems and treatment plants

PFAS chemicals enter the wastewater treatment process from upstream industrial and manufacturing discharges to wastewater utilities, as well as through everyday domestic source contributions from consumers using and rinsing PFAS-coated products down the drain

Clean water utilities are described as:

Not designed or constructed with PFAS treatment in mind

Currently possess no technology available that is capable of removing PFAS from the hundreds of millions of gallons of influent

Biosolids are generated continuously as a byproduct of the treatment process and can only be managed through a limited set of pathways, including:

Land application

Landfill disposal

Incineration

text:
Tesla has signed a 140 MWac power purchase agreement (PPA) with Spanish renewable energy company Zelestra for electricity from a planned solar project in northeast Texas, expanding their existing renewable energy partnership into the US.

The agreement covers power from Zelestra’s Lumen Farm solar project, which is located in northeast Texas. Zelestra expects to begin construction in 2027 and bring the project into full operation by 2029.

The deal comes as Tesla’s energy needs in Texas continue to grow. It also gives Zelestra a new opportunity to expand its renewable energy business in the US and work with large corporate customers seeking long-term clean power supplies.

Phil North, Zelestra’s US CEO, said: “As a trusted global partner, we can deliver bespoke solutions for clients in multiple geographies. As such, we are excited to expand our relationship with Tesla to the US.”

Tesla secures Texas solar power

Under the agreement, Tesla will receive electricity generated by the planned 140 MWac solar project once it becomes operational. The long-term PPA is expected to support the development of the Lumen Farm project while giving Tesla access to renewable power in Texas.
