title: North Carolina Formally Recognizes Composting as Agriculture in Landmark Farm Act
description:
Paula Luu Governor Josh Stein signed Senate Bill 401 into law on June 22, 2026, making North Carolina one of the few states to formally include composting within its statutory definition of agriculture.
The law also creates a pathway for qualifying operations to pursue bona fide farm status under North Carolina General Statute 160D-903.
For the North Carolina Composting Council, the law is both a hard-won policy victory and a springboard for future industry growth.
“Now that permitted Type 1, 2, and 3 composting facilities are recognized as agriculture under North Carolina law, the industry is better positioned to grow,” said Kat Polk, Executive Director of the North Carolina Composting Council (NCCC).
Showing how composting supports agriculture, waste reduction, and economic development helped broaden the coalition and create a stronger foundation for lasting policy change.
text:
Paula Luu

Governor Josh Stein signed Senate Bill 401 into law on June 22, 2026, making North Carolina one of the few states to formally include composting within its statutory definition of agriculture. The change gives permitted composting facilities a stronger legal and economic footing while offering a policy model that advocates hope other states will follow.

The legislation, known as the NC Farm Act of 2025-2026, expands the state’s definition of agriculture to include the production, processing, storage, use, and sale of compost made from yard and food waste. It applies to permitted Small and Large Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 composting facilities.

The law also creates a pathway for qualifying operations to pursue bona fide farm status under North Carolina General Statute 160D-903. That designation can provide protections historically reserved for conventional agricultural producers, including stronger standing in land use disputes, potential property tax benefits, and protections from certain nuisance lawsuits.

For the North Carolina Composting Council, the law is both a hard-won policy victory and a springboard for future industry growth.

“Now that permitted Type 1, 2, and 3 composting facilities are recognized as agriculture under North Carolina law, the industry is better positioned to grow,” said Kat Polk, Executive Director of the North Carolina Composting Council (NCCC). “This designation can help reduce some of the financial and regulatory barriers to starting or expanding a composting operation while also strengthening confidence in compost use as an agricultural product.”

From Waste Diversion Goal to Infrastructure Need

The policy arrives as North Carolina faces increasing pressure on its remaining landfill capacity. The North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality’s (NCDEQ) 2025 Waste Characterization Study found that 30% of material being sent to landfills could have been composted instead.

That finding helped advocates frame composting as both a waste management solution and an agricultural opportunity. In June 2026, at the invitation of Representative Jimmy Dixon of Duplin County, the NCCC’s Advocacy and Access Committee presented directly to the North Carolina House Committee on Agriculture and Environment. However, legal recognition alone will not create the processing capacity needed to divert that material.

“To scale fast enough to make a meaningful dent in the organic waste gap, the industry needs access to start-up and expansion capital, as well as continued development of end markets to ensure sustained demand for the finished product,” Polk said.

NCDEQ offers annual grants that can help private companies and municipalities offset the cost of composting infrastructure. Polk said those programs are valuable, but public grants will not be enough to build the industry at the scale the state needs.

“Local banks and investors also need to recognize the value of composting in order to provide the low-interest loans needed to help companies get started and scale up,” she said.

Just as important is demand for the finished compost. Polk pointed to significant untapped opportunities in agriculture, transportation projects, green infrastructure, landscaping, and new development. State and local policies could help expand those markets through procurement requirements or specifications that encourage compost use.

“There need to be strong end-markets to close the economic loop and seal the deal for composters and investors to come into the business,” Polk said. “Either way, compost quality must remain consistently high in order for demand to grow.”

She added that trained operators will remain central to the industry’s success. “Skilled and dedicated composters who learn the trade and mentor others are at the heart of bridging the gap,” she said.

A Four-Year Legislative Strategy

The Farm Act provision did not emerge from a single legislative session. The NCCC’s Advocacy and Access Committee spent four years building relationships and advancing compost provisions through three consecutive Farm Acts.

In 2023, the Council helped secure a sales tax exemption on compost purchased by farmers. In 2024, Type 1 composting facilities were included under the state’s Right to Farm Act. The 2026 legislation went further by placing composting within the core statutory definition of agriculture.

“These relationships proved to be the foundation of our success,” Polk said. “We learned early on that identifying and cultivating legislative champions, particularly committee chairs and other key decision-makers who shape policy behind the scenes, was just as important as building broad support.”

She added that one lesson was that advocates should engage agricultural institutions early on, not only lawmakers.

“If we could do anything differently, we would have engaged other key stakeholders earlier in the process, including the Department of Agriculture, the Farm Bureau, and other agricultural partners,” she said.

Showing how composting supports agriculture, waste reduction, and economic development helped broaden the coalition and create a stronger foundation for lasting policy change. The Council also had to accept that progress would come incrementally. “There were times when we didn’t achieve everything we hoped for in a single legislative session, and we had to be willing to accept incremental progress rather than a perfect outcome,” Polk said. “Each Farm Act built on the last, and every step forward created new opportunities for the next.”

An Industry-Driven Effort

The legislative agenda was shaped by composting businesses, start-ups, experienced operators, and other industry leaders who were willing to explain their barriers directly to policymakers.

“These leaders are the same experts who have been willing and able to go to the North Carolina General Assembly to share their authentic experience in person,” Polk said. “These genuine connections, from communities that are well known by state lawmakers, have made the difference.”

The Council credited the outcome to collaboration among state legislators, NCDEQ, the Farm Bureau, industry partners, and composting advocates.

The strategy was deliberate, incremental, and built around relationships. North Carolina’s approach offers a replicable model for other states. By positioning composting within agricultural law rather than treating it solely as waste management, the state has created new pathways for legal protection, financing, infrastructure development, and market growth.

text:
SALT LAKE CITY (ABC4) — The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has announced the selection of Utah, among four other states, as potential sites for major nuclear development.

Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses, as the DOE calls them, are a part of an effort to modernize the nation’s full nuclear fuel cycle. The campuses will bring in “significant investment,” expanding domestic manufacturing and creating thousands of new high-paying jobs in their respective regions, the DOE said.

Utah is among Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana, and Idaho as potential host states. The energy department selected the five states after reviewing 28 applications from 26 states.

“Utah welcomes the chance to help America reclaim its leadership in civil nuclear energy,” said Gov. Spencer Cox. “We’re building the advanced technologies that will drive affordable, abundant power across our country. Through Operation Gigawatt, Utah is developing the entire nuclear lifecycle, from fuel production to advanced reactor deployment—strengthening our national security while helping secure America’s energy independence. This campus will accelerate that work.”

The department believes these nuclear sites will be massive generators of economic growth. Specifically they are engineered to support the full nuclear fuel lifecycle, meaning fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel, and final disposition of used nuclear fuel.

Depending on state priorities and capabilities, the campuses may also host advanced reactor deployment, power generation, advanced manufacturing, and co-located data centers.

The energy department said the campuses have the potential to attract up to $50 billion in capital investment and generate as much as $10 billion in state and local tax revenue. Additionally, each campus could create nearly 25,000 jobs.

name: North Carolina American Energy
title: Where Do We Go From Here, Part 2 - Southern Alliance for Clean Energy (SACE)
description:
We have never gone on an electric road trip of this length or in such remote conditions.
My wife and I have been driving EVs for over a decade, so we feel up for the challenge.
You could look at an EV as slowing down the road trip, but I see it as deepening it.
Already, the road trip is generating its own momentum and accumulating the weight of its expectations.
It’s a long road ahead.
text:
This article is Part Two of a three-part series about my 5,000-mile sabbatical road trip in an EV from my home in the southern Appalachians to the island of Newfoundland, and my reflections on what it means to be citizens and climate advocates as the planet overheats. Part One can be found here.

The EV is packed. The route is set. We run through the final checklist. All boxes checked. We pull down our driveway and head north, ironically, into a heatwave toasting the east coast that is so severe, prolonged, and far-reaching that researchers have concluded it is “virtually impossible” that it could have occurred before humans began warming the planet.

My wife and I have been planning this six-week sabbatical road trip for a year, researching where we will go and how we will get there, leaving just enough to chance to maintain the element of surprise. As the tires start to turn down the highway, we are giddy with anticipation of the adventure ahead; it has been 30 years since either of us last took a road trip as sprawling as this one. We are headed to Canada’s Maritime provinces and the island of Newfoundland, 2,500 miles away, to camp amidst the splendor of national parks — Fundy, Cape Brenton Highlands, Kejimkujik, Terra Nova, Gros Morne — and explore remote and culturally rich towns like Chéticamp, St. John’s, Cow Head, Wolfville, and Annapolis Royal. We are raring to smell and taste the North Atlantic; to walk through boreal forests, over taiga highlands, and into deep fjords; to listen to Acadian sea shanties sung in old, wood-clad pubs.

This sabbatical trip will give me the experience of driving an EV for 40 days and 5,000 miles beginning on US highways and ending in the Canadian sticks. We have never gone on an electric road trip of this length or in such remote conditions. We will be relying on a network of public charging infrastructure that, at times, will be sparse. My wife and I have been driving EVs for over a decade, so we feel up for the challenge. As an advocate for the rapid electrification of our nation’s transportation system, I need to test the technology’s limitations and demonstrate its viability; I need to know what I am selling.

The trip will also put distance between me and the daily reminders of Hurricane Helene — eroded riverbanks, fallen forests, broken bridges, closed trails, condemned buildings — and give me room to sort through what a climate-induced disaster does to a person. I grew up trusting the planet to be stable. I knew, from the textbooks, that humanity’s flourishing had ridden on millennia of climate stability. I assumed that stability would hold for at least my lifetime. Hurricane Helene proved that assumption wrong.

The storm left me disquieted and vulnerable; angry at the politicians who sell us out to the polluters cooking the planet; sad about climate change’s human costs, whether from the floods in Texas, the fires in Los Angeles, or the storm in my own backyard; bitter about the plants and animals losing ground they can’t get back; and frustrated that solar, wind, energy storage, and EVs — the tools sitting right in front of us — aren’t being deployed fast enough to bend the curve. I packed these feelings into the car along with the tent, the food, the clothes, and the maps. They take up just as much room as anything else we’re bringing.

Driving Away

As we head north out of Western North Carolina and climb the steep igneous and sedimentary spine of the Blue Ridge, the sunrise backlights the high peaks to the east, rays shooting into the valleys, basking the misty morning canopy in butterscotch. We climb two thousand feet, crest over Sam’s Gap, and descend into Tennessee and the scoured Nolichucky River valley where floodwaters from Hurricane Helene surrounded the Unicoi County hospital and, in a daring helicopter rescue, 54 employees and patients were airlifted from the roof to safety. The six workers who died at the Impact Plastics factory further downstream were not so lucky. A pit opens in my stomach. Helene is riding our bumper like a tailgater.

Two and a half hours into the drive, we stop in Wytheville, Virginia, to charge the EV, which is down to 10% capacity. We get out and plug in. The charger makes its whirling sound as it pushes 250 kW of power into our hungry battery. The landscape has subtly changed. We’ve entered the rugged sandstone-and-shale ridges and rolling valleys of the Allegheny Range. A patchwork of green pastures and rows of knee-high corn fields unfolds in all directions. Lush hardwood trees meander like ribbons tracing the creeks. The smell of fresh-cut hay and dank cow dung wafts as the morning dew evaporates. The sun is still gentle on the skin, but you can tell the day will be a scorcher.

After twelve minutes of charging, we get back on the road, battery charged to 70%, bathroom visited, body stretched. We climb the ridge to the Continental Divide. We descend the other side and leave the last of the waterways that drain from the high North Carolina peaks where Hurricane Helene dumped feet of rain. We weave through a tight, forested gorge, and emerge into the Roanoke River Basin. Long north-south-running ridgelines emerge above the wide, silo-studded Shenandoah Valley, and the telltale signs of disaster vanish; green mosses still cover the river rocks, bridges and roads show no signs of washouts, and buildings still stand at the edge of the floodplain. We are 200 miles from home, and finally, the storm is in the rearview mirror.

The Electric Journey

Driving our EV on this road trip will require us to charge our battery dozens of times, sometimes plugging into fast chargers along the highway like in Wytheville, and sometimes plugging into a wall outlet outside a quaint ocean-side inn overnight while we sleep. The fact that we need to charge means we have to look much more intently at the road ahead. If we were driving a gas car, we wouldn’t even think about it; we would just stop for gas at the nearest gas station whenever we needed to. But with an EV, even before we leave home, we know where we must stop to charge to reach our destination. There will be charging stops at breweries serving award-winning IPAs, at trailheads where we will hike to waterfalls, at visitor centers with exhibits we will wander through, and at towns off the beaten path that we would not otherwise have discovered. You could look at an EV as slowing down the road trip, but I see it as deepening it.

What I love most about driving an EV is that it emits up to 80% less climate pollution over its lifetime than a gas car. Heck, when we get to Newfoundland, where 97% of the electricity is generated by hydropower, we will be driving on water. Whereas electricity can be clean, oil is always dirty. An EV is a way to clean up at least some of my conflicted climate complicity. I love to travel to exotic places by plane, which creates a lot of emissions. I eat meat, and although I try to eat local, my diet adds more emissions. I have an energy-efficient home with a little plug-in solar system in the backyard, but that’s not enough. I grow a garden, which doesn’t amount to a climate hill of beans. I am part of the problem. We all are. And while we should take stock and work to minimize our individual impacts, the blame for the climate predicament does not lie at our feet.

The Problem Is Bigger Than Us

We are living in an economic system that gives us few options: electric utilities keep burning fossil fuels instead of fully embracing renewable energy; automakers keep sending gas-burning cars to showrooms instead of doubling down on EVs; airlines keep burning refined kerosene instead of demanding biofuels; industrial agriculture keeps mechanizing and chemicalizing our food system; oil companies keep drilling for more fossil swamp goo. Technology innovation drives industry, but industry also gets the technological innovations it asks for. Our climate impact is the output of our personal choices multiplied by far weightier political and corporate decisions. We can’t fix this problem person by person; we need system-level change to address the systemic challenge of climate change.

Despite our individual limitations, I have always felt motivated to do my part. My motivation stems from my childhood: I grew up in Guilford, Connecticut, near the shores of Long Island Sound, on a landscape of rocks long ago dumped by retreating glaciers. When I was a child, I ran wild through the woods. I played on and around the thousands of boulders sitting stoically in the forests, or stacked into piles, creating fissure caves and their Fat Man Squeezes. I leaped over the hundreds of miles of rock walls laid by pioneers after they’d plowed the stony ground. I asked the adults, “Where did all these stones and boulders come from?” Most didn’t know, but some did, and they would say, “Canada.” They would tell the story of the last ice age and the mile-high ice sheet that scraped across Canada and northern New England, stopping where I stood and dumping plowed earth. My imagination was sparked; I would stand at the edge of my yard, look back at my family’s 1970s ranch-style house, and imagine the glaciers moving towards me like a giant snowplow coming to dump rocks and boulders on our doorstep. The thought made me shiver; if I were alive then, the Earth would have killed me. But that awareness also gave me comfort; the ice age was long ago; I am safe now.

Reckoning With The Tensions

The long drive through Virginia tightens the back and cramps the legs. Morning gives way to afternoon by the time we arrive in Martinsburg, West Virginia, and we’re ready for a break. We stop to charge the EV at a Sheetz convenience store before crossing the Potomac River into Maryland. I step out of the car and am awash in hot air rising off the asphalt parking lot and the acrid smell of the upwind gasoline vapors from the dozen pumps in use. We are the only EV plugged in at the eight chargers. I wonder when this will flip — when the gas pumps sit idle and the chargers are overwhelmed with demand. Someday.

We get back on the highway, and I zoom out the map display on the car’s screen to see the full stretch of highway between here and Canada; 200 miles more to go today, another 400 tomorrow, and 320 the next. Are we crazy? I zoom out further to see the 2,000 miles beyond that, through Canada, still to come. Are we really driving to Newfoundland? Is this going to work in an EV?

I stop focusing on the distant bucolic scenery and hone in on the detritus at the edge of the highway, which has been there all along, but ignored. The towering billboard ahead reads, “Unleaded $3.66, Diesel $4.80,” in bright green and red LEDs. The next one welcomes truckers with hot showers. The next promises to turn your wreckage into a windfall: “I’ll fight for you!” On another, a cartoon beaver tells me, “You can hold it, only 177 miles!”

My grip on the wheel tightens. Driving the highway doesn’t feel like a choice anymore. I feel the other end of the journey reaching back in time and yanking us forward. We chose to take this trip, mapped it out, made the reservations, carved out the time, but I can feel inertia creeping in. Already, the road trip is generating its own momentum and accumulating the weight of its expectations. I push down on the pedal. It feels like there is no turning back, like when I was a little boy standing on the edge of a pool, slowly leaning ever more forward until gravity took hold and plunged me in.

At the same time, I feel the tension between me as a person making individual choices, and as a consumer strapped into an economy that, like this highway, is built to keep us moving and burning fossil fuels. The problem is if America keeps traveling down its current energy path, by 2050, climate-polluting fossil fuels will account for 77% of energy production and renewables only 22%. That won’t work: the world’s climate scientists agree that avoiding catastrophic warming means slashing fossil fuel use and getting almost all our electricity from renewables by 2050. That’s our conundrum: will we make new choices, or will we let the inertia of the systems and structures we have built over the past 250 years propel us into an ever warmer world?

I think again of the boulders in the woods of my childhood. The visceral awareness that the Earth’s climate has been violently different in the past hones my awareness and deepens my perception of what we are messing with. The climate’s remarkable stability over the past 12,000 years is what has allowed our species to thrive. Sure, there have been moments of chaos; winters that lasted for years, volcanoes that covered the planet in soot, earthquakes that swallowed cities. But at the macro level, there has been balance. Today, there is increasing chaos. And what I know from growing up amidst the boulders of the last ice age is that the Earth’s climatic system sustains life, and it takes it away.

Maybe part of the answer to where we go from here is to start claiming our agency, to start owning the fact that climate change results from choices we make as consumers, and more impactfully as voters who continue to elect leaders unwilling to lead on climate. We can make different choices. We can elect different leaders. We can pump the brakes, take the exit ramp, and leave our fossil-fuel past behind. Or maybe the inertia is too strong.

As I sit with my own tension between agency and inertia, I also wonder how the Canadians we will meet are reckoning with theirs, how they are experiencing and adapting to climate change, and where they hope we go from here. Before I can find out, my wife and I have to ride America’s highways along the East Coast’s Appalachian chain, traversing Pennsylvania’s Pocono Mountains before crossing New York’s Taconic range, following Connecticut’s Litchfield Hills, and into Massachusetts’ Berkshires and Maine’s coastal Longfellow Mountains. It’s a long road ahead.

Stay tuned for Part 3.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy has left South Carolina off a list of finalists for a multi-billion dollar nuclear campus that officials had sought as part of their efforts to revive and expand the state’s nuclear capabilities.

Five other states – Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Idaho – were announced as potential host states for nuclear lifecycle campuses. These campuses would be developed to strengthen and modernize the country’s nuclear fuel cycle, according to a DOE news release Tuesday, July 28.

South Carolina was among 26 states that had sought consideration for nuclear campuses. Not making the list is a blow to those who said a nuclear lifecycle campus could produce thousands of jobs and result in billions of dollars in investment in South Carolina.

The DOE release did not say what factors left South Carolina and other states out, but one lawmaker said it may have been the state’s opposition to taking nuclear waste from other places as part of the campus plan.

In addition to focusing on developing facilities to support making nuclear fuel, as well as enrichment, the campuses would support reprocessing used fuel and potentially be sites for nuclear waste disposal.

The State reported last week that South Carolina’s proposal for a life cycle campus included support for “boreholes,’’ deep cuts in the ground where high level radioactive waste could be stored. The state Commerce Department submitted the proposal. But the state Senate has passed legislation against taking the nation’s nuclear waste.

“There was no interest in South Carolina opening itself up or being the receptacle for nuclear waste outside of its existing legal obligations,’’ state Sen. Tom Davis said, recalling his discussions with the Commerce Department about taking atomic refuse.

Politico reported this week that President Donald Trump is seeking changes in the law that would make it easier for states to become repositories for nuclear waste. Plans are underway to revamp the classification of nuclear waste to provide more flexibility, Politico reported, basing its story on a government document obtained by its journalists.

Spokespeople for the Commerce Department and Gov. Henry McMaster were not available.

The federal government has been searching for years for a permanent solution to high level waste disposal. The material, the byproduct of making nuclear power and atomic weapons, contains deadly contaminants that can linger in the environment for thousands of years.

Former President Barack Obama shut down a planned high-level nuclear waste burial ground in Nevada more than 15 years ago as environmental concerns in that state mounted. Since then, atomic waste that was supposed to be disposed of in Nevada’s Yucca Mountain has been building up at nuclear power plants across the country. Waste from weapons complexes like South Carolina’s Savannah River Site also was to go to Yucca Mountain.

Tom Clements, a critic of nuclear weapons and atomic energy, said last week South Carolina could have become a dumping ground for the nation’s high-level atomic garbage if the boreholes disposal concept went through.

“That was the implication,’’ Clements said Tuesday of the Commerce Department plan. “They didn’t say we’ll deal only with our own state’s waste. They left it open-ended.’’

The South Carolina nuclear campus would presumably have been at the Savannah River Site, a 310-square mile atomic weapons production facility near Aiken.

Aside from the waste issue, landing a nuclear lifecycle campus in South Carolina was projected to be an economic boon for the state.

“These campuses will be massive generators of economic growth, create thousands of high-paying jobs, and be crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance,’’ Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in Tuesday’s news release. “The innovative concept is a direct result of President Trump’s leadership and ambitious directives to restore the domestic nuclear fuel cycle and get America’s nuclear industry growing again.”

In South Carolina, the Department of Commerce said a nuclear innovation campus could contribute to $60 billion in private investment and 15,000 direct jobs for South Carolina.

The department said little to explain why it had included the support for boreholes in its nuclear campus plan when there is ample opposition in the state for importing waste.

South Carolina was once a repository for a variety of noxious and toxic waste, with a low-level nuclear waste dump, a hazardous landfill, a medical waste incinerator and multiple “mega’’ garbage dumps.

Officials in the five states chosen as contenders for nuclear lifecycle campuses were ecstatic Tuesday over their selection by the Department of Energy. Those states signed memorandums of understanding with the DOE to continue exploring a chance to have a campus, the news release said.

“As the global epicenter of nuclear energy, Tennessee is honored to be selected as a potential host for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus,” Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said in the news release. “As our state answered the call during the Manhattan Project and helped shape the course of history, Tennessee stands ready once again to advance the safe, reliable energy solutions our nation depends on.’’

title: Australia built the receiver for a solar tower running on liquid sodium, a metal liquid from 208 ...
description:
Every commercial solar tower built so far moves its heat with steam or molten salt.
Solar salt, the sodium and potassium nitrate blend the tower industry standardized on, sets solid at around 430 degrees.
Every pipe, valve and tank in a salt plant has to be kept warm so the working fluid never turns into a plug.
Sodium is also a far better conductor of heat than salt, and that is the property Vast built its whole machine around.
That is the trade the solar tower business keeps losing.
text:
Solar panels have gotten cheap enough that making electricity is no longer the hard part. Making it at 9pm is. That gap is the only reason anyone still builds the other kind of solar plant, the one with a field of mirrors aimed at a tower, because heat sits in a tank overnight far more happily than electrons sit in a battery.

Australia had a bet running on that idea, and it was an odd one. Every commercial solar tower built so far moves its heat with steam or molten salt. Vast Solar’s VS1, a 30-megawatt plant planned for a stretch of scrub north of Port Augusta, South Australia, was designed around liquid sodium instead.

The receiver got built. The engineering got finished. The federal government committed up to A$180 million, which is roughly US$118 million and, for the record, every dollar figure below is Australian. Not one mirror went into the ground.

On November 13, 2025, KPMG partners Peter Gothard and Amanda Coneyworth were appointed voluntary administrators of Vast Renewables Limited and ten Australian subsidiaries, including the company set up to own VS1. What the administrators have proposed since then ends somewhere failed energy startups almost never end: with the government taking the patents.

Liquid metal was the entire point

Sodium melts at about 208 degrees Fahrenheit and stays liquid all the way up to 1,621. Solar salt, the sodium and potassium nitrate blend the tower industry standardized on, sets solid at around 430 degrees. Every pipe, valve and tank in a salt plant has to be kept warm so the working fluid never turns into a plug.

Sodium is also a far better conductor of heat than salt, and that is the property Vast built its whole machine around. It is not a free lunch. Sodium reacts hard with water and with air, so a sodium plant is a plumbing problem before it is anything else, and Vast’s own engineering documentation describes sloped piping runs designed so that more than 1,600 feet of sodium line could be drained.

VS1 was never going to be one big tower. The design called for eight modular arrays, each with its own mirror field, its own receiver and its own controls, all feeding a shared insulated header. Concentrated sunlight heated sodium at the receivers, a heat exchanger handed that heat over to molten salt, and the salt sat in tanks rated at 288 megawatt-hours feeding a steam generator and a 30-megawatt turbine.

Mirrors that steer sunlight onto a single point are not new, and at small scale they do genuinely absurd things. The 57-year-old solar furnace in the French Pyrenees concentrates a full megawatt of sunlight onto a spot the size of a dinner plate. The engineering problem has never been collecting the heat. It has been moving it, storing it, and doing that for thirty years without the plant eating itself.

The pilot that got Vast this far was small: 3,500 mirrors in five arrays around 88-foot towers at Jemalong, near Forbes in New South Wales, good for 1.1 megawatts. It ran for 32 months and won the International Energy Agency’s SolarPACES innovation award in 2019.

The receiver for the real thing was designed and built in Goodna, a suburb of Brisbane, and finished in February 2025. It is still there. The administrators’ February 2026 report says they stopped running the business after December’s creditors meeting, except for keeping up the leased Goodna premises, which hold plant and equipment tied to the group’s intellectual property.

The same ground already lost a much bigger tower

Port Augusta has done this before, at larger scale and with a louder ending.

In 2017 the South Australian government signed a 20-year supply deal with American developer SolarReserve at A$78 a megawatt-hour, for a 150-megawatt tower with 1,100 megawatt-hours of molten salt storage north of the city. The project was costed at around A$650 million and carried a A$110 million federal concessional loan, negotiated that year as part of a deal with independent senator Nick Xenophon.

SolarReserve got development approval in January 2019. On April 5 of that year, then state energy minister Dan van Holst Pellekaan announced the project was over, because the company could not reach financial close. Adelaide firm 1414 Degrees bought the site later that year for about A$2 million.

Here is the part that ties the two failures together. That A$110 million concessional loan did not die with SolarReserve. It was recommitted in 2022 for Vast’s much smaller plant on the same ground, and it was still sitting there unspent when ARENA topped the package up in March 2025 with up to A$180 million in grant funding, replacing an earlier A$65 million commitment.

Two companies, two technologies, one paddock, one pot of federal money, nothing built. The grant was conditional anyway. Vast still had to raise the rest of the A$360 to A$390 million the plant was costed at, and it never did.

ARENA is the largest single creditor, and the proposal hands it the patents

The numbers in the administrators’ supplementary report of February 17, 2026 are blunt. Unsecured claims against the group came to A$58.4 million. ARENA, the federal agency that had backed the project since 2023, is owed A$24.5 million of that, more than 40 percent.

The deed of company arrangement put to creditors was proposed by Nabors Lux 2, the Luxembourg entity through which Houston-based drilling contractor Nabors Industries lent money to Vast. It puts A$100,000 of fresh cash on the table, half from Nabors and half from Taloumbi Station Pastoral, a company the report links to two former directors and officers, Alec Waugh and Craig Wood.

The mechanism that makes it work for everybody else is subtraction. ARENA and Nabors agreed not to take a cent out of the deed fund, which drops the pool of participating claims from A$58.4 million to A$30.6 million and lifts the estimated return for remaining unsecured creditors to somewhere between 3.2 and 4.2 cents in the dollar. Straight liquidation was estimated at 1.6 to 2.9 cents. Employee entitlements, about A$2.1 million of them, were expected to be paid in full either way.

In exchange, the intellectual property goes to ARENA or an entity ARENA nominates. The report gives the reason in a single line, saying the transfer is meant “to maximise the chances of its commercialisation in Australia.”

The administrators were straight about the trade-off. Signing the deed means creditors give up any claim on recoveries a liquidator might have chased, including any possible insolvent trading action against directors. No such claim has been made and the report does not allege one.

A second sales process had already run, reopened on December 22 with binding bids due January 14. Indicative offers came in for the intellectual property, for some plant and equipment, and for Vast’s 50 percent share of the joint venture that holds the land. None of them turned into a binding bid, and the administrators put a value of A$260,000 on the joint venture shares.

Creditors were due to vote on February 25, 2026. The outcome has not been announced publicly, and the most recent document on KPMG’s creditor page for the group is still that February 17 report.

The mirrors never came. A data center operator did

The land itself is doing fine, which is the strangest part of all this.

The Aurora precinct is held by SiliconAurora, a joint venture between 1414 Degrees and the Vast subsidiary now in administration. In January 2026 the 140-megawatt, 280-megawatt-hour battery approved for the site cleared the Australian Energy Market Operator’s generator performance standards, the last technical gate before transmission negotiations.

Then on July 27, 1414 Degrees told the market it had signed a heads of agreement with an unnamed Australian data center operator to build up to a gigawatt of AI computing capacity there. The operator gets exclusivity over an initial 40-hectare parcel, just under 100 acres, inside a landholding of 15.8 square kilometers, about six square miles.

The staging is modest at the front and enormous at the back. A 17-megawatt starter campus on an existing 33-kilovolt connection, a 200-megawatt anchor campus once the 275-kilovolt line is hooked up, then a longer path to a full gigawatt as generation gets built out. 1414 Degrees brings the land, the power and the fiber. The partner brings the money and knows how to run the racks.

It is a heads of agreement, not a contract. Definitive terms covering land access, behind-the-meter power, storage, grid connection and precinct services all still have to be negotiated, and the company said as much in its own announcement.

Put the two storage numbers on that site side by side and the whole shift is right there. VS1’s salt tanks were rated at 288 megawatt-hours, roughly nine and a half hours of output. The lithium battery that actually cleared its approvals is rated at 280 megawatt-hours, eight less, delivered in two.

That is the trade the solar tower business keeps losing. Longer storage on paper, for a plant nobody will finance. Shorter storage on the grid, for a plant a bank already understands. Tower advocates argue the technology gives you something batteries do not, a real spinning turbine holding the grid’s frequency steady, which is the same job Australia now pays for with 300-ton machines built to spin in place and generate nothing at all.

The counterargument is sitting in California, where a $2.2 billion tower plant that opened in 2014 now spends its time being talked about by regulators rather than by engineers.

The receiver in Goodna is the piece anyone would actually want. Under the proposal it goes, along with the patents behind it, to the agency that helped pay for it, which beats a scrap merchant and falls a long way short of a working power station. Two companies have now tried to put a tower on that ground, and both got stuck at exactly the same step, the one where somebody has to sign the check.

text:
WASHINGTON — Last week, U.S. Sens. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) and Chris Coons (D-Del.) introduced the Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology (FIRST) Act to codify the U.S. State Department’s FIRST program advocating for the responsible deployment of civil nuclear energy around the world.

The bipartisan bill would ensure that U.S. economic and national security interests are prioritized as we advance our nuclear industry and continue supporting the partnerships American companies have with other countries working to expand their nuclear energy programs.

“The responsible development of civil nuclear energy, on an international scale, contributes to U.S. national security and bolsters our economy,” Budd said. “The FIRST program has been a productive way for our nation to partner with good-faith actors who are building their nuclear arsenals, and continuing to leverage these public and private partnerships will help us advance our own energy dominance. Since North Carolina is a leader in next-generation nuclear technology, I am proud to partner with Senator Coons to bring this bipartisan solution forward and codify this program that will expand markets for our great innovators into law,” said Senator Budd.

Launched in 2019, the State Department’s FIRST program is a multiagency initiative that leverages public-private partnerships to strengthen U.S. leadership in civil nuclear energy. Through engagement with more than 50 partner countries seeking to deploy advanced nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors (SMRs), the program supports the development of civilian nuclear power programs that adhere to the highest international standards for nuclear security, safety, and nonproliferation.

Budd chairs hearing to examine U.S. competition with China in science and technology

Last week, Budd chaired a hearing in the Senate Subcommittee on Science, Manufacturing, and Competitiveness yesterday entitled Measuring What Matters: Science, Standards, and Strategic Competition to discuss how the U.S. can more strategically align our scientific research, federal science agencies and assets, and the private sector to compete with China.

In his opening statement, Senator Budd emphasized three priorities to pave the way for stronger American competition: prioritizing outcome-based metrics, streamlining our world-class science agencies, and identifying Chinese intellectual property theft undermining our national security.

“First, we need to better prioritize outcome-based metrics as a gauge of impact and competitiveness,” Budd said. “Influencing international standards, leading in high-impact research and measuring technology adoption and diffusion are paramount. Additionally, evaluating the strength of public-private partnerships and instances of industry funding university research could signal which lines of applied research are most valuable and making the greatest impact.

“Second, this committee should look at ways to streamline, focus, and improve agencies under its jurisdiction, like the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the National Science Foundation. Dr. Copan, during your time as NIST Director, you authored an important 3 white paper titled, ‘Return on Investment Initiative for Unleashing American Innovation,’ which recommended improving tech transfer, strengthening R&D partnerships with the private sector, and improving access to federal R&D assets for businesses.

“Given (China’s) significant focus on standards development, I look forward to discussing ways in which NIST’s world-class talent in metrology can be better targeted to enhance U.S. competitiveness in emerging technologies.

“Finally, this committee should look carefully at Chinese scientific and intellectual property theft, which significantly undermines American economic dominance and national security. I firmly believe that the U.S. is well positioned to continue to lead the world in the amazing discoveries and breakthroughs that inspire countless young men and women to engage in science and build the technologies and companies that shape the future.”

text:
Emily Tench, MBA ’25, built her career launching clean energy projects, but she was repeatedly surprised and frustrated by how often they failed to take off.

As a consultant at Geneva-based Dalberg Advisors and Sustainable Ventures, advising on over $100 million of energy transition and infrastructure projects, Tench witnessed a common pattern: Communities wanted energy solutions, investors wanted to fund them, and developers wanted to build them. Yet despite these tailwinds, many projects never materialized.

The disconnect fascinated Tench: “I wanted to understand why it was so hard to turn good ideas into real infrastructure,” she says.

With support from the Stanford Impact Founder (SIF) Fellowship program, Tench has spent the year since graduation from Stanford GSB working on this problem. Her solution was to create PermitPal, a company that uses artificial intelligence to help infrastructure project developers and investors identify development risks earlier and navigate permitting and political challenges.

“We’re building an AI partner for the people developing and financing infrastructure,” says Tench. “The earlier you understand risk, the more likely you are to get good projects built.”

A Global Perspective

Tench brings a global perspective to the problem. At Dalberg, she led projects in more than 10 countries across Europe, North America, Africa, and Asia. Her work spanned clean energy, nature-based solutions, and infrastructure development.

While the details differed across regions, the narrative was the same. Local communities worldwide were eager to take action on climate change, she says, based on her interactions on the ground. “I remember walking in the Seychelles, bleached corals crunching under my feet, and hearing our guide speak about his community’s concerns about the future. It was a similar refrain from farmers in Cambodia and in Madagascar.”

Tench emerged from this work convinced that accelerating the deployment of climate and infrastructure projects could benefit communities worldwide.

The Path to PermitPal

Tench arrived at Stanford GSB thinking about what role she could play in accelerating climate and infrastructure projects. She had already started several companies before arriving at Stanford — including one at age 18, for which she was awarded Oxford University’s Social Enterprise Award.

While pursuing her MBA alongside a master’s in public policy at Harvard Kennedy School, Tench explored a range of climate venture ideas, including through Stanford Climate Ventures and LaunchPad. During this time, she teamed up with Camila Nicollier, who was pursuing her master’s degree in statistics and data science at Stanford and eventually became PermitPal’s AI and data lead.

Tench and Nicollier set out to identify the primary barrier for energy infrastructure projects. Through hundreds of interviews with project developers, they found that permitting was a manual process, often conducted with incomplete information.

In the U.S. alone, 43,000 different local jurisdictions oversee new projects. Elected officials constantly change, and community sentiment is dynamic. As a result, tens of billions of dollars for renewable energyopen in new window and storage have been canceled in recent years. More than 90% of clean energy developers cited permitting as a cause of project delays or cancellations, according to a recent Crux surveyopen in new window.

As a result of their research, Tench and Nicollier focused on tackling permitting, with AI underpinning platform operations. PermitPal’s first product, Clara, is an AI permitting consultant that analyzes more than a million scattered government documents each month related to zoning, planning, and infrastructure. By trawling through official records, Clara uncovers what local watchdogs or lawmakers have said about, say, solar power, or how related projects have fared in the past. Beyond unearthing policies and hard data, the service supports developers to listen to the needs of local residents and decision-makers.

The SIF Fellowship: A Lifeline for PermitPal

Tench was awarded the SIF Fellowship to work on PermitPal in the year following graduation. She and Nicollier also received a TomKat Grantopen in new window to support their work.

After running pilots through early 2026 and launching officially in March, PermitPal has already increased its monthly revenue tenfold. It now provides geographic coverage for every state, county, and township in the U.S. and has helped to de-risk $100 million in project capital for developers and investors.

But PermitPal’s path has not been without obstacles. When Tench graduated, changing renewable energy policies presented headwinds to new renewable deployments in the U.S. The SIF Fellowship was critical, providing the financial and tactical support Tench needed to stick to PermitPal’s vision.

“For us at that moment, SIF was a lifeline for the company,” Tench said. “It gave us the ability to stay with the renewables sector during a time that was quite challenging for the industry.”Fellowship support helped Tench troubleshoot early startup issues and build new skills, such as in sales. It also helped smooth out the roller coaster of entrepreneurship by connecting Tench with a peer community.

Building the Operating System for Infrastructure Development

With a year of experience under her belt, Tench now sees permitting as only the first chapter. Her vision is for PermitPal to become the intelligence layer that supports every stage of infrastructure development.

Bringing a major infrastructure project to life requires dozens of specialists, from permitting consultants and environmental advisors to land agents, lawyers, engineers, and financial analysts. Critical decisions are spread across disconnected software, spreadsheets, and millions of fragmented documents.

“We think infrastructure development is one of the last trillion-dollar industries that is still largely manual — and for good reason,” Tench says. “Unlike consumer applications, where occasional mistakes are acceptable, project development decisions involve millions of dollars in capital and years of development. A single incorrect answer can derail an entire project.”

Moving beyond Clara, customers have already begun asking PermitPal to solve adjacent problems, from screening acquisition data rooms to identifying promising sites before land is purchased. For Tench, the opportunity is transforming how the world plans and delivers the infrastructure it needs, more quickly and in closer partnership with the communities it serves.

As the company scales, Tench says she wants growth to remain tied to projects she and Nicollier believe in. She also wants the projects to match the needs of the communities where they’re sited.“We want to try and prove that there’s a different way of doing business — that you can be a hugely financially successful company but also do it in a way that is good to people and good to the world,” Tench says.

Ford has inked a deal with Geely to secure the future of its Spanish factory by announcing the pair will work together to create a Ford-branded SUV and two all-electric Geely SUVs.

As part of the joint venture, Ford will own 66 per cent of the new company, with China’s Geely Auto owning the final 34 per cent share, and the first vehicle will roll out of its plant in Valencia as soon as 2028.

To cope with the new models, production at Ford’s European facility will ramp up to its maximum 500,000 capacity, with four vehicles set to join the existing Kuga SUV that’s made there now.

READ MORE: Ford’s Super Mustang Mach-E the only EV running at Pikes Peak Hill Climb. Guess who won?

READ MORE: First details of next Ford Puma EV revealed: Compact electric SUV is gonna be a Renault 4 under the skin

READ MORE: Ford Bronco right-hand drive confirmed: It will be electrified, but will it come to Australia?

As previously revealed, the first Ford to be created in partnership will be a European take on the Bronco already on sale in the US.

Early reports suggest the new SUV will be based on the same upgraded C2 platform that currently underpins the Kuga and has been in use since 2018.

Alongside the Euro Bronco will be another “multi-energy Ford family crossover” that is also scheduled for 2028, which will introduce a “rally-bred crossover in the C-segment”, the Blue Oval says.

Insiders have already ruled out any badge-engineered models as part of the new collaboration with the Chinese car-maker, with the Ford vehicles set to feature completely unique bodies.

The new Bronco and second SUV are two of five new “rally-inspired” models that the US car-maker has confirmed it will introduce by 2029 as part of plans to revive its fortunes in Europe.

Two small SUVs will also be among the mix and will be produced by Renault as part of another joint venture.

It’s unknown where the fifth model will come from, but it’s almost certain it will be built outside Valencia.

Geely was attracted to the new partnership as it will help it build two all-electric SUVs at Valencia that won’t be subject to any of the hefty tariffs levied on Chinese-built cars.

Ford said the new partnership would help leverage scale.

Commenting on the new deal, Ford Europe boss Jim Baumbick said: “The battle we’re in and the environment in Europe has changed forever. It’s at a new level of cost. What we’re trying to do is ensure that we can actually demonstrate the lowest possible cost while building products specifically in Europe for European customers.

“It’s no different than what the Geely team is trying to do is to get costs that they see in China actually in Europe, and collectively we’re taking choices that are congruent with made-in-Europe.”

text:
The BMW Group is preparing to launch series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) batteries for electric vehicles – starting with high-voltage batteries for the all-electric BMW iX5, which will begin at its Woodruff plant this December. The facility is a cornerstone for the North American market and was built near the Spartanburg vehicle plant, where the iX5 will be manufactured, in line with the ‘Local for Local’ principle. From there, the vehicle will also be exported to Europe.

To achieve this, the carmaker has implemented cutting-edge processes. The new cylindrical cells in the 46120 format from battery cell manufacturer AESC are integrated directly into the battery pack using the ‘Cell-to-Pack’ method. All production steps are monitored seamlessly in real time. Specially developed AI assistants process data alongside more than 300 employees and 250 robots to ensure zero-defect production.

Even during the planning and ramp-up phases, BMW consistently relied on digital tools. Digital twins and virtual reality applications facilitated factory planning, while employees completed a specially developed VR training programme. This allowed them to practice real-world processes and equipment operations in a highly detailed virtual environment.

“Plant Woodruff plays a key role in the ramp-up of electromobility in the US,” said BMW Production Director Raymond Wittmann. “With our Gen6 high-voltage battery, we’re not only taking a major technological leap – we are also setting new standards in production. In Woodruff, we are combining cutting-edge processes, artificial intelligence and the expertise of our employees to create a production facility designed for the highest quality.”

Technologically, the system is based on an 800-volt architecture. The BMW iX5 60 xDrive offers a usable net energy content of 144kWh in the USA and 141kWh in Europe. In terms of sustainability, the Gen6 battery cell reduces CO₂e emissions by around 28 per cent compared to the previous generation. This reduction is achieved through the use of secondary materials for cobalt, lithium, and nickel, as well as green electricity in cell production. The Woodruff plant itself operates entirely without fossil fuels during normal operations, while its material handling equipment is powered by hydrogen.

The foundation for the project was laid in June 2023 with the groundbreaking ceremony for the Woodruff plant. Construction commenced in September 2023, followed by the installation of equipment in autumn 2024. Pre-series test runs began in summer 2025. The investments in Woodruff are part of a comprehensive US strategy, in which BMW invested approximately $1.7 billion in electromobility in the Spartanburg region, including partnerships with local cell suppliers such as AESC.

DOE’s direct final rule was designed to implement Executive Order 14270, “Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American Energy,” issued April 9, 2025.
[3] The proposed rule is, by DOE’s own description, substantively identical to the direct final rule: the NOPR’s summary states that it “proposes regulatory revisions identical to those set forth in a direct final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register.” DOE’s procedural and regulatory review analyses for the NOPR likewise mirror those conducted for the direct final rule, with the NOPR expressly incorporating the direct final rule’s analysis by reference.

text:
On July 9, 2026, the Department of Energy (DOE) withdrew its direct final rule that would have implemented, starting July 13, 2026, “zero-based regulating” sunset provisions across a range of DOE regulations. DOE did so after receiving adverse comments during the public comment period on the direct final rule, as it committed to do when it issued the rule on May 29, 2026. However, DOE issued the direct final rule alongside a companion notice of proposed rulemaking (NOPR) with the same goal, meaning that the DOE may still act to sunset the relevant regulations sometime in the future.

What is Zero-Based Regulating?

DOE’s direct final rule was designed to implement Executive Order 14270, “Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American Energy,” issued April 9, 2025. The executive order directed DOE, along with the Environmental Protection Agency, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, to insert “sunset provisions” into regulations issued under specified energy statutes. For DOE specifically, the order applies to regulations issued under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, the National Appliance Energy Conservation Act of 1987, the Energy Policy Act of 1992, the Energy Policy Act of 2005, and the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007.

“Zero-based regulating” is a system where each regulation must be affirmatively justified on a recurring basis rather than assumed to continue simply because it existed in a prior period. The executive order requires covered agencies to build a “Conditional Sunset Date” into each covered regulation, defined as the date on which the regulation will cease to be effective and be removed from the Code of Federal Regulations unless the issuing agency affirmatively extends it. Before allowing a regulation to expire, the agency must offer the public an opportunity to comment on the costs and benefits of the regulation, and it may extend the sunset date only after finding that an extension is warranted. The stated goal of this framework is to compel agencies to reexamine their regulations periodically, on the theory that some regulations otherwise persist for decades without renewed scrutiny and may, over time, become unnecessary, unduly burdensome, or contrary to policy.

DOE’s direct final rule would have amended 21 parts[1] in Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations affecting areas as varied as greenhouse gas reporting guidelines, access to DOE computers, contractor legal management, and the domestic uranium program, adding a sunset provision stating that each identified part would automatically expire one year from the rule’s effective date unless extended, rescinded, or otherwise addressed before that date.[2] The rule also would have added a new general sunset provision, codified at 10 C.F.R. part 1061, applicable to covered regulations more broadly, providing that DOE could extend a conditional sunset date by written determination of the Secretary of Energy for periods not exceeding five years, but that amendments to an existing regulation would not themselves extend its sunset date.

Virtually Identical Sunsetting Provisions in the NOPR

DOE elected to use the direct final rule procedure because it did not anticipate significant public comment and considered the action non-controversial, with an effective date of July 13, 2026. Consistent with that procedure, DOE provided a comment period running through June 29, 2026, and stated that if it received significant adverse comments by that date, it would publish a timely withdrawal and instead address the comments through a final rule responding to the companion NOPR published the same day.

DOE did, in fact, receive adverse comments on the direct final rule. Commenters raised concerns that the sunset process bypasses meaningful public input and fails to adequately assess whether the sunsets are consistent with underlying statutory mandates or serve the public interest. For example, one commenter argued that DOE’s rule offered little analysis or explanation for why the identified regulations should sunset, and that the proposed amendments would allow the targeted rules to expire automatically even if DOE failed to provide the promised future comment periods or to announce decisions on the regulations’ fate, rendering the rule arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

As a contingency, DOE published the NOPR on the same day.[3] The proposed rule is, by DOE’s own description, substantively identical to the direct final rule: the NOPR’s summary states that it “proposes regulatory revisions identical to those set forth in a direct final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register.” DOE’s procedural and regulatory review analyses for the NOPR likewise mirror those conducted for the direct final rule, with the NOPR expressly incorporating the direct final rule’s analysis by reference. DOE has confirmed it will respond to the timely comments on the direct final rule and the NOPR as part of any final action taken on the proposed rule.

Rulemaking Timeline and Next Steps

With the direct final rule now off the table, the proposed rule remains pending before DOE. The agency’s stated next step is to review and respond to the comments submitted by June 29, 2026, and to issue a final rule addressing those comments in connection with the proposed rulemaking. DOE has not announced a specific timeline for issuing that final rule. Given the adverse comments received, including arguments that the sunset framework lacks adequate reasoned explanation and risks automatic expiration of regulations without the promised comment opportunities, DOE’s final rule may include additional analysis of or modifications responsive to those concerns, or even an additional public notice period if significant modifications are made.

The Foley energy team will continue to track developments in this area and welcomes questions on these issues.

[1] For context, there are over 150 parts contained in Title 10. Chapter I alone has 54 active parts.

[2] See Pt 300, Voluntary Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program: General Guidelines; Pt 602, Epidemiology and Other Health Studies Financial Assistance Program; Pt 605, The Office of Science Financial Assistance Program; Pt 706, Security Policies and Practices Relating to Labor-Management Relations; Pt 708, DOE Contractor Employee Protection Program; Pt 719, Contractor Legal Management Requirements; Pt 727, Consent for Access to Information on Department of Energy Computers; Pt 733, Allegations of Research Misconduct; Pt 760, Domestic Uranium Program; Pt 766, Uranium Enrichment Decontamination and Decommissioning Fund; Procedures for Special Assessment of Domestic Utilities; Pt 782, Claims for Patent and Copyright Infringement; Pt 783, Waiver of Patent Rights; Pt 784, Patent Waiver Regulation; Pt 824, Procedural Rules for the Assessment of Civil Penalties for Classified Information Security Violations; Pt 840, Extraordinary Nuclear Occurrences; Pt 861, Control of Traffic at Nevada Test Site; Pt 950, Standby Support for Certain Nuclear Plant Delays; Pt 960, General Guidelines for the Preliminary Screening of Potential Sites for a Nuclear Waste Repository; Pt 963, Yucca Mountain Site Suitability Guidelines; Pt 1009, General Policy for Pricing and Charging for Materials and Services Sold by DOE; and Pt 1015, Collection of Claims Owed the United States. (All parts are in Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations.)
