title: With Texas' Data Center Boom, Uncertainty Is the Business Plan
description:
The usual worry about Texas’ data center boom is that the state is flying partly blind.
Data centers account for almost 90 percent, with cryptomining operations and industrial plants making up most of the rest.
Separate estimates put the capacity that data centers have actually connected and are drawing today at closer to 7.5 gigawatts.
Data center developers had filed roughly 30 gigawatts of interconnection requests with AEP Ohio.
The point is not that a data center is an oil well, or that the industry did anything wrong.
text:
The usual worry about Texas’ data center boom is that the state is flying partly blind. It does not yet know how much electricity these projects will actually need, how much water they will take, or whether the tax breaks offered in the name of growth will return enough to justify their cost.

That sounds, at first, like a paperwork problem: collect better numbers, build a better spreadsheet, close the gap, and the problem is solved. But the longer you sit with the missing information, the less accidental it looks. The uncertainty does not fall evenly. Again and again, it gives developers room to maneuver while leaving the public to plan around promises it cannot fully test.

Start with demand. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) has a queue of large-load requests, meaning any single site asking to draw more than 75 megawatts, that now totals roughly 439 gigawatts. Data centers account for almost 90 percent, with cryptomining operations and industrial plants making up most of the rest. For scale, the most electricity Texas has ever drawn at one time is 87,403 megawatts, set on July 21 of this year. The queue is more than five times that. Separate estimates put the capacity that data centers have actually connected and are drawing today at closer to 7.5 gigawatts.

For years the development queue cost little to join and bound no one to build, but that inflated total did real work by manufacturing a sense of inevitability that pressured the grid to build ahead of it. Texas has only just now begun closing that door, requiring large-load applicants to post real financial security and prove land control before a request counts. It’s a genuine fix, but it only touches one ledger.

Water is the project resource that Texas has always asked about but never tied to a real requirement, and it works the same way demand once did—only more brazenly. Data centers heavily consume water in order to cool servers and to run the plants that power them. When the state asked the industry to report how much it is using, fewer than a third of the companies queried responded. The Texas Water Development Board runs a separate, mandatory survey, yet only 17 percent of data centers answered in 2025 (despite the penalty for ignoring it being a Class C misdemeanor). Required or not, the number never arrives, and a figure the state never receives is one it cannot price, cap, or otherwise meaningfully regulate. That silence is less a gap in the record than a form of leverage. Vagueness here is not a hole in the industry’s case; it is the entire case.

The gas plants are hardest to hide, and yet developers still have a sanctioned way around scrutiny. Rather than wait in line, they increasingly build their own power on site—with some 38 gigawatts of it in development—and the same reform that now demands firm commitments from the grid queue leaves this exact path open. Those plants still need air permits, so the pollution does get counted. But a permit only measures what comes out of the stack. It never asks whether the data center it serves is real, or who covers the cost of the infrastructure if it never arrives. Those questions belong to the grid connection process, and a company that builds its own power never has to enter it. The smoke gets measured. The gamble does not.

The media coverage of the boom keeps arriving at this pattern and stopping short of naming it. Whatever any one company intends, the pattern is too consistent to pass for accident. The lever is not missing information. Sometimes the industry files far too much, like that padded queue of connection requests, and sometimes it files almost nothing, like the water usage survey. What runs through both is asymmetry: The developer usually knows more than the state and reveals only what suits the project. Call it what it is: a system that rewards whoever controls the information, and never the public. That same imbalance lets Texas grant a sales tax exemption now on pace to become the nation’s costliest, without a clear account of what it was buying. “Gather more data” assumes the data is lying around waiting to be picked up, when really it sits with whoever profits from Texas never getting its hands on it.

Texas has courted this industry, and that exemption is one measure of the welcome. So it was notable when Governor Greg Abbott wrote to state regulators in June about data center costs. Look at what carries a deadline and what does not. The Public Utilities Commission (PUC) must make data centers fund their own infrastructure; the PUC and ERCOT must file a joint memo; the commission must act on transmission costs by July 31. All electricity, all with dates attached. Then come the water items, and the register shifts. Water reporting, water-efficient cooling, an end to outdated tax incentives, these are things the governor pledged to take up with the Legislature next session. That session convenes in January 2027. The mandatory water survey Texas already has, the one 17 percent of data centers bothered to answer, is already law. (Abbott also recently touted that a controversial East Texas data center project was pulling its plans because it didn’t meet the governor’s requirements, providing him a useful pelt to hold up to anti-data center voters as proof that his recent actions are having an effect.)

None of this means the data demand surge is imaginary. AI computing is growing fast, and some of those filings will become real buildings pulling real power off the grid. The industry brings real investment, and Texas has reason to want it. That was never the question. The question is whether Texas should commit decades of generation and water to requests never guaranteed by the companies making them. Growth does not become a public obligation just because it sounds inevitable. In an interconnection queue, a firm plan and a hedged bet look exactly alike. Only one of them should be enough to break ground.

The useful move is not to plead for numbers. It is to make the absence of them expensive for whoever withholds them. And on energy demand, Texas has finally started doing that. Ohio ran the same test, and the result was striking. Data center developers had filed roughly 30 gigawatts of interconnection requests with AEP Ohio. Once regulators required binding contracts backed by real collateral, just 5.6 gigawatts signed. The rest evaporated, which was the point.

Water deserves the same treatment, and so does the on-site generation path left open alongside it. Tie either hookup to real disclosure so that a company earns it by opening its books. And when a speculative plant winds up half-used, let the company that built it swallow the loss, not the ratepayer who never asked for it. None of that requires predicting the future. None of this is theoretical either. Texas has run into it before. Oil and gas has powered the state for a century, and most of its wells are plugged and retired properly. The trouble was always narrower than the industry: Bonds have long been set below what plugging a well actually costs, so when a company fails, the well becomes the state’s. More than 11,000 now sit orphaned on the state’s rolls, and recent watchdog estimates put the state-funded plugging cost above $55,000 per well, with taxpayer dollars covering the difference. The point is not that a data center is an oil well, or that the industry did anything wrong. It is that Texas already knows what happens when a cost is not secured up front, and the current boom is a chance to secure it early instead of late.

Texas does not have to know the future to guard against it. It has to ask for firmer commitments before public systems plan around a company’s word, and make the people selling the boom carry the risk if it fails to arrive. The computing is real, and it is not going anywhere. The only open question is who pays when the promise outgrows the thing beneath it.

Dive Brief:

Massachusetts is awarding $23 million in clean energy grants at nine public colleges and state facilities, the state announced Monday.

The awards will cover up to 45% of the cost for projects that include connecting geothermal systems and implementing energy efficiency measures at the University of Massachusetts’ Dartmouth, Boston and Amherst campuses; Massachusetts Maritime Academy; Salem State University; and the state Department of Conservation and Recreation and Development Services.

When taken together, the projects are expected to reduce annual greenhouse gas emissions by 21,000 metric tons and lower long-term costs for taxpayers, Gov. Maura Healey said in a press release.

Dive Insight:

The grants were awarded under the Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources’ Leading by Example Decarbonization Implementation Program. The executive order creating the program directs the state to reduce on-site fossil fuel emissions 35% by 2030.

Key awards include $7.35 million to support the installation of a 5-MW industrial heat pump at the UMass Amherst central heating plant that will use waste heat to produce low-pressure steam.Fewer than two dozen of these systems are installed across the U.S., “putting [the university] at the forefront of a growing field,” the state said.

UMass Boston is receiving $5.3 million to support a campuswide decarbonization plan. As part of that plan, the campus will replace gas boilers at its central power plant with three electric heat shift chillers that use an existing sea water pump to cool and heat the campus. The plan ultimately will reduce the campus’s natural gas consumption and associated greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels by over half, the state said.

UMass Dartmouth was awarded $1.1 million to establish a new connection to a geothermal system being installed at one of its buildings to leverage excess heating and cooling capacity.

The state’s Division of Capital Asset Management and Maintenance received $7.5 million to support geothermal projects at the Massachusetts Maritime Academy and Salem State University, connecting several buildings on each campus to the system.

The grants to the Department of Conservation and Recreational Services and Development Services, or DCR, support projects at three public recreation sites: almost $1 million for an energy retrofit at the headquarters building for a Boston park, more than $400,000 at one skating rink to replace a natural gas-fueled heating and hot water system with a variable refrigerant flow system and more than $400,000 to a second rink to replace a natural gas hot water system with a heat pump and energy recovery ventilation.

The rinks are the largest consumers of fossil fuels in the DCR rink portfolio, so the retrofits are seen as proving grounds for future decarbonization efforts at other rinks, the release says.

title: Sunrise co-founder bets on data centers in House bid - E&E News by POLITICO
authors: Timothy Cama, Kelsey Tamborrino, Christa Marshall, Zack Colman, Jason Plautz, Jeffrey Tomich, Katherine Long, Shelby Webb
description:
A co-founder of the Sunrise Movement is betting that data center opposition will propel his progressive campaign over more-centrist Democrats, despite his underdog status.
He’s calling for a nationwide moratorium on data center construction and has focused on the issue in his first video advertisement of the campaign.
Advertisement The race serves as a key indicator of whether voters want Democrats leaning more left on data centers and climate change.

text:
A co-founder of the Sunrise Movement is betting that data center opposition will propel his progressive campaign over more-centrist Democrats, despite his underdog status.

William Lawrence, a community organizer who help launch the youth-led climate change action group nearly a decade ago, is in a three-way Democratic primary in Michigan’s Lansing-area 7th District, where President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by the slimmest of margins. The winner will face incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Barrett in what is likely to be one of the nation’s closest general election races this November.

Lawrence — who has support from Sunrise, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed — has tried to put significant attention on data centers. He’s calling for a nationwide moratorium on data center construction and has focused on the issue in his first video advertisement of the campaign.

Advertisement

The race serves as a key indicator of whether voters want Democrats leaning more left on data centers and climate change. Lawrence hasn’t raised as much money as either of his primary opponents — Bridget Brink, former ambassador to Ukraine, and Matt Maasdam, a former Navy SEAL — who have also gotten high-profile endorsements.

Michigan is home to a number of high-profile data center construction projects, such as ones in Saline Township and Dowagiac that have, at times, split communities and state leaders over their potential impacts to the electric grid, water supplies and surrounding area.

“It wasn’t something I expected to be talking about last August when I got into the race because it really wasn’t on folks’ radar here in Michigan. But there were then four data centers proposed in my district alone after I declared my candidacy,” Lawrence said in an interview.

Riding a wave

Lawrence said he went to local planning meetings to listen to data center companies pitch their projects and hear what Michiganders were saying about them.

“It was clear to me that this is an abuse of power that is taking advantage of communities without the resources to fully fight back on their own,” he said.

Lawrence’s campaign launched an ad featuring him at a farm, saying, “Tech billionaires want to turn this field into a massive data center that’ll jack up our energy bills and ruin our home values.”

“I’m running for U.S. Congress because I’ve never been afraid to stand up to corporate power,” Lawrence said in the ad.

Michigan is a hot market for data centers, owing to its location near the middle of the country and favorable tax treatments for the facilities. Out of the United States’ 4,668 data centers in operation or development, 79 are in Michigan, ranking it No. 18 among states, according to Data Center Map. A POLITICO analysis of Data Center Map’s data found that 12 projects are in Michigan’s 7th District, half in operation and half in development.

El-Sayed, who is running as a progressive in Michigan’s Democratic primary for the Senate, is making data centers a high priority in his race as well, although he has not endorsed a nationwide moratorium. Many top Democrats have endorsed the more-moderate Rep. Haley Stevens. The Democratic primary winner will likely take on former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers.

Pitching climate

Lawrence is also carrying on his advocacy for the Green New Deal, the rapid decarbonization proposal that Sunrise is best known for, as part of his campaign for the House.

“The foundation of green industrial policy remains a strong prescription to continue the work of cutting climate pollution while creating good jobs building things here in this country,” he said.

While the Democrats’ 2022 Inflation Reduction Act — the largest federal investment in renewable energy ever — had “a lot” of what the Green New Deal hoped to accomplish, Lawrence wants to focus on securing other pieces, like expanding the child tax credit, investing billions of dollars in green housing and making union organizing easier. The Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill last year rolled back major parts of the IRA.

Lawrence’s Green New Deal push puts him in line with a series of insurgent Democrats who have won primaries this year in safe Democratic congressional seats and are poised to advance to Congress next year, breathing new life into the climate proposal for the artificial intelligence and data center age.

“He has a shot at proving that someone who is backed by Bernie Sanders and the Working Families Party, who is the Sunrise Movement co-founder, who is a proud progressive and very uncompromising in those ideals…can win in a seat that Trump won,” said Denae Ávila-Dickson, spokesperson for Sunrise.

Lawrence may be tapping into real concerns that voters aren’t hearing from other politicians, said Nazita Lajevardi, a political science professor at the University of Michigan, but he’s risking alienating certain voters.

“It’s kind of a gamble, because some of the issues he’s talking about might appeal to the left wing of the Democratic Party,” she said, pointing to his support for the Green New Deal, Medicare for All and other progressive concepts.

Uphill battle

Lawrence has raised $1.1 million, far behind his primary opponents. Brink has raised $3 million and Maasdam $2.1 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.

No independent polling on the race has been released. One poll taken in June by GQR, commissioned by Brink’s campaign, had her at 30 percent to Lawrence’s 23 percent. But an April survey by Data for Progress, commissioned by Lawrence’s campaign, had him ahead at 20 percent to Brink’s 14 percent.

Maasdam has support from Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D), who used to represent the 7th District. Brink has the backing of former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who was also once Michigan governor.

Sunrise activists have confronted both candidates in recent weeks to push them on data center issues. Both said they would not support a nationwide data center moratorium.

“I think that’s a local issue to decide,” Maasdam told Sunrise. In response to the activist saying he’s accepted support from organizations funded by technology companies, he said, “I don’t know where all that comes from.”

Massdam’s campaign didn’t make him available for an interview. In a recent video on the subject, he said, “I share people’s concerns and skepticism that these giant behemoth companies are coming into the district and pushing local governments around with an army of lawyers.”

Maasdam said he supports work the state Legislature has done recently to try to keep data centers from increasing electric bills and to crack down on nondisclosure agreements companies sign with politicians.

“I want to make sure that the municipalities and local governments have the tools and the resources at their disposal to handle the negotiations with these big companies,” he said.

When Sunrise confronted Brink, she similarly deferred to local municipalities. “My view is that we should leave that to communities as to what they want to do,” she said.

At a candidate forum in June, Brink also called for environmental, electricity and transparency standards. “It requires an open and transparent conversation between those who want to come in and the people of our community and the people of our districts, and that’s what I would stand behind in Congress.”

Trump visited the district Monday, holding an event at a General Motors facility in Milford, where Barrett spoke to the crowd to boast about the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Trump called Barrett a “congressman who’s doing really, really good. He’s going to have a tough race. You’ve got to help him.”

text:
As summer temperatures continue to rise, air conditioners will start running full blast and lead to an increase in electricity usage. However, staying cool and comfortable does not have to come at the cost of high energy bills. By making a few simple changes around your home, you can improve its energy efficiency and beat the heat while keeping costs down.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, home heating and cooling costs can make up more than 52% of an average customer’s electric bill. In some cases, poor insulation, air leaks and inefficient HVAC systems can lead to even greater energy costs each year. To keep your home cool without significantly raising the thermostat and save money on your bill at the same time, try these low to no-cost tips.

Improving energy efficiency with low-to-no-cost tips

Change air filters. Air filters on some air conditioning units require monthly cleaning or replacing.

Set your thermostat to the highest comfortable temperature.The smaller the difference between the inside and outside temperatures, the lower your energy usage and bill will be.

Buy a programmable thermostat. A programmable thermostat can help manage costs, is controllable, and can help monitor usage.

Use fans to cool off. Ceiling fans, box fans and oscillating fans use very little electricity to circulate the air. Make sure ceiling fans are rotating in the right direction – counter-clockwise during summer – to push cooler air down into the room. Be sure to turn all fans off in unused rooms.

Close blinds, shades and curtains to keep the sun out and the cool air in. Also, close air conditioning vents in rooms that are not in use.

Seal cracks and holes around doors, windows and ductwork. Weather stripping and caulk will help keep the cold air in and the hot air out.

Use the myAdvisor tool. The usage and cost tool can compare usage history by month, day and hour.

By following these simple steps, you can stay cool and comfortable all summer long while keeping your bills under control. We also offer free comprehensive residential energy audits and rebates to help reduce the upfront cost of installing energy-efficient equipment.

Exploring resources through Bill Toolkit

To ensure customers have quick access to energy efficiency, bill management and financial assistance resources, Entergy offers an online platform called Bill Toolkit. The platform consolidates helpful resources for customers interested in exploring ways to lower their electric use and costs and learn more about different payment options the company offers. It also provides information on our energy efficiency programs and incentives and rebates associated with these programs.

Tracking energy use through myAdvisor

Entergy customers can set electric usage alerts and monitor how much energy they use each day through bill management tools like myAdvisor, which is available through their myEntergy account online. Tracking usage over time can help customers identify trends that contribute to higher usage and budget their monthly expenses. With the myAdvisor dashboard, customers have access to not only usage and cost details, but also bill history and projections, analyzer tools and more. On the Entergy mobile app this information can be found by tapping the “usage” tab.

Managing bills through payment and assistance options

Entergy offers several flexible payment options so customers can choose when, where and how they receive their bills.

Pick-A-Date allows customers to pay their bills when it works best for them.

Level Billing allows customers to “level out” seasonal energy use fluctuations, making their bills more consistent every month.

PaperFREE billing allows customers to get their bills emailed as soon as they post and instant access to two years of billing history.

AutoPay allows customers to avoid late fees, writing checks and paying for postage by having bills automatically deduct from their bank accounts.

We also offer flexible payment options such as deferred payment arrangements or payment extensions. Customers can find out if they qualify for these options through our mobile app or myEntergy online.

About Entergy Louisiana

Entergy Louisiana provides electric service to more than 1.1 million customers in 58 parishes.

About Entergy New Orleans

Entergy New Orleans is an electric service that serves Louisiana’s Orleans Parish. The company provides electricity to more than 209,000 customers.

Both companies are subsidiaries of Entergy Corporation. Entergy produces, transmits and distributes electricity to power life for 3 million customers through our operating companies in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas. We’re investing for growth and improved reliability and resilience of our energy system while working to keep energy rates affordable for our customers. We’re also investing in cleaner energy generation like modern natural gas, nuclear and renewable energy. A nationally recognized leader in sustainability and corporate citizenship, we deliver more than $100 million in economic benefits each year to the communities we serve through philanthropy, volunteerism and advocacy. Entergy is a Fortune 500 company headquartered in New Orleans, Louisiana, and has approximately 12,000 employees.

title: Thea Energy lands $20M federal grant to build its magnets for fusion reactors | TechCrunch
description:
Now, Thea Energy has a leg up courtesy of a Department of Energy grant.
The fusion power startup told TechCrunch Monday that it has received a $20 million award from ARPA-E to help manufacture its modular high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets.
Thea is among the top funded fusion power startups, having raised $100 million in May on top of a $20 million Series A it raised in 2024.
Like many of its peers, Thea has plans to build a commercial-scale fusion power plant in the mid-2030s.

text:
For hard-tech startups, manufacturing is a pricey endeavor. Now, Thea Energy has a leg up courtesy of a Department of Energy grant.

The fusion power startup told TechCrunch Monday that it has received a $20 million award from ARPA-E to help manufacture its modular high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets.

HTS magnets are costly but important components in any magnetic confinement reactor, one of the two main ways startups are attempting to harness fusion power for commercial purposes. In magnetic confinement reactors, powerful magnetic fields contain and compress plasma, helping to heat the particles until the fuel can fuse and release large amounts of energy.

Thea’s reactor is based on a design known as a stellarator. Stellarators look like inner tubes that have been twisted and squeezed in ways that help it confine the plasma more effectively. Most stellarators use magnets that are built to mimic those twists and turns, which makes them expensive to manufacture.

To minimize manufacturing costs, Thea uses fewer variants. The 12 large magnets that do the heavy lifting are made from four different templates, and the more than 300 smaller magnets used to fine tune the plasma are all identical. They’re arrayed around the periphery of the reactor, similar to how pixels are distributed across a computer display.

The small magnets are controlled by software, an arrangement that should allow for more forgiving construction tolerances, which could lower costs, Thea says.

Thea is among the top funded fusion power startups, having raised $100 million in May on top of a $20 million Series A it raised in 2024. Like many of its peers, Thea has plans to build a commercial-scale fusion power plant in the mid-2030s.

Update 7/28: Thea is planning to build a commercial power plant in the mid-2030s, not the mid 2040s.

text:
Confidence Infrastructure plans to raise Tk300 crore through an initial public offering (IPO) to finance electric vehicle (EV) battery production, business expansion, debt repayment and investments in new sectors, including food.

The company has appointed UCB Investment Limited as issue manager for the proposed IPO. The two companies signed the issue management agreement on Tuesday at Confidence Infrastructure's corporate headquarters in Dhaka. The agreement was signed by Imran Karim, chairman of Confidence Infrastructure, and Tanzim Alamgir, managing director and chief executive officer of UCB Investment.

Speaking to The Business Standard, Karim said the group's affiliate, Confidence Batteries Limited, currently manufactures lead-acid batteries for the automotive, industrial, telecommunications, solar power and backup power sectors. The company now plans to enter EV battery manufacturing to meet growing domestic demand, reduce import dependence and build local capabilities in advanced battery production.

The company is targeting the electric motorcycle, three-wheeler, passenger car, bus and energy storage system markets. It also plans to invest part of the IPO proceeds in modern food production, processing and supply chains as part of its strategy to diversify into high-growth sectors.

Subject to regulatory approval, UCB Investment will provide due diligence, financial and legal reviews, prospectus preparation and other IPO advisory services.

According to company officials, the IPO proceeds will finance EV battery manufacturing, new infrastructure and energy projects, debt repayment and investments in the food business.

Confidence Infrastructure reported Tk3,606 crore in consolidated revenue and Tk275 crore in net profit for FY25, with earnings per share of Tk19.92. It has a paid-up capital of Tk138.12 crore and an authorised capital of Tk500 crore.

The company operates across infrastructure development, manufacturing, storage, electricity, power generation, telecommunications and paint production. Its planned expansion into EV batteries is aimed at strengthening its position in the clean energy and future mobility market.

Confidence Group already has a listed company – Confidence Cement PLC, which has been trading on the Dhaka Stock Exchange since 1995. The cement maker recently declared a 10% cash dividend for FY25, reported Tk97 crore in net profit and was trading at around Tk69.10 per share. If approved, Confidence Infrastructure will become the group's second listed company.

Capital market analysts say large industrial IPOs have become increasingly rare, limiting investment opportunities in fundamentally strong companies. They believe Confidence Infrastructure's listing would deepen the market, while its planned investment in EV battery manufacturing could strengthen future earnings and support Bangladesh's emerging electric vehicle supply chain.

The IPO is subject to approval by the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC), which will review the company's audited financial statements, due diligence reports, prospectus, asset valuation and proposed use of proceeds before granting approval.

name: IRA Tax Credits
title: How the Big Beautiful Bill became law: Energy tax credits spark intra-party feud
authors: Callie Patteson, Maydeen Merino, Ramsey Touchberry
description:
Yet, the White House refused to budge on cutting cold turkey the hundreds of billions of dollars in clean energy tax credits.
Finding the perfect balance between centrists and conservatives on energy tax credits was extremely difficult, lawmakers and aides said.
“There was no issue that the president emphasized as wasteful spending more than the green energy tax subsidies,” Arrington told the Washington Examiner.
To Wright’s surprise, the biggest revolt was on the clean energy tax credits.
Months earlier, Rep. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY) organized a letter alongside 20 other House Republicans urging against wholesale repeal of the clean energy tax credits.
text:
Still, Curtis recognized he was the new guy on the block as he sought changes to the legislation.

HOW THE BIG BEAUTIFUL BILL BECAME LAW: READ MORE FROM THE WASHINGTON EXAMINER’S 10-PART SERIES

“I found myself saying to the industry, to one of my colleagues who had asked me about it, ‘Don’t worry, I got this,’” Curtis recalled to the Washington Examiner. “They’re looking at a brand-new senator saying, ‘Don’t worry, I got this.’ Very skeptical.”

Curtis knew that the hundreds of billions of dollars in subsidies were without a doubt on the chopping block. They were, after all, from the largest-ever climate bill passed and championed by Democrats.

But he also knew that “how they go away is everything.” Curtis argued that businesses would be “decimated” if they were not given time to adjust to ending federal subsidies. As it turned out, many Republicans quietly agreed with him, despite it meaning they were at odds with most in their party and, more importantly, Trump.

The ensuing tug-of-war policy battle would rage for weeks over clean energy, constantly nearing the brink of disaster against the backdrop of other contentious negotiations that could crumble the entire legislation at any time.

Just a week before the law’s passage, Trump was about to lose another Republican vote. Curtis had leverage. Yet, the White House refused to budge on cutting cold turkey the hundreds of billions of dollars in clean energy tax credits.

“Put a fork in me. I’m done,” Curtis recalled telling White House staff. “This is not logical, it’s emotional. And you’ve lost my support for the bill.”

Right says cuts don’t go far enough

Tensions over the clean energy tax credits, established under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, had been brewing for weeks as a key provision in the bill set to deliver on Trump’s tax agenda. A group of conservatives blocked the measure from hitting the floor in the House until the subsidies were completely scrapped.

Initially, the bill included fairly gentle terminations of the clean energy tax credits, phasing out the subsidies in the early 2030s — several years after Trump leaves office. Centrist Republicans had for months urged leadership to handle the repeal of the credits with a scalpel, to prevent any significant losses of investments in their districts. The hardliners wanted a sledgehammer to decimate the Biden-era policies.

There were many obstacles that Trump and Republican congressional leaders faced before they passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Finding the perfect balance between centrists and conservatives on energy tax credits was extremely difficult, lawmakers and aides said.

Sen. James Lankford (R-OK), a member of the GOP leadership team, said he was surprised that much of the energy-related negotiations weren’t ironed out until the last possible moment, calling it “a really big battle at the end.”

He added, “I would have never guessed that would have been the final battle.”

At various times, as Republicans got close to a tentative deal, Trump pushed harder.

Sean Clerget, who served as chief tax counsel to House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith (R-MO) and helped craft the energy tax language, said, “Trump was very aggressive on wind.”

Indeed. Trump has aggressively and consistently moved to halt offshore wind projects and repeal policies that help to bolster renewable energy throughout his second administration, while also rolling back regulations to prop up the fossil fuel industry as part of his energy dominance agenda.

Trump has many staples to his stump speeches, and one of his so-called greatest hits is railing on wind energy. Attracting rebuttals from fact checkers, Trump has claimed wind energy kills eagles, causes cancer, and isn’t used by “smart countries.”

Emboldened by their party leader, fiscal hawks in the Freedom Caucus called for stronger cuts to minimize the federal deficit and offset other tax credit extensions. And — as a bonus — stronger cuts to green subsidies helped deliver on Trump’s campaign promise to kill the so-called Green New Deal.

“We were making progress, but the vote was called, and the problems were not resolved, so I voted no,” Rep. Chip Roy (R-TX) said in a post on X after blocking a crucial committee vote. “I am staying in Washington this weekend to deliver. Medicaid Work requirements must start NOW not 2029 & the Green New Scam must be fully repealed, as President Trump called for.”

Trump phoned Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX), chairman of the House Budget Committee, from Air Force One while traveling back to the United States from his diplomatic and economic tour of the Middle East in mid-May.

The call came just after the panel had held its last markup on the measure, and it was headed to the floor for a vote. The final House vote count was still up in the air, as some members were not satisfied with how quickly the legislation would repeal the wind and solar energy tax credits.

“There was no issue that the president emphasized as wasteful spending more than the green energy tax subsidies,” Arrington told the Washington Examiner. “So it seemed like some of my colleagues, some of my fellow budget committee members, were aligned with what the president wanted to do. And they didn’t think we had gone far enough.”

Arrington said he agreed with their sentiment. However, the legislation needed to move forward. “But I also knew we could make some changes in [the] rules committee,” he said.

A big problem for the speaker

With a single-digit majority in the House, dual pushback from the Freedom Caucus and centrists threatened to tank the entire bill. It was a major problem for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA), who had his energy expert on speed dial.

Johnson would call Energy Secretary Chris Wright as late as 11 p.m. or even 2 a.m. to talk strategy on getting the votes. Sometimes these were individual calls with the speaker, and other times with groups of members.

Most lawmakers didn’t need much convincing about stripping tax credits for things such as electric vehicles or preserving subsidies for technologies such as nuclear and geothermal energy.

To Wright’s surprise, the biggest revolt was on the clean energy tax credits. This was partly because legislators didn’t want to see less money going to their districts, as Republican-led states were attracting private sector investments in renewable energy projects during the Biden administration.

In the immediate years after the Democrats’ climate law was passed, roughly 80% of total investments made went to Republican congressional districts. This included new manufacturing facilities, utility-scale clean energy projects, and decarbonization sites in states such as South Carolina, Kentucky, Tennessee, and Ohio. Many of these projects were expected to generate tens of thousands of jobs in the states.

At the same time, solar and wind lobbyists had the ear of many legislators on Capitol Hill. One solar industry advocate recalled various lobby days and fundraisers that involved offering education to members about the industry and bringing constituents together from their respective districts.

“Reconciliation Bill Risks Devastating Job Losses in Every U.S. State if Senate Fails to Change Course,” the Solar Energy Industries Association wrote in a report released in early June, a month before the July 4, 2025, legislative deadline.

And the industry saw some success. Months earlier, Rep. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY) organized a letter alongside 20 other House Republicans urging against wholesale repeal of the clean energy tax credits.

“The solar lobby just came in and brought new data and new arguments, and then they were bombarding senators and House members constantly,” Wright recalled, saying it led to a lot of back and forth between himself and Congress. “The trade groups, the lobbyists, fought tooth and nail to the end … that was the biggest battle.”

Republican infighting

Curtis, the Utah Republican senator, was taking a calculated political risk in being the point man to save some of the energy credits.

He served eight years in the House before coming to the other side of the Capitol. But in many ways, it was a whole different ball game that left Curtis wondering how much to wield the newfound leverage that he lacked in the lower chamber.

“As a newbie, as the new senator, I didn’t really have a good sense of how hard to push my feelings and work to exert myself,” Curtis said. “But as it unfolded, it was clear that the bill text had gone too far, and I literally came — it was not a bluff — I came to the point where I was not willing to support it because it had gone too far.”

He wasn’t alone. Republicans including Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), Thom Tillis (R-NC), and Jerry Moran (R-KS) also pushed heavily against the House-proposed cuts.

Conservatives succeeded in accelerating the repeal of the green subsidies, with the House-passed bill ending tax credits for all projects — regardless of whether they were for wind, solar, or other alternative energies — unless they start construction within 60 days of the bill’s enactment and are placed in service by the end of 2028. Only nuclear developers saw relief, with the measure ordering those projects to start construction by 2028 to qualify for energy subsidies.

The stiff arm from the Republicans in the Senate surprised Wright just a “little bit.” The secretary spoke with both Curtis and Murkowski specifically as the vote neared, aiming to find a compromise.

“We all agreed the subsidies should go away,” Wright said. “The question was just the pathway, and so even when there was a meaningful disagreement in the pathway, it was always polite. It may have been firm … but they were polite.”

Murkowski’s office declined to comment.

Curtis knew he was going against the grain: “It was clear that it was in opposition to the White House. It was clear it was in opposition to some of my colleagues.”

The notion of immediately nixing renewable energy credits and subsidies “didn’t fit with a strategy of being energy dominant” and seemed “more punitive,” Curtis said. Funds or tax breaks already committed to the wind and solar industries meant companies were expecting the money for ongoing projects.

In June 2025, Rhodium Group and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Center for Energy and Environment Policy Research reported that about $522 billion worth of clean energy investments were announced between mid-2022 and the first quarter of 2025, though they have yet to come online.

The investments included the expansion of solar generation, geothermal plants, sustainable aviation fuel, hydrogen facilities, wind turbines, EVs, and much more.

Trump steps in

With such a slim majority in both chambers, a few votes against the bill could tank the entire legislation.

So about 36 hours before the bill hit the Senate floor, Trump stepped up his involvement.

Wright recalled huddling with the president, Johnson, and a few others in the Oval Office. The president was “pretty clear” on what he would and wouldn’t support during the meeting, Wright said.

While the secretary didn’t elaborate on what Trump specifically told leadership during the meeting, it is well known that the president viewed any tax credits for renewable energy projects, such as wind and solar, as wasteful government spending and that his signature tax bill would not pass without those rollbacks.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) wasn’t present at the meeting, but later met with the president that night to discuss how they could secure the votes in the upper chamber.

The following morning, Thune called Wright to explain his conversation with the president, where he thought negotiations in the upper chamber had landed, and how many more senators they needed to get to passage.

Wright, a career oil and gas executive and fracking pioneer, recalled that Thune had made “great progress” and that the budget reconciliation bill was finally at a place that would work with the administration’s priorities.

The secretary wasn’t getting everything he wanted, but he knew that would always be the case. He had succeeded in securing federal subsidies for nuclear and geothermal technologies, and had long pushed for sharp rollbacks for renewable energy alternatives, which he called unreliable and overly expensive.

With Thune searching for votes, the Senate wasn’t going to be able to pass the dramatic subsidy repeals outlined in the House version. But for Wright, the bill was finally in a position to slash Democrats’ climate change legislative agenda significantly.

Wright’s conversation with Thune left him in good spirits, allowing him, for the first time in a long time, to have a “relatively relaxed” day, walking along the river with his wife.

Looking back, Wright described the day as a “false calm,” as the Senate prepared to enter a more than 24-hour vote-a-rama to get a final version of the legislation on the floor, with key Republicans going back and forth right up to the moment they cast their votes.

“Then the night came,” Wright said, as he and Thune would soon again be forced to negotiate with members for their votes.

Crunch time

Just one day after Thune met one-on-one with the president, the wheels in the Senate started to come off.

The upper chamber was headed into its closely watched vote-a-rama marathon amendment session, providing a last chance for senators of either party to propose changes and force votes.

This series of votes stretched late into the evening on June 30, 2025, and well into the early hours of July 1, with the majority leader attempting to please both fiscal hawks and moderate Republicans pushing for softer cuts.

Confidence was wavering over whether Thune could corral the centrist votes. Murkowski, the Alaska Republican who often butts heads with Trump, was among those on the fence.

With their votes up in the air, Wright went back to the phones.

The energy secretary made a “couple” of calls late that night, telling certain members that “if we have to take a step back, we’ll take a step back, but we can’t blow up the core of what we’re doing.”

Thune spoke with Murkowski throughout the night and the following morning. She ultimately succeeded in squeezing in an amendment that allowed projects beginning construction less than one year after the bill was enacted to claim the federal subsidies. The amendment also slashed a new tax proposed by GOP hardliners in the Senate that would have been imposed on solar and wind projects that fail to meet restrictions on the use of Chinese materials.

With Murkowski’s amendment added to the bill, Republicans appeared to have a deal on slowly removing the green tax provisions, where enough senators were satisfied. Murkowski ultimately and reluctantly voted for final passage.

HOUSE JAMS THROUGH FUNDING PATCH TO AVERT SHUTDOWN THROUGH DECEMBER

“There were plenty of times I thought she was going to vote no,” a GOP aide told the Washington Examiner.

Fiscal hawks in the House criticized the Senate-passed bill. Roy accused the upper chamber of offering a “giveaway” to the renewable energy industry. While the changes were a “deal killer” for him, Johnson called his bluff by putting the bill to a vote. And ultimately, Roy voted in favor of the final package.

Members of the Washington Examiner’s staff who have worked on this series over the past several months are Haris Alic, Hailey Bullis, Bob Cusack, Christian Datoc, James A. Downs, Gabrielle M. Etzel, Lauren Green, Zach Halaschak, Chris Irvine, Joseph Lawler, Naomi Lim, Maydeen Merino, Callie Patteson, Mabinty Quarshie, Samantha-Jo Roth, David Sivak, and Ramsey Touchberry.

text:
GE Vernova is investing in the modernisation of its Veresegyház manufacturing facility in Hungary as the site – the energy company’s largest gas power plant outside the US – celebrates its 25th anniversary.

The overhaul programme includes new renewable energy infrastructure, expanded production capacity and plans to recruit more than 80 new employees.

The Veresegyház plant plays a central role in the company's global operations, manufacturing and repairing critical gas turbine components used in power generation projects worldwide. It specialises in advanced processes including robotic welding, precision machining and thermal coating technologies for both new equipment and refurbishment work.

A key element of the latest investment is the construction of a large on-site solar power system designed to reduce the plant's dependence on grid electricity. The project is being delivered in phases, with the first stage already completed through the installation of a 2MW solar carport covering more than 500 parking spaces.

The second phase includes the installation of 14.5MW of solar PV capacity alongside a 40MWh battery . More than 21,000 solar panels are being installed across a 15-hectare site, with grid connection expected later this year.

Once fully operational, the combined solar and battery system is expected to supply almost half of the facility's annual electricity demand, which currently stands at around 33GWh, considerably improving the site's energy self-sufficiency while reducing carbon emissions from manufacturing operations.

Leaning in

GE Vernova says that this sustainability milestone coincides with a period of intense growth for the facility as it works to address the global electricity "investment supercycle".

To meet surging demand, in 2025 a $24,5 million investment, supported by a planned significant contribution of the Hungarian Investment Promotion (HIPA), set the foundation for the site's ongoing modernisation, which now includes the successful installation of new lean production lines and the commissioning of high-performance precision machinery. Additionally, five advanced coating booths equipped with vacuum furnaces are now operational to bolster repair and manufacturing output.

Exposing the hidden resiliency risk in standby power systems

The company is also continuing to expand its workforce. Following the recruitment of around 100 employees over the past year, GE Vernova now plans to hire a further 80 skilled workers, including machinists, welders, fitters and assembly operators, to support increased production.

Viktoria Fodor, GE Vernova’s Veresegyház plant manager, said: "We are not just expanding our capabilities, energy independence and talents; we are building a more sustainable and efficient future. By blending advanced manufacturing technology with renewable energy, we are ensuring that Veresegyház remains a core element of GE Vernova’s global gas power manufacturing operations for decades to come."

More modernisation

GE Vernova maintains a substantial operational presence in Hungary, with several key locations that support its global energy work. The company’s footprint is centred around the facility in Veresegyház. The site’s modernisation was announced soon after the company received a significant order for gas turbines from Hawaiian Electric.

GE Vernova has also just received a contract for another type of modernisation project – this one at a pumped storage hydropower plant in North Wales.

The Dinorwig pumped storage hydropower plant is set to undergo the next stage of a major refurbishment programme aimed at extending the operational life of one of the UK's most strategically important energy assets by at least 25 years.

First Hydro Company – the joint venture between energy company Engie and investment firm La Caisse that owns and operates the facility – has awarded GE Vernova a contract to modernise two of the plant's six pumped storage generating units.

The work forms part of a long-term investment programme to replace ageing equipment, improve reliability and maintain the station's ability to provide rapid-response electricity to the national grid.

Now more than 40 years old, Dinorwig remains one of Europe's largest pumped storage hydroelectric facilities. The station can deliver up to 1,320MW of electricity within 12 seconds of being called upon and reach its full output of 1,800MW in less than a minute, making it a key source of flexibility for balancing electricity supply and demand. At full capacity, the plant can generate enough electricity to supply the equivalent of around one million homes.

The wider modernisation programme includes the replacement of key plant components across all six generating units, alongside substantial infrastructure upgrades. The modernisation forms part of one of the UK's largest hydro refurbishment and replanting programme, helping to strengthen long-term grid resilience and support the integration of renewable energy in the UK's evolving electricity system. This programme is expected to extend the plant’s life by at least 25 years.

Major milestone

Delphine Cherel-Sparham, managing director of Engie Hydro UK, said: "This contract marks an important milestone in our long-term investment programme at Dinorwig.

"As majority owner and operator of the plant, Engie is committed to ensuring Dinorwig continues to provide the flexibility, resilience and energy storage capabilities that the UK electricity system increasingly depends upon. Together with GE Vernova, we are investing in the modernisation of key generating units to help secure the plant's performance for decades to come.”

Presenting GE Vernova’s view, Emmanuel Mercier, the firm’s Hydro Power EMEA leader, said: “This project is a strong example of how GE Vernova can bring innovation and engineering expertise to a landmark hydro asset. Dinorwig is a highly strategic facility for the UK power system, and we are proud to support First Hydro Company in strengthening the reliability and performance of this important plant.”

Private equity-backed Momentum Environmental acquired Corbett Industrial Cleaning Services. The deal advances Momentum’s goal to be a vertically integrated leader in environmental services and non-hazardous waste in the U.S. Northeast.

Momentum was co-founded in 2024 by Bill Hunter, who is the company’s CEO. It operates with a fleet of 152 vehicles based in seven locations across New York state that extend into neighboring states. The company also owns two centralized wastewater treatment plants with solidification pits and infrastructure for managing solids, as well as a soil recycling facility.

Hunter said Momentum’s current service footprint spans from Erie, Pennsylvania, to Worcester, Massachusetts. Its acquisition of Corbett densifies its services in the eastern portion of its existing footprint. That’s by design — Hunter said he sees abundant opportunity for growth in New England.

This is Momentum’s fourth acquisition over the last two years. Hunter said he sees plenty of runway to expand in the region both through acquisitions and organic growth. The rise of solar and wind manufacturing has created new business for Momentum, and Hunter expects artificial intelligence-related industries to also spur the creation of new manufacturing capacity with waste and recycling needs.

He also said tight disposal regulations in the Northeast create further opportunities for Momentum, especially with its water and soil treatment facilities.

“There’s a lot of laws that have hit the books in both Massachusetts and New York that makes it tighter for the materials that are eligible for landfill disposal. So we’re focused on that,” Hunter said.

“Becoming part of a larger, vertically integrated organization allows us to broaden what we’ve created while preserving the relationships that have defined our business for more than a decade. Hunter said he remained a shareholder in Terra Nova but departed amicably to work closer to his home in New York. Clean Harbors announced it acquired Terra Nova in May for $225 million.

text:
Microgrids are a hot topic these days, and with good reason—supporting EV charging infrastructure with battery storage, on-site generation and V2X technology can overcome grid constraints and reduce costs.

Cenex has published new research detailing how DC-coupled smart energy hubs can help organisations accelerate fleet electrification while unlock substantial energy savings, lower peak demand and overcome grid constraints.

The report explores the performance of the 3ti Papilio3 V2X DC FastHub across a range of commercial and public-sector use cases, including fleet depots, factories, offices and leisure destinations.

Using Cenex’s EIGER energy modelling tool, the study assessed how DC-coupled energy systems can optimise energy use behind the meter.

The report found that peak site demand can be reduced by between 5 kW and 150 kW, depending on the site and operational profile, and predicts that annual energy cost savings of £2,600–£3,700 could be achieved at office, leisure and depot sites operating on two-rate tariffs. For high-demand factory sites, annual savings could be as much as £18,000.

Battery energy storage is a central component of any microgrid. Cenex found that using a DC-coupled architecture reduces energy conversion losses, improving overall system efficiency and renewable energy utilization.

“Cenex modelling demonstrated how smart DC microgrids integrating solar, storage and bidirectional EV charging can significantly reduce energy costs, lower peak demand and support fleet electrification,” said Steve Carroll, Cenex’s Head of Research and Technical Services. “Solutions like the Fasthub will be essential if we are to electrify transport operations and optimize energy use in today’s grid-constrained environments.”

“This research makes a compelling value case for bidirectional charging hubs in fleet depots, factories and sites with limited grid capacity,” said Mark Potter, CTO, 3ti. “The HALO V2X Hub brings solar generation, battery storage and bidirectional EV charging together in a behind-the-meter DC microgrid, and Cenex’s modelling shows the tangible savings and grid benefits that delivers.”

text:
CenterPoint Energy submitted more than 17 GW of large load projects to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas’ new large-load interconnection process and expects 14 GW to be eligible as base load or studied load, officials said Tuesday in the company’s second quarter earnings call.

Texas regulators approved the new rules in June. The first set of projects to navigate the new process is called “Batch Zero.”

The 14 GW would represent a more than 65% increase from the company’s current Houston-area peak system demand of 21 GW, company officials said. The utility is anticipating 50% load growth by the end of 2029.

“Based on projected load ramps sought by customers, we expect nearly all of these projects to be energized by the end of 2030,” CenterPoint CEO Jason Wells told analysts. “We are confident the combined 14 GW of base load and study load are well positioned to move forward in the Batch Zero process, given the level of customer commitments already secured.”

Of the 14 GW, approximately 10 GW of projects have all required ERCOT studies approved and are eligible for base load designation, Wells said. The remaining 4 GW “are positioned to qualify as studied load because they have one of the two required studies already approved.”

The 14 GW are supported by signed facility extension agreements with long-term end-user commitments, approximately $900 million of customer cash commitments and deposits, and “clear line of sight to the materials execution capability and system capacity to serve,” Wells said. The remaining 3 GW of Batch Zero submissions “represent additional customer demand that is pending ERCOT approval of the required studies.”

CenterPoint increased its 10-year capital investment plan by $1.2 billion, to $66.7 billion, through 2035. The increase reflects incremental investment to support accelerating demand from large-load customers in Houston and higher costs around the utility’s Downtown Houston Revitalization project.

CenterPoint expects the growth to help keep utility bills affordable. The 14 GW of higher demand from large loads will result in residential and commercial savings over $5 billion over the next decade, Wells said.

Besides the transmission-level demand CenterPoint is seeing from large-load customers, the utility anticipates an additional 2 GW of increased distribution-level demand over the next several years, “driven by reshoring of advanced manufacturing and continued population growth in the Greater Houston area,” Wells noted.

While Texas is CenterPoint’s largest service territory, where it serves almost 2.8 million metered customers and dozens of retail providers, the company also sees the potential for “transformational” large-load opportunities in its Indiana electric territory. CenterPoint serves more than 150,000 customers in Southwestern Indiana and has begun work to serve a new customer that would represent the “single largest load we serve in the region,” Wells said.

“As a result of commitment from the customer, we have already begun work to serve this load. Outside of the project identified, we are engaged with multiple counterparties for additional large load projects in that area,” he said. “The related investments required to serve these large loads would be incremental and outside of our current base plan.”

CenterPoint Energy has been planning for the retirement of the coal-fired F.B. Culley Unit 2 in Indiana, but the U.S. Department of Energy issued emergency orders in December, March and June directing the utility to continue operating the unit through Sept. 19.

The utility filed a complaint with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission “to request creation of a cost recovery/cost allocation mechanism,” CenterPoint said in a quarterly report filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. In March, FERC directed the Midcontinent Independent System Operator to adopt a tariff amendment that would authorize the F.B. Culley unit to recover costs.

“A separate filing will be made at a later date with the FERC to seek recovery of all costs incurred to comply with the U.S. Department of Energy’s emergency 202(c) orders,” CenterPoint said. The utility said it has also filed an application with regulators in Indiana “to recover any compliance costs associated with the emergency 202(c) orders that are not recovered through the FERC proceedings.”

title: Manish Bapna's Post - LinkedIn
description:
According to new analysis from E2, federal actions targeting clean energy have cost more than 460,000 potential jobs and $90 billion in economic activity across the United States.
E2 examined the impacts of recent federal actions, including the freezing of clean energy funding and provisions in the recently enacted budget law that rolled back key clean energy incentives and programs.
At a time when electricity demand is rising rapidly, hundreds of clean energy manufacturing and power generation projects have been delayed, canceled, or scaled back.
The economics of clean energy continue to improve.
The question is how quickly we will get there and whether the United States will decide to lead or be forced to catch up.
text: We now have the numbers. According to new analysis from E2, federal actions targeting clean energy have cost more than 460,000 potential jobs and $90 billion in economic activity across the United States. E2 examined the impacts of recent federal actions, including the freezing of clean energy funding and provisions in the recently enacted budget law that rolled back key clean energy incentives and programs. The consequences are significant. At a time when electricity demand is rising rapidly, hundreds of clean energy manufacturing and power generation projects have been delayed, canceled, or scaled back. Together, these projects would have generated enough electricity to power more than 3 million homes, supported tens of billions of dollars in worker income, and produced billions in annual tax revenue for communities across the country. These losses are not just numbers on a spreadsheet. They represent jobs not created, investments not made, and economic opportunities missed. But there is also reason for optimism. The economics of clean energy continue to improve. Solar, wind, and battery storage technologies are becoming more affordable and competitive every year. While recent U.S. federal policies have created strong headwinds, many states across the country and countries around the world continue to invest in the clean energy transition—driving innovation, strengthening energy security, and building more productive and resilient economies. The clean energy future is inevitable. The question is how quickly we will get there and whether the United States will decide to lead or be forced to catch up. title: Oklahoma a finalist in U.S. Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus competition
description:
The White House named Oklahoma as one of five finalist states to compete for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus, a first of its kind project that would bring the full cycle nuclear energy ecosystem together in one location if ultimately selected.
“I’m pleased to announce that after reviewing 28 applications from 26 states, the Energy Department has selected five initial contenders to further explore building Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses,” Secretary Wright said.
“These campuses will be massive generators of economic growth, create thousands of high-paying jobs, and be crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance.
This would be the first ever full nuclear lifecycle campus in the United States.
“Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses give us the opportunity to work directly with states on regional priorities that support President Trump’s vision to revitalize America’s nuclear base.” The proposed campuses could support activities across the full nuclear fuel lifecycle, including fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel, and disposition of waste.
text:
The White House named Oklahoma as one of five finalist states to compete for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus, a first of its kind project that would bring the full cycle nuclear energy ecosystem together in one location if ultimately selected.

According to U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, the four other finalists are Utah, Tennessee, Idaho and Louisiana. Following record levels of interest in the application process, Wright signed Memorandums of Understanding with Oklahoma and the four other five states to continue exploring opportunities to host Innovation Campuses and support President Trump’s bold vision for American energy dominance and national energy security.

“I’m pleased to announce that after reviewing 28 applications from 26 states, the Energy Department has selected five initial contenders to further explore building Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses,” Secretary Wright said. “These campuses will be massive generators of economic growth, create thousands of high-paying jobs, and be crucial to unleashing America’s nuclear renaissance. The innovative concept is a direct result of President Trump’s leadership and ambitious directives to restore the domestic nuclear fuel cycle and get America’s nuclear industry growing again.”

“Oklahoma has been America’s energy state for more than a hundred years, and we’re not slowing down now,” said Governor Kevin Stitt. “We built this state by leading, first in oil, then natural gas, then renewables, and now we have the chance to lead again. This is about creating more high paying jobs, driving innovation, and making Oklahoma a Top Ten state.”

The Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus is designed to bring the nuclear industry together from start to finish, including fuel fabrication, electricity generation, medical isotope production for cancer and other treatments, fuel recycling, and permanent material management. This would be the first ever full nuclear lifecycle campus in the United States.

Oklahoma has made the final cut for one of as many as three campuses the Department of Energy will likely choose by the end of 2026. State leaders emphasized that this is not a final site selection, but it is a major step forward as Oklahoma enters the next phase of host agreement negotiations.

“This is a major opportunity for Oklahoma. If awarded, this project would bring billions of dollars in investment in Oklahoma, add research opportunities for our Oklahoma universities, and bring additional electricity generation through the deployment of advanced small modular reactors,” said Oklahoma Secretary of Energy and Environment Jeff Starling. “Oklahoma has partnered with leading U.S. companies in the advanced nuclear space, and we look forward to competing for and winning this generational opportunity.”

According to federal energy experts and industry leaders, nuclear technology is not new. It is proven, safe, and clean, and the top companies in the industry are ready to partner with Oklahoma to build this campus.

“This is not the finish line. It is the next round,” Stitt said. “We are excited, we are prepared, and we are going to keep working with communities, industry leaders, and the federal government to put Oklahoma in the strongest position possible.”

U.S. Energy Secretary Wright announced the effort in January, asking states to express interest in hosting a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses, a new effort to modernize the nation’s full nuclear fuel cycle and strengthen America’s leadership in advanced nuclear energy.

The action marked the first step towards potentially establishing voluntary Federal-State partnerships designed to advance regional economic growth, enhance national energy security, and build a coherent, end-to-end nuclear energy strategy for the country.

“Unleashing the next American nuclear renaissance will drive innovation, fuel economic growth, and create good-paying American jobs while delivering the affordable, reliable and secure energy America needs to power its future,” said Wright. “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses give us the opportunity to work directly with states on regional priorities that support President Trump’s vision to revitalize America’s nuclear base.”

The proposed campuses could support activities across the full nuclear fuel lifecycle, including fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel, and disposition of waste. Depending on state priorities and regional capabilities, the sites could also host advanced reactor deployment, power generation, advanced manufacturing, and co located data centers.

text:
Beginning with an essay in the Atlantic magazine and later in a best-selling book, authors Derek Thompson and Ezra Klein argued that combining the power of unrestrained technological development with an activist government could unleash a new era of overwhelming material prosperity. Since then, a so-called “Abundance movement” has worked to dismantle rules and regulations believed to be standing in the way of that vision.

Frontier Group has long questioned the core assumptions of “Abundance” – that America’s most critical problem is scarcity, that “more” is always and everywhere better, and that longstanding environmental and other protections are bumps in the road to prosperity, not essential to safeguarding our future.

* * *

In February 2022, a month after Derek Thompson’s article in the Atlantic, Tony Dutzik argued that “abundance often comes at a cost. And if we’re not careful and thoughtful, we might end up with too much of the wrong things.” He proposed an alternative “abundance agenda” focused on “creating abundance where it will do real good” and recognizing the abundance we already enjoy.

When is enough enough? The “abundance agenda” America needs

New economy

When is enough enough? The “abundance agenda” America needs

February 17, 2022

Is more energy always better? Citing examples ranging from drafty households to America’s energy-intensive transportation system, Tony Dutzik argued that the answer is “no.” This March 2023 essay argues that the answer to America’s energy challenges isn’t “superabundance,” but “more of the right kinds of energy applied to the right kinds of work in the right places at the right times.”

Is more energy always better? Why pursuit of “energy abundance” risks missing the point

Clean energy

Is more energy always better? Why pursuit of “energy abundance” risks missing the point

March 6, 2023

Some rules and regulations are necessary to protect the public and the environment. Sometimes, though, unnecessary regulations really do get in the way of things we want more of, like rooftop solar panels. Our 2026 scorecard grades states based on their efforts to make it quick, easy and hassle-free to “go solar” – an illustration that, when it comes to solving specific problems, policy tools favored by “abundance” advocates can sometimes be useful.

Solar permitting scorecard

Clean energy

Solar permitting scorecard

March 25, 2026

But the pursuit of material abundance often has ecological and other impacts that need to be understood and recognized. Our March 2025 review of “Abundance” found that the book’s assumption that “the technologies of the future will be ecologically benign in a way the last generation’s technologies have turned out not to be” could lead to tremendous mistakes.

The problems of “Abundance”

New economy

The problems of “Abundance”

March 20, 2025

And when the pursuit of material abundance ignores or conflicts with deeply held non-material values – faith, love of place, protection of nature – it can even be self-defeating on its own terms, wrecking the delicate coalitions needed to transition to a more sustainable future, as Tony Dutzik wrote in 2026.

“Machine environmentalism” is failing. What comes next?

Global warming solutions

“Machine environmentalism” is failing. What comes next?

March 20, 2026

True abundance isn’t about more stuff – especially in a country that often seems to be buried in it. It’s about preserving the richness and abundance of the natural world, creating time and space for the things in life that truly matter, and building enough of the right kinds of technologies to limit the damage caused by our economy to the climate, our environment and ourselves.

description:
If Elon Musk’s sprawling xAI data center campus in Memphis were included in that lineup, it would rank second.
What’s driving those emissions amounts to a private fossil fuel power plant to keep Musk’s artificial intelligence facilities running.
Regionally, only Tennessee’s largest coal plant, Cumberland, which at 2.4 GW is double the size of typical coal plants, produces more climate pollution than xAI.
No other power plant currently produces as much greenhouse gas emissions in TVA’s entire seven-state service area.
The Shawnee Fossil Plant, a coal plant owned by TVA in Kentucky, was the second-biggest emitter in 2023 with 5.8 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions.
text:
Courtesy Steve Jones, Flight by Southwings for SELC

Power plants, an oil refinery and a chemical plant are among Tennessee’s top climate polluters. If Elon Musk’s sprawling xAI data center campus in Memphis were included in that lineup, it would rank second.

What’s driving those emissions amounts to a private fossil fuel power plant to keep Musk’s artificial intelligence facilities running.

The xAI site currently has two buildings, Colossus 1 and Colossus 2, that support Grok, the AI for the social platform X. The first data center gets power from about a dozen on-site gas turbines, along with about 300 megawatts of power generated by the Tennessee Valley Authority, the utility that serves 10 million people in a seven-state region.

The second data center is powered just across the state line in Mississippi by 59 gas turbines with a generating capacity of 1.4 gigawatts, or 1,400 megawatts.

More: What DC BLOX’s murky plans in Nashville signal for electricity costs, environmental impacts | WPLN News

Those turbines will release between 7 and 8 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions in a given year, based on the turbine makes and models, emissions rates listed in xAI and TVA permits, and an assumption that the turbines operate full time, according to calculations by the Southern Environmental Law Center, a nonpartisan law firm.

“What is happening in Mississippi is on an unprecedented scale. There is nothing else like this out there,” said Patrick Anderson, an attorney with SELC.

On the lower end, the xAI site’s level of emissions is equivalent to the energy use of nearly 1 million homes or 1.6 million gasoline-powered vehicles driven for one year.

Regionally, only Tennessee’s largest coal plant, Cumberland, which at 2.4 GW is double the size of typical coal plants, produces more climate pollution than xAI. That plant produced about 9.4 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions in 2023, according to the latest data available from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

No other power plant currently produces as much greenhouse gas emissions in TVA’s entire seven-state service area. The Shawnee Fossil Plant, a coal plant owned by TVA in Kentucky, was the second-biggest emitter in 2023 with 5.8 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions.

xAI is the largest NOx polluter in Tennessee

For one type of air pollution, xAI’s Mississippi gas turbines, many of which do not have pollution control equipment installed, rank even higher among industries in the Memphis region.

The turbines produce more nitrogen oxides than any facility in Tennessee, Mississippi or Arkansas.

xAI’s own emission data would translate to about 4,400 tons of NOx emissions annually — and an analyst from the Environmental Integrity Project estimated a total closer to 5,300 tons, based on the turbine model type seen in aerial images of the facility. For comparison, the Cumberland Fossil Plant produces 3,921 tons of NOx emissions annually, according to EPA data.

Nitrogen oxides are a group of gases emitted into the air from fossil fuels burning in vehicles, buildings and power plants. This pollution is linked to higher rates of heart disease, lung disease and asthma.

Air pollution causes hundreds of thousands of premature deaths in the U.S. each year, with a significant number attributed to nitrogen dioxide, one form of NOx pollution.

Power plants have greatly reduced their NOx pollution over the years due to government requirements for pollution controls.

But many of the turbines powering xAI’s Colossus 2 do not have pollution controls, according to SELC.

NAACP suing xAI

The NAACP, represented by SELC and Earthjustice, sued the company in April for running some turbines without permits and pollution controls.

The groups argue that the mobile turbines represent a stationary facility, due to an EPA rule published in January. The agency wrote that “the EPA has not regulated combustion turbines, even those that may be portable, as nonroad engines, but rather as stationary sources.”

The U.S. Department of Justice intervened in the case, later adding EPA to its petition after the groups pointed out that the Clean Air Act only gives EPA the right to intervene.

EPA’s top official Lee Zeldin seemed to confuse details of the case when talking to WPLN on July 14.

“In Mississippi, (the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality) is the permitting authority for these projects,” Zeldin said. “In this particular case in Tennessee, it’s specifically Shelby County. EPA isn’t the permitting authority for these projects in Tennessee. It’s delegated to the state and local level.”

The lawsuit only pertains to the turbines in Mississippi, however.
